cases.prompt: How has New Zealand's freshwater management policy changed over the past decade, and what are the main points of disagreement?

rubric.what_it_isolates: Multiple search queries, wide retrieval across time, genuine synthesis across many chunks. The case where a stronger answer model might pay off.
rubric.expected_ttft_profile: Highest pre-answer TTFT. Heavy topic-gen + eval; synthesis starts late.

response.response_text:
# Freshwater Policy in Aotearoa: A Decade of Change and Controversy

New Zealand's freshwater management has undergone significant and contested shifts over the past decade — swinging between tighter environmental protections and industry-friendly deregulation, with Māori rights to water running as a persistent and unresolved thread throughout.

## The Foundation: Resource Management Act and Regional Councils

The bedrock of freshwater governance remains the Resource Management Act (RMA) 1991, which gives regional and unitary councils responsibility for managing water resources with a long-term goal of sustainability [[1]](cite://1/1). However, critics have long argued the system was inadequate — Fish & Game's Neil Deans noted that water management plans weren't even compulsory until 2011, meaning tens of thousands of permits were issued over 35 years without any overarching plan [[2]](cite://2/1).

## The 2020 Essential Freshwater Package

The most significant reform of recent years came under the previous Labour-led government. An updated National Policy Statement (NPS) for Freshwater Management came into force in 2020, introducing new requirements for local authorities to improve river quality and halt further degradation of waterways and wetlands [[3]](cite://3/1).

Central to that package was *Te Mana o te Wai* — a concept introduced to freshwater policy in 2014 that prioritises the health and wellbeing of the waterway first, the health needs of people second, and social, economic and cultural wellbeing third [[4]](cite://4/1). The 2020 update also introduced freshwater farm plans, requiring farmers with 20 or more hectares in arable or pastoral use to develop plans reducing the harm of farming on freshwater [[5]](cite://5/1).

## The National-Led Government's Rollback (2023–Present)

Since coming to power in late 2023, the National-led coalition government has moved decisively to wind back many of those protections, framing the changes as reducing regulatory burden on the primary sector.

Key steps have included:

- The **Resource Management (Freshwater and Other Matters) Amendment Bill**, passed in October 2024, which excluded the Te Mana o te Wai hierarchy of obligations from resource consent processes, relaxed rules keeping farm animals out of waterways, amended winter grazing regulations, paused identification of new Significant Natural Areas, and restricted councils from notifying freshwater plans until the current NPS is replaced [[6]](cite://6/1).
- A **review of freshwater farm plans**, with the government flagging the system as too costly, complex, and broadly applied [[5]](cite://5/2).
- In May 2025, the government opened public consultation on **sweeping new national direction** — proposing to replace the NPS for Freshwater Management entirely and 'rebalance' Te Mana o te Wai to better reflect the interests of all water users, not just the health of the waterway [[7]](cite://7/1). Changes to wetland regulations, water storage rules, fish passage requirements, and synthetic fertiliser rules were also proposed [[8]](cite://8/1).

RMA Reform minister Chris Bishop framed the goal as replacing the RMA with new legislation premised on property rights, expected to come into force in 2027 [[8]](cite://8/2).

## The Main Points of Disagreement

The debate is sharp, and cuts across several fault lines.

### Economy vs. Environment

The starkest tension is between agricultural productivity and environmental protection. Federated Farmers has welcomed the deregulatory changes, with freshwater spokesperson Colin Hurst calling the previous rules 'completely unworkable' and saying they had been amended eight times in three years [[4]](cite://4/2)[[7]](cite://7/2). Beef + Lamb and farming advocates argue incentives and catchment-specific farm plans are more effective than top-down regulation [[9]](cite://9/1).

On the other side, freshwater ecologist Mike Joy warned that most lowland rivers are no longer swimmable or fishable, and that 'things are going to get worse' under the proposed changes [[7]](cite://7/3). The Green Party described the reforms as a 'comprehensive dismantling' of environmental protections [[7]](cite://7/4), while Greenpeace warned the changes would increase nitrate contamination of drinking water, linking higher nitrate levels to bowel cancer and pre-term birth risks [[9]](cite://9/2).

A 2026 report, *Our Freshwater 2026*, confirmed the state of freshwater continues to deteriorate, with ecologist Nick Ling describing the findings as 'sobering' — and warning that freshwater quality failures could eventually undermine New Zealand's tourism reputation [[10]](cite://10/1).

### Te Mana o te Wai and Māori Rights

Perhaps the most constitutionally significant conflict concerns the role of Māori as kaitiaki (guardians) of water. Coalition partner ACT has called for Te Mana o te Wai to be scrapped entirely, while Ngāi Tahu rūnanga chair Justin Tipa called its removal from the hierarchy 'absolutely unacceptable' [[9]](cite://9/3).

The dispute goes deeper than policy settings. In November 2025, a landmark High Court case was brought by *Wai Manawa Whenua*, a coalition of Māori landowners, hapū and iwi, challenging the Crown's continued use of a 'first in, first served' water allocation system that they argue shuts Māori out and ignores their authority as kaitiaki [[11]](cite://11/1)[[12]](cite://12/1). Federation of Māori Authorities chairperson Traci Houpapa noted that in many catchments water has been fully or over-allocated, leaving Māori authorities unable to access water for their own farms and landholdings [[11]](cite://11/2).

Wai Manawa Whenua chairperson Kingi Smiler said the Crown gave 'solemn promises' in the Supreme Court in 2012 to address Māori rights in water allocation — promises he described as 'cynical' and 'empty' in the absence of action [[11]](cite://11/3).

### Central vs. Local Control

There is also genuine tension over whether environmental standards should be set nationally or locally. Some regional councils, like Otago, were 'cornered' by central government when the 2024 legislation blocked their plans to introduce stronger freshwater protections [[13]](cite://13/1). Mid Canterbury farmers, by contrast, welcomed the pause, with Federated Farmers president David Acland arguing that change should be 'led by the rural community, not by Wellington' [[13]](cite://13/2).

### Drinking Water Safety

A further concern centres on public health. Researcher Marnie Prickett from Otago University warned that the proposed RMA changes de-prioritise drinking water sources, weakening protections that were put in place specifically in response to the deadly 2016 Havelock North campylobacter outbreak [[14]](cite://14/1).

The debate, in short, is not just about water — it's about who gets to use it, who protects it, and whose values get to shape the country New Zealand wants to be.

Would you like to explore the specific legal arguments Māori groups are making about water rights and the Crown's obligations in more depth?

1.text:
[Page 9] Water in New Zealand is protected by legislation, principally the Resource Management Act 1991. It provides a legal framework for using water, managing its quality, and balancing the needs of different groups who affect or use water. For example, fishers and swimmers want the lakes and rivers to be clear, while factory owners need to dispose of waste material. Regional councils throughout the country monitor water quality, and then decide how to manage land and effluent. In consultation with the local community, a council might decide to maintain high water quality in upland rivers and lakes for recreation and biodiversity, but allow some runoff and waste into lowland rivers and estuaries.

1.document_title: Water Quality in New Zealand: Comprehensive Assessment of Threats, Management Strategies, and Case Studies
1.document_summary: This comprehensive document examines water quality in New Zealand, addressing freshwater management and protection challenges. While New Zealand has high-quality freshwater by global standards, it faces significant threats from soil erosion, sewage, farm fertilizers, and algae growth. Major pollution sources include point sources (sewage pipes) and non-point sources (farm runoff), with contaminants encompassing sediments, organic matter, and dissolved chemicals like nitrate and phosphate. High nitrate levels pose particular health risks for infants. The document presents case studies of Lake Rotorua, Lake Taupō, and the Manawatū River, illustrating how human activities have degraded water quality. Management strategies outlined under the Resource Management Act 1991 include regional council monitoring, water-quality standards, and weed control methods. Key issues addressed include excessive nutrient levels causing algal blooms, invasive species like hornwort and didymo, and disease-causing organisms. Solutions involve multiple approaches: grass carp for vegetation control, restoring riparian shade, reducing nutrient inputs, improving farming practices, and implementing legislative protections. The document emphasizes voluntary farm management practices, including dairy farmer initiatives using effluent spraying and wetland treatment systems, a voluntary accord between Fonterra Co-operative Group and government entities to minimize dairying's environmental impact, and a Code of Practice for Fertiliser Use to mitigate agricultural harm.

2.text:
[Page 16] After a review of New Zealand’s soil conservation in 1964, the Water and Soil Conservation Act was passed in 1967. A Water and Soil Division was set up within the Ministry of Works and Development. Under its control were the Soil Conservation and Rivers Control Council, the Water Pollution Control Council and the Water Allocation Council. Importantly, at local level the control lay with each catchment authority, via the regional water boards. Emphasis was placed on measuring the extent and types of erosion through land inventory surveys and land capability assessments.

2.document_title: Soil Erosion and Conservation in New Zealand: Comprehensive Analysis of Causes, Types, Management, and Control Methods
2.document_summary: This comprehensive document examines soil erosion and conservation in New Zealand from the 1940s to modern times. It explains that soil contains vital nutrients essential to farming and describes natural erosion processes including wind, rain, floods, and earthquakes. The document categorizes erosion into four main types: surface erosion (sheet and wind), fluvial erosion (rill and gully), mass-movement erosion (slips and earth flows), and streambank erosion. Human activities significantly accelerated erosion—settlers cleared forests and introduced grazing animals, exposing soil. By 1997, 50% of New Zealand experienced moderate to slight erosion, with 10% severe. New Zealand loses approximately 210 million tonnes of soil annually to rivers—about 10 times the global average. Hill country erosion costs $100-150 million annually, damaging infrastructure and aquatic ecosystems. The document traces management history from early surveys (Raeside and Gibbs, 1945) through key legislation including the Soil Conservation and Rivers Control Act (1941), Water and Soil Conservation Act (1967), and Resource Management Act (1991). Conservation methods implemented since the 1940s include tree planting, aerial topdressing, new farming techniques, and dam construction. Biological control methods include reforestation with poplars and pines, riparian strips, and shelter belts. Mechanical techniques include flumes, debris dams, bulldozing, and conservation tillage. Research demonstrates that reforestation successfully controls erosion while dense pasture reduces sheet erosion but cannot prevent slips and gullies.

3.text:
[Page 1] How we use water Compared to many countries, New Zealand’s lakes and rivers are clean and clear, and the tap water is of good quality. People have contact with fresh water in many ways, including: wading in streams or rivers while tramping or fishing boating, swimming or fishing in lakes washing or drinking farm irrigation. Water quality can vary for instance, it may not be drinkable, but is usable for washing. Soil erosion When early settlers cut down the forests to make farmland, many hillsides began to erode. Soil was washed down and began to build up in rivers and lakes, sometimes smothering plants and fish. Sewage Sewage and factory waste was once piped directly into rivers and lakes. This brought unwanted nutrients, damaged the water and wildlife, and caused health problems in people. Today most sewage is treated with chemicals first. Farm fertilisers Fertilisers put onto farms contain nutrients such as nitrate and phosphate. Any that are washed into lakes and rivers upset the natural balance of nutrients in the water. Fish are harmed and some water plants (e.g. algae) grow too much. Algae and other problem plants Algae are tiny water plants. Excess nutrients in the water (e.g. from city waste or farming) can make them grow too quickly. They clog lakes and rivers, reduce water clarity and starve fish of oxygen. During low flows and high summer temperatures in the 1980s the Manawatū River had so much algae that fish were dying. There is now less pollution, but water runoff from farms still damages the water quality. Hornwort is the worst water weed. It can reach 10 metres tall underwater, smothering other plants. Protecting the water There are laws that protect New Zealand’s water, and control how it is used. The strictest standards are for drinking water. Councils test lakes and rivers for pollution, and sometimes certain fish species are used to eat up unwanted water weed. Farmers have to follow guidelines about using fertiliser and effluent, to reduce pollution in streams and lakes.
{}

[Page 15] Fluoridation Fluoride is added to some public water supplies to reduce dental decay. The Department of Health first conducted fluoride trials in Hastings in 1953. By 1978, 54% of New Zealand communities had fluoridated water; by 2016, the figure was 58%. Christchurch and New Plymouth were the only major cities without fluoridated water. A 2009 survey found that children living in fluoridated areas had 40% less severe tooth decay than children in unfluoridated areas. Local councils made decisions about the fluoridation of drinking water until the Health (Fluoridation of Drinking Water) Amendment Act 2021 transferred this responsibility to district health boards. Fluoridation illustrates how public health measures are often politicised and fiercely contested on ideological and philosophical grounds. Some people have argued that fluoridation of water supplies breaches individual rights and limits choices. In 1980 the Human Rights Commission ruled that it did not contravene human rights. In the 2010s there were further legal challenges to the fluoridation of water supplies. Consumer advocacy group, New Health New Zealand Inc., claimed in 2014 that fluoridation of water breached the right to refuse medical treatment under the Bill of Rights Act. They argued that fluoridation was a form of medical treatment that should not be compulsory. They also challenged the right of the South Taranaki District Council to add fluoride to the water supplies of Patea and Waverley. In 2018 these cases reached the Supreme Court, where a majority of judges, sometimes for different reasons, dismissed them.

7.document_title: New Zealand Aquaculture: Industry Overview, Farming Practices, and Regulatory Framework
7.document_summary: This comprehensive document provides an in-depth analysis of New Zealand's aquaculture industry, covering its development, major farming practices, and regulatory landscape. The industry, valued at $280 million by 2001, primarily focuses on three export species: green-lipped mussels, quinnat salmon, and Pacific oysters. Green-lipped mussels are cultivated using the Japanese longline system, becoming New Zealand's second most important seafood export by 2000, sold to over 60 countries. Salmon farming evolved through three methods: ocean ranching (1976), sea-cage ranching (1983) in Big Glory Bay and Marlborough Sounds, and freshwater farming in South Island hydroelectric canals, producing 8,500 tonnes in 2001 with 65% exported. Pacific oysters, cultivated starting in 1970, reached 3,500 tonnes annually by 2001 and generated $13.6 million in exports. Additional species include pāua shellfish, scallops, and sea horses. The industry operates under a dual licensing system managed by regional councils and the Ministry of Fisheries, with a government moratorium on marine farm expansion by 2002. Key challenges include regional concentration, toxic algal blooms, and tensions between farmers and Māori groups regarding seabed ownership. Despite these challenges, the industry has strong future prospects for diversifying into high-value species such as pāua, kingfish, and crayfish.

[Page 1] Water quality in New Zealand By world standards New Zealand has high quality water available for many uses. A plentiful supply is something that New Zealanders have taken for granted since the days of early settlement. Maintaining the quality has, for a long time, been largely due to the low population and the low level of contaminants from farming and urban development.

9.document_title: New Zealand Lakes: Formation, Ecology, Management, and Māori Land Rights
9.document_summary: This comprehensive document explores New Zealand's 775 lakes (at least 0.5 km long), covering their formation, ecology, management, and Māori land rights. Lake Taupō is the largest at 623 km², while Lake Hauroko is the deepest at 462 meters. Lakes form through diverse processes: 38% by glaciers (South Island), 16% by rivers, 15% by dunes, 8% artificially, and others by volcanoes, landslides, and coastal barriers. Glacial lakes like Tekapo display distinctive turquoise colors. Native fauna includes fish species, freshwater crayfish, and waterfowl such as ducks, grebes, and introduced species like black swans and Canada geese. Environmental challenges include nutrient overload from agricultural runoff and sewage causing algal blooms and oxygen depletion, particularly affecting lakes near Rotorua and Te Waihora since the 1950s. Recreational uses include boating, fishing, waterskiing, and game-bird hunting, managed by Fish and Game New Zealand. The document explores complex legal ownership of lake beds under the Treaty of Waitangi, highlighting the 1992 Crown return of Lake Taupō's bed to Ngāti Tūwharetoa and the 2006 agreement for Rotorua lakes. 11.document_title: Māori Land Tenure and Customary Rights Systems
11.document_summary: This document explores the traditional Māori system of land tenure and property rights known as "take whenua." Land was historically held communally by tribal groups (hapū) with individual and family use rights for specific purposes. Key principles included discovery (whenua kite hou), ancestral rights (take tupuna), conquest (take raupatu), and gifting (take tuku). Mana whenua refers to tribal authority over land and water bodies. Continuous occupation (ahi kā), symbolized by keeping fires burning, was essential to maintain land rights. The principle of ringa kaha meant victors had to actively defend conquered lands. Abandonment caused rights to diminish from ahi kā to ahi tere to ahi mataotao. Land transfers included conditions confirmed through ceremonies and taonga (treasures). The Native Land Court, established in 1865, resolved disputes but often simplified Māori customs, preferring conquest-based claims. By 1847, Chief Justice William Martin noted Māori had appropriated all valuable land through these customary systems. The system was fluid and accommodated changing tribal relationships, with disputed lands arising from migration and inter-tribal marriage.

[Page 7] Categories of water In traditional Māori knowledge, wai (water) is classified in a number of ways. Some of these categories include: waikino dangerous water, sometimes inclement seas or swollen rivers waitapu sacred water, waters used for ceremonial purposes waimāori pure water, water rich in mauri , used for cleansing and for ceremonial purposes waitai sea water, saline water waimanawa whenua water from under the land waikarakia water for ritual purposes waiwhakaika, waikotikoti water to assist in the cutting of hair.

14.document_title: Agricultural and Horticultural Research in New Zealand: From Colonial Times to Modern Crown Research Institutes
14.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the development of agricultural and horticultural research in New Zealand from early colonial times through the 1990s. It chronicles how farmers adapted introduced plants and animals to local conditions, leading to the establishment of government research institutions beginning with the Department of Agriculture in 1892. Key scientific achievements include solving 'bush sickness' through cobalt supplementation, developing phosphate fertiliser trials, breeding improved livestock varieties (Halfbred, Drysdale, Corriedale, Perendale, and Coopworth sheep), and implementing biological pest control. The document details the crucial role of the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research (DSIR), established in 1926, which coordinated research through specialized institutes including the Dairy Research Institute (1927) and Wheat Research Institute (1928). Major breakthroughs include solving cheesemaking problems through bacteriophage research, developing improved wheat varieties (Cross 7 and Hilgendorf), and establishing the grasslands revolution through pasture plant research. Notable achievements in fruit breeding include the development of world-renowned apple varieties: Gala, Pacific Rose, and Jazz. The document also covers Gladys Reid's 1965 discovery of zinc treatment for facial eczema, advances in dairy productivity through herd recording and artificial insemination, and the discovery of endophytic fungus benefits in ryegrass. In 1992, Crown research institutes replaced the DSIR, including AgResearch, HortResearch, Plant & Food Research, Landcare Research, and NIWA, continuing research in sustainable agriculture, animal health, biotechnology, horticulture, and crop science.

15.document_title: Te Tiriti o Waitangi: A Comprehensive History from 1840 to Modern Legal Recognition
15.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the history of Te Tiriti o Waitangi (Treaty of Waitangi) from its signing in 1840 through to modern legal recognition. The treaty, signed between the British Crown and over 500 Māori chiefs on 5-6 February 1840, was drafted in English and translated to Māori by missionary Henry Williams. Critical differences between versions created ongoing disputes: Article One differed on sovereignty versus governance; Article Two guaranteed chiefs "te tino rangatiratanga" (chieftainship) while giving the Crown land-buying rights; Article Three granted Māori British subject protections. From 1860-1940, the Crown systematically dishonored treaty promises through land confiscation, the Native Land Court, and legislation undermining Māori rights, despite Māori resistance through the Kīngitanga (Māori King movement), petitions, and alternative institutions. The pivotal transformation occurred with the Treaty of Waitangi Act 1975, which established the Waitangi Tribunal to investigate Crown breaches. The tribunal's jurisdiction expanded in 1985 to cover all Crown actions since 1840, fundamentally changing the treaty's role from a largely ignored historical document to a central element of New Zealand law and governance. Subsequent parliamentary legislation incorporated treaty principles into law, leading to widespread legal recognition and formal settlements between the Crown and iwi.

Allocation was hotly debated for over a decade, but was finalised with the passing of the Māori Fisheries Act 2004. Tribal coastline and numbers of members were factored into the allocation of deep sea fisheries. Half the settlement assets ($300 million in quota) were allocated to tribes, and the assets of the Treaty of Waitangi Fisheries Commission $300 million were allocated to a new company, Aotearoa Fisheries Limited (AFL).

16.document_title: Ngā haumi a iwi – Māori Investment: Treaty Settlements, Economic Development, and Corporate Structures
16.document_summary: This document examines Māori economic development and investment in New Zealand, tracing evolution from traditional systems to modern tribal enterprises. It covers the historical context of European trade, significant land losses from the 1840s onwards, and the Waitangi Tribunal established in 1975. Key developments include Treaty settlements restoring land and fisheries to tribal ownership, with major settlements like Tainui (1995, $170 million) and Ngāi Tahu (1998, $170 million). Fisheries settlements (1989, 1992) granted Māori control over one-third of New Zealand's commercial fisheries, with the Māori Fisheries Commission allocating $600 million in assets. Major entities like Aotearoa Fisheries Limited and tribal companies such as Ngāi Tahu Seafood emerged as significant players. By 2008, Ngāi Tahu Holdings had $644 million in assets with $31 million operating surplus. The document explains how Māori tribes manage investments through land incorporations and trusts, with examples like Lake Taupo Forestry Trust and Wakatu Incorporation. By 2004, Māori owned 5% of New Zealand's land, with $16.5 billion in commercial assets across primary (52%), secondary (8%), and tertiary (40%) industries. Successful Māori businesses share characteristics including low debt-equity ratios, structural separation of commercial functions, diversified investments, and collaborative relationships. Māori investors prioritize land ownership, local employment, environmental sustainability, intergenerational wealth creation, and balanced traditional tikanga with corporate management structures.

Around $500 million of taxpayer and ratepayer funding has been earmarked to clean up just eight lakes and rivers. The Protecting Lake Taupo Project, which by 2080 aims to cut nitrogen loads into the lake by 20 per cent, was projected in 2004 to cost $81.3 million, but has received further Government top ups. Then there’s the $210 million Waikato clean up. Cleaning up Lake Rotorua will cost about the same. That would be done by imposing caps on surrounding farms, as with Horizons’ One Plan, but just like the Manawatu Wanganui initiative, the Bay of Plenty council has faced dogged opposition. 17.document_title: New Zealand's Water Crisis: Economic Growth, Environmental Degradation, and Governance Challenges
17.document_summary: This comprehensive document collection examines New Zealand's freshwater crisis, exploring tensions between economic development and environmental sustainability. The collection analyzes water's dual role as a natural resource and economic commodity, detailing how hydroelectric schemes and irrigation power New Zealand's agricultural economy, particularly dairy which generates $11.4 billion in exports but requires 900 liters of water per liter of milk. Key findings include: 28% of assessed lakes worsened between 2005-2009, the Manawatu River identified as the most polluted in the Western world, and 68% of freshwater fish species threatened. The documents reveal that 60% of national water usage occurs in Canterbury, with 86% dedicated to agricultural irrigation. Government policies, including the $400 million Irrigation Acceleration Fund and appointment of commissioners to bypass democratic processes, have prioritized short-term economic gains over sustainability. Water contamination with E.coli and toxic algal blooms has forced boil-water notices affecting over 880,000 New Zealanders. The collection highlights historical injustices including the 1863 Waikato land confiscation and inadequate settlements, while exploring Māori perspectives on water stewardship and cultural loss. Climate change projections indicate increased extreme weather and volatile river flows, yet governance frameworks remain inadequate. The collection presents sustainable farming practices as potential solutions while emphasizing that intensive dairy farming and healthy waterways appear mutually exclusive, requiring urgent integrated policy responses.

18.text:
[Page 11] A 2010 report from MfE assessed water quality trends in 112 New Zealand lakes between 2005 and 2009. Over the study period, 12 per cent of the lakes assessed had improved, while 28 per cent had worsened. The report then extrapolated those findings across 4000 lakes smaller than a hectare, and found that 32 per cent were likely to have poor or very poor (nutrient enriched) water quality. Those surrounded by farmland fared worst: 44 per cent were eutrophic (meaning they carried excessive nutrient loads) or worse. When extrapolated, the study concluded that out of 3820 New Zealand lakes, more than a third would be eutrophic or worse. For 35 years, Levin poured its treated sewage into Lake Horowhenua. The abuses stopped in 1987, but still the lake looks jaundiced. The town now spreads its sewage over land, but some of it has been found to leach into the lake anyway. When it reflects a blue sky, it might pass a postcard test. Catch it on the wrong day, however, and it morphs into something green and glowering. In waters opaque with slime, suspended sediment and algae—“probably the result of faecal contamination from farmland runoff,” according to MfE—you wouldn’t see your hand at arm’s length. In fact, such a test would be unwise: last summer, NIWA freshwater scientist Max Gibbs warned Horizons Regional Council, which covers ManawatuWanganui, that after heavy rain, Lake Horowhenua’s waters, deemed among the 10 most polluted in the country, might well kill a small child. The problem is not just in lakes. In 2010, NIWA reported that water quality in our major rivers had declined between 1989 and 2007. Over that period, nitrogen and phosphorus loadings (see sidebar) had increased greatly at many sites. Nitrogen had increased by about 1.4 per cent each year over most of the country, and no sites recorded a drop. Climbing trends for temperature, nitrogen and phosphorus had accelerated, commensurate with a surge in nitrogen fertiliser use—which has doubled since the mid 1990s—and dairy cow numbers. Twenty years ago, Mike Joy took his niece and nephew for a swim in the Oroua River, in Manawatu. They soon succumbed to vomiting and diarrhoea, and when Joy mentioned this to locals, they looked at him in disbelief: everyone knew that river was full of Feilding’s sewage, in breach of a discharge consent. “That started my fight with regional councils, and got me into wanting to study it more, to find out what was going on,” he says. Joy, now a senior lecturer in ecology and environmental science at Massey University, has become one of water’s most pugnacious advocates. Inevitably, his tireless campaigning—notably for long finned eels—has taken the gloss off the clean, green narrative. When he told The New York Times in November last year that there were “two worlds in New Zealand—the picture postcard world, and the reality”— he was pilloried by a Wellington marketing executive as “the foot and mouth disease of the tourism industry” and branded a traitor on talkback radio. Joy and I sit in the drizzle, watching the most polluted river in the Western world shuffle past, listless and grey. Of 300 rivers and streams across North America, Europe, Australia and New Zealand assessed by the Cawthron Institute, this one—the Manawatu—was found to be the sickest: so fouled with treated sewage, industrial waste and farm run off that it scored twice as poorly as the next worst river, sampled downstream from a Berlin sewage outfall. And still, there are some people doggedly fighting efforts to clean it up. In May 2007, Horizons Regional Council announced its One Plan, ostensibly a blueprint for environmental management in the region for the next decade. Part of the plan proposed caps on nutrient and pollu tion discharges to fresh water in the district, effectively dictating land use options and curbing intensification. Federated Farmers condemned it as “Farmageddon” and took the council to the Environment Court, challenging the plan on a contention, among others, that there was no need to improve the region’s water quality as it was no worse than that of some rivers elsewhere. Farmers were quick to invoke economic calamity. Dannevirke businessman Allan Benbow told a public meeting last year that the One Plan—by his own extrapolations—would cost the Tararua District $60 million and 300 jobs.

19.document_title: The Secret Life of Slime: Comprehensive Exploration of Biofilms, Microorganisms, and Microscopic Ecosystems
19.document_summary: This comprehensive document explores the fascinating world of microbial biofilms and microscopic life in aquatic ecosystems. It traces biofilm discovery from Antony van Leeuwenhoek's 17th-century observations to modern science, revealing biofilms as complex communities of bacteria, protozoa, algae, fungi, and viruses on wet surfaces. At microscopic magnifications, bacterial biofilms appear as sophisticated "cities" with water channels and micro-colonies facilitating nutrient exchange and protection. The document details diverse microscopic organisms including rotifers, gastrotrichs, nematodes, ciliates, amoebae, and flagellates, explaining their structures, feeding mechanisms, and ecological roles. Biofilms are essential for aquatic ecosystems, supporting food chains through photosynthesis, decomposition, and nutrient cycling. The document addresses biofilm significance for human health, including antibiotic-resistant bacteria and medical device infections. However, human activities—pollution, deforestation, agricultural runoff, and invasive species—threaten these ecosystems. Research shows urban streams have degraded biofilm communities with toxic metal accumulation. The document concludes by highlighting biofilms' potential for environmental remediation, as microbes can remove pollutants from water through wetlands and wastewater treatment systems.

21.document_title: How to Fix the Manawatū River
21.document_summary: The Manawatū River, home to one of New Zealand's six Ramsar-listed wetlands of international significance, has become one of the country's most polluted waterways. Originally cloaked in native forests, the river's degradation began with European settlement through deforestation, industrial waste discharge, and intensive agriculture. Pollution evolved from visible sewage and industrial waste in the early 20th century to diffuse pollution from nitrogen and phosphorus runoff from farms. Current challenges include unsafe swimming conditions, sedimentation from eroded hill country, and habitat destruction for native fish species like kōaro. Key solutions include: returning nutrients to land through better farm practices and wetland restoration; upgrading sewage infrastructure to prevent wastewater discharge during heavy rainfall; retiring marginal hill country through reforestation to reduce erosion and sedimentation; and implementing stricter land-use regulations. The 2009 "worst in the west" designation prompted initiatives including Horizons Regional Council's One Plan (2010) and the Manawatū River Leaders' Forum, offering hope for restoration despite ongoing tensions between commercial enterprise, farming, and environmental protection. Climate change threatens to intensify these challenges through increased rainfall.

22.text:
[Page 22] “The Water Conservation Order was in the way,” says Snoyink, “so they had it gutted. People had the foresight to campaign for protection of that river and now, because we’ve already taken all the easy water, they’re overturning these protection orders. And DOC is nowhere to be seen—we don’t have that voice for the natural environment any more.” That’s possibly because it was Nick Smith as Minister of Conservation who facilitated the amendment, then put the application before the commissioners he had appointed at Environment Canterbury. “There is this absurd contention,” says Eugenie Sage, “that you can simply re plumb an entire region. So the rivers are reduced simply to canals to convey water from point A to point B so it can be used to grow grass.” She argues that supposedly sacrosanct measures such as Water Conservation Orders can be overturned only because New Zealand rivers still have no effective legal framework to protect them. “We need more effective regulation and binding national standards, because they have the strength of rule. Christchurch was able to clean up its air because of a national environmental standard for particulate matter. Where there’s been central government leadership on environmental quality issues, things have improved. Where there hasn’t, such as with water quality, things continue to decline.” Neil Deans, Fish & Game’s Nelson Marlborough manager, points out that the Government’s 2011 National Policy Statement, which compels councils to produce water management plans, is 30 years late. Historically, plans have not been compulsory. “We didn’t get one in Canterbury until about 2010. So what happened in the meantime? Tens of thousands of permits were allocated in that space, for 35 years. The problem is that this is effects based legislation, and the effect of one more little straw on the camel’s back is very hard to measure. But the effect of all those straws has well and truly broken the camel’s back in many of our catchments throughout New Zealand, particularly in areas like Canterbury.”

[Page 33] “I’d like to see some rivers flow free, all the way to the sea. I want our rivers to be restored to good ecological health. I want people to be able to enjoy our rivers, without worrying about getting sick. Is that too much to ask?” The Rakaia writhes like a hydra across the Canterbury plains, turquoise with glacial silt. An important breeding site for wrybill plovers, in 1988 the river was granted a Water Conservation Order—the country’s most stringent protection measure—that guaranteed minimum flows. Under provisions in the ECan Act, TrustPower secured an amendment early last year that exempted Lake Coleridge from the flow restrictions, allowing water to be used instead by Central Plains Water to irrigate 30,000 hectares of central Canterbury. Murray Rodgers doesn’t want to obstruct farming, but he wants to see it done differently, through low intensity biological or organic principles, “because otherwise, we’ll be living with contaminated water across the whole region. Our grand kids will probably find that their drinking water slowly becomes undrinkable across large swathes of the plains.” Blind faith in bounty, it turns out, is misplaced. What we once thought inexhaustible is now spent. What we assumed would always be pure is now polluted. Having drained and drawn and dammed and dirtied, the solution we have shunned self imposed limits—now confronts us as our one remaining option. The water coursing through your body and mine will eventually move on: it will return to the atmosphere, to rain down again in some new place, to nourish a crop, bear a kayaker down a foaming rapid or lend sanctity to some ritual. We can secure all the consents for water we like; trade it, channel it, keep it prisoner, but it will not be owned. It will simply be mutable, perhaps defiled, but undiminished. We need water, but it does not need us. Our urgent charge is to find our proper place in the water cycle, and live within its bounds. The Waikato River roils before plunging over the Huka Falls. [Page 19] one place to another. Scott Larned, a NIWA ecologist with a strong interest in how ecosystems interact with water, told me it can take 60 to 100 years for rainwater falling on the upper Canterbury Plains to percolate to the ocean, picking up and transporting contaminants from farmland as it moves through the ground. We were standing next to the Halswell River, which runs through Lincoln, at the time. He said that if you took a beaker of water from the Halswell and aged every molecule, the average age would be 60 years, which means the water bears the signature of 60 year old farm activities. “Since that was prior to a lot of intensification,” he said, “it means we haven’t seen the most contaminated groundwater yet.” Davies Colley agreed the full impact of agricultural intensification on river water quality will not be felt for several decades: there is still a half century of nutrients to leak into rivers. When it comes to water quality, “we all live downstream,” says Canadian environmentalist David Suzuki. It is relatively easy to prevent pollution of waterways from concentrated sources such as a milking shed, but much harder to contain contamination from leaky soils. New Zealand looks to innovative science, strong regulatory frameworks and an energised public to protect this precious commodity: fresh water. Meanwhile, the government has set a goal of doubling exports by 2025, which could mean more hooves on paddocks, more fertiliser and supplemental feed, and more risk of eutrophication to rivers. How can New Zealand avoid a hard landing on freshwater, I asked Davies Colley. “Across the board recognition that land use affects both water quality and our greenhouse gas footprint, and that we have to control what happens on land. In some catchments, meeting freshwater targets will involve combinations of mitigations such as riparian fencing and planting, treatment wetlands and denitrification filters. In other catchments, it may be necessary to de stock or change to lower footprint enterprises.” “But it’s no good just shutting down half of New Zealand’s export income,” added Chris Tanner, NIWA’s principal scientist for aquatic pollution. “You’ve got to find a positive way to solve this.” Tanner, who co leads the challenge’s innovative and resilient land use theme, says part of the problem is the fact that land values have not reflected the cost of environmental impacts. “Two properties, one very leaky and the other which retains contaminants, are likely to be valued the same if they produce the same milk solids per hectare,” he said. Perhaps all land in New Zealand is overpriced relative to what can be produced from it, he added, because the costs of mitigating environmental damage haven’t been taken into account. “The whole system has been allowed to drift,” he said, “because it’s hard, and it takes political will, and it’s against the tide of growth incentives. But the further out you get on a limb, the harder it is to come back.” But come back we must. For Tanner, that means learning to look at land in a different way—“not just at how many kilograms of milkfat per hectare it might yield, but asking, ‘How susceptible is it to contaminant loss? 26.document_title: Between Two Worlds: The Extraordinary Life Cycle and Conservation of Mayflies
26.document_summary: This comprehensive collection explores the fascinating world of mayflies, examining their extraordinary lifecycle, ecological significance, and conservation challenges. Mayflies spend nearly their entire lives underwater as nymphs before emerging for a brief aerial existence lasting only one to two days. Mass mayfly hatches on New Zealand's Waiau River demonstrate their ecological importance. The articles reveal how mayflies serve as crucial bioindicators of freshwater ecosystem health, with researcher Whelan hand-planting mayflies to restore populations in Irish lakes. New Zealand's Macroinvertebrate Community Index (MCI) system uses mayflies to assess water quality. Research by Otago University ecologist Andreas Bruder demonstrates how agricultural stressors—including nutrient levels, sediment, reduced flow, and chemical pollutants—affect aquatic ecosystems, identifying excessive fine sediment as a primary cause of riverine degradation. New Zealand's unique endemic mayfly fauna is highlighted through the work of retired teacher Hitchings, emphasizing that many of the country's mayflies are found nowhere else on Earth. Despite surviving virtually unchanged for 350 million years, mayflies face significant threats from habitat reduction and increasing economic value of water resources. These insects serve as crucial ecosystem links and represent one of nature's most remarkable evolutionary successes.

[Page 8] “I brought up two daughters,” says Rodgers. “With my love of the back country, I naturally wanted to give them the same experiences I’d had. In the 1980s,when they were growing up, we’d go out for picnics on lowland rivers like the Selwyn, the Opihi, the Orari. We never thought about any risks of getting sick; we just took clean water for granted. It was part of our life. You just don’t go picnicking on a Canterbury lowland stream any more.” Something intrinsic, he says, has been lost. “We’re talking about what many people, of my generation anyway, see as being the rightful heritage for their offspring. Something that I’d accepted as one of the reasons I’m a New Zealander and a Cantabrian—the freedom to go out onto a river and enjoy it for what it is. That’s been taken away without even asking the question, ‘Can we have it?’ That’s the injustice of the whole thing.” Last summer, residents of Waiau farther to the north were warned to boil all their drinking water after town supplies were found to be brimming with E.coli . There is precious little deep groundwater in the Waiau Hurunui district: people must draw from shallow springs and bores fed by river water. But that river is itself fed by surface run off which, as stock numbers climb, is passing through more and more manure before it reaches the river. Without a reduction in stock loadings, the only solution is to upgrade water treatment facilities, a cost borne by typically small ratepayer bases. Next, it was Hororata. An E.coli bloom forced residents to boil—and the Selwyn District Council to chlorinate—water that was once the envy of the country. Cheviot, which draws its water almost entirely from an aquifer just 15 metres below the Waiau Gorge, was put on permanent ‘boil water’ notice in 2005, until an improved treatment system costing $46,000 was commissioned in 2009. Ratepayers are still footing the extra costs of more intensive water management. But no system can neutralise the toxins produced by cyanobacteria, which thrive in the shallower waters of depleted streams and rivers, warmed to excess after shady streamside vegetation has been cleared. Toxic algal mats are becoming a summer phenomenon as the tiny plants gorge on burgeoning levels of nitrates washed into rivers from farms. Phormidium , a blue green alga that coats stream and riverbeds with noxious brown or black mats, can cause rashes, irritate skin and eyes and trigger allergic reactions. It can, and has, killed dogs. “In the last 18 months, Darfield had over a hundred cases of gastroenteritis,” says Eugenie Sage. “The community is paying the price in terms of water supply contamination and increased costs of water treatment.” And while the community pays, industry benefits. Irrigation can add between $6000 and $10,000 of value to a farm hectare, essentially privatising a community asset. Furthermore, farmers can sell any unused portions of water consents what they were allocated for the cost of an application fee, they can sell at a price. “It’s intensive agriculture freeloading on the environment, because polluted rivers, streams and groundwater are not accounted for,” says Sage. “The loss of natural values and character, the loss of healthy ecosystems, none of that is taken into account.” “Water is a public good, and a lot of us are quite happy to leave that water in the river,” says Snoyink. “We appreciate the amenity value. But, just as we feel we have a fundamental right to that water, farmers feel they have a right to use it too. But the users of that water are not paying for the environmental damage, nor the cost of lost social amenity. The community pays for it; it’s their loss.”

27.document_title: New Zealand's Water Crisis: Economic Growth, Environmental Degradation, and Governance Challenges
27.document_summary: This comprehensive document collection examines New Zealand's freshwater crisis, exploring tensions between economic development and environmental sustainability. The collection analyzes water's dual role as a natural resource and economic commodity, detailing how hydroelectric schemes and irrigation power New Zealand's agricultural economy, particularly dairy which generates $11.4 billion in exports but requires 900 liters of water per liter of milk. Key findings include: 28% of assessed lakes worsened between 2005-2009, the Manawatu River identified as the most polluted in the Western world, and 68% of freshwater fish species threatened. The documents reveal that 60% of national water usage occurs in Canterbury, with 86% dedicated to agricultural irrigation. Government policies, including the $400 million Irrigation Acceleration Fund and appointment of commissioners to bypass democratic processes, have prioritized short-term economic gains over sustainability. Water contamination with E.coli and toxic algal blooms has forced boil-water notices affecting over 880,000 New Zealanders. The collection highlights historical injustices including the 1863 Waikato land confiscation and inadequate settlements, while exploring Māori perspectives on water stewardship and cultural loss. Climate change projections indicate increased extreme weather and volatile river flows, yet governance frameworks remain inadequate. The collection presents sustainable farming practices as potential solutions while emphasizing that intensive dairy farming and healthy waterways appear mutually exclusive, requiring urgent integrated policy responses.

28.document_title: How to Fix Te Waihora/Lake Ellesmere: Restoration Strategies for New Zealand's Degraded Lake
28.document_summary: Te Waihora/Lake Ellesmere is one of New Zealand's most important yet severely degraded wetland habitats. The lake supports over 160 bird species and 45 fish species, including critically endangered species like kōtuku (white heron) and kakī (black stilt), but bird counts have declined from 92,000 in the 1980s to 49,000 annually since 2013. The lake has shrunk to less than half its original size due to drainage and land reclamation. Four main contaminants—nitrogen, phosphorus, sediment, and faecal microbes—from intensive farming degrade water quality, causing algal blooms. Comprehensive restoration strategies include Environment Canterbury's Selwyn Te Waihora Water Plan requiring 30% nitrogen reductions, recreating wetlands (which could reduce nitrogen load by 40%), replacing invasive plants with wetland forests, and engineering solutions like floating wetlands. The Ahuriri Lagoon exemplifies successful wetland reconstruction. Following Ngāi Tahu's regaining of lake bed ownership in 1998, the restoration programme Whakaora Te Waihora aims to restore the lake's ecosystems and its original name: te kete ika o Rākaihautū (the fish basket of Rākaihautū). While restoration is expected to take generations, it is achievable.

This comprehensive document collection explores New Zealand's paua (abalone) industry from multiple perspectives. It covers the ecological and cultural significance of paua as New Zealand's iconic shellfish, describing its life cycle, habitat, and status as a national symbol. The paua industry is worth approximately $80 million annually, particularly in Asian markets where premium prices reach up to $2000 per serving in Hong Kong.

The document traces the paua fishery's history from early commercial ventures in 1848 through the post-WWII boom driven by mother-of-pearl demand, examining regional variations in shell quality and the decline of the jewelry industry due to Asian competition. It details modern management challenges, including the collapse of global abalone fisheries and New Zealand's efforts to prevent similar decline through quota systems and research-based stock assessments.

Research by marine ecologist Reyn Naylor and NIWA reveals critical sustainability concerns, showing that landings data alone poorly indicate stock health as skilled fishers can maintain high catches while overall populations decline. Serial depletion has been identified across eight quota management areas, particularly in PAU 5 (Fiordland, Stewart Island, Catlins/Otago). Commercial catch is set at 1,200 tonnes annually.

A significant focus addresses illegal poaching, which accounts for approximately 33% of the total allowable commercial catch, with limited Ministry of Fisheries staff resulting in substantial unreported illegal harvests. The document also explores the emerging paua farming industry, with around 75 sea-based licenses and 24 land-based farms approved. Innovative products like paua pearls, commanding retail prices of $500-$3500, represent new commercial opportunities. The collection emphasizes the complex balance between commercial exploitation, cultural significance, and resource conservation.

32.document_title: Mussel Power: New Zealand's Greenshell Mussel Farming Industry - Production, Ecology, and Environmental Impacts
32.document_summary: This comprehensive document explores New Zealand's greenshell mussel farming industry, covering its evolution, production methods, ecological significance, and environmental challenges. The industry has grown from a fledgling enterprise in the 1970s to a dominant aquaculture sector, harvesting 35,000-40,000 tonnes annually and generating approximately $40-52 million in export revenue. The document details the industry's origins through pioneers like Stuart McFarlane and Keith Yealands, who adapted Spanish and Japanese cultivation techniques, and describes modern longline farming systems that cultivate 300-350 mussels per metre. Production methods include mechanized seeding using biodegradable stockings and harvesting operations using large vessels capable of processing 90 tonnes daily. Key quality control practices emphasize strict hygiene, traceability standards, and quarantine procedures. The industry faces significant challenges including toxic algae blooms, fish predation, blue mussel competition, and unpredictable mussel spawning. Environmental concerns include aesthetic impacts from farming infrastructure, potential nutrient depletion, and unknown long-term ecological effects. The document also explores mussel adaptations, including their use of byssus threads for anchoring and larval dispersal mechanisms. Despite profitability challenges, the industry continues to expand, particularly in the Coromandel Peninsula and Marlborough Sounds regions, employing approximately 900 people in Marlborough.

[Page 7] was created from vast areas of wetland. Thames historian Alistair Isdale wrote of the region, “It lay sleeping, awaiting the magic kiss of a golden prince. It awoke instead to the warm breath of a cow licking its face.” But the watercourses that brought wealth are also the plumbing for pollutants. Reports commissioned into the state of the region’s rivers and streams—such as the Waitoa, pictured, a tributary of the Piako River—paint a poor picture of their overall health. Water quality is deteriorating as nutrient concentrations increase and sediment and faecal levels maintain a high average. Levels of bacteria in many rivers and streams may make water unsuitable for recreational purposes. Barry Flint milks 1000 cows, split into several herds Miranda Kaiaua area. His family have been on at least some of the property since the 1930s. Flint is proud that he’s lifted the carrying capacity of the land from 2.5 cows per hectare to 3.2, though it’s cost him $1000 a hectare to do so. in the “Drainage is the big thing,” he explained. “I’m on heavy marine clays and by gently humping and hollowing the paddocks, we improve drainage considerably. I’m now growing twice as much grass as 30 years ago. I’ve also switched from Friesian cows to lighter Jerseys. They cause less pugging damage and suffer less footrot, which means they can forage better. “My father used to get 400 pounds of butterfat to the acre, which was pretty good, but I now get 1000 kilograms of milk solids per hectare.” I try to do the maths: 400 lbs fat/acre = 790 kg total milk solids (which also includes protein). If he’s doubled grass growth, he’s only increased milk solids by a quarter, which is less than I would have expected. Like elsewhere, potable water is a major issue on the plains. “It used to cost 22 cents per cubic metre, but now it’s increased to $1.88,” says Flint, who received an annual water bill from the council for more than $35,000 until he put down his own bore. That also cost $35,000, but promised to be only $3000 annually to run. He’s since discovered, however, that the bore water contains toxic levels of iron and boron, which costs as much to remove as the annual council water bill. “I’m stymied,” he says. With bitter irony, Flint also pays the council to maintain stopbanks and drains to keep unwanted water out. As environmental scrutiny has increased on the plains, farmers have come under pressure to comply, no matter what their circumstances or the lay of their land—even Flint has had a run in with Environment Waikato, the regional council. “From their surveillance helicopter, they saw I was grazing an area of about 20 acres beyond the seawall that I’d cleared the mangroves from,” he says. “Turned up here like the FBI in three vehicles flashing their IDs. Wouldn’t believe that I owned the land. It grew grass really well out there—I reckon it produced 8000 kilograms of milk solids.” Flint withdrew his stock from the area but remains adamant that his family have owned it for some 80 years. That night, I slept in my van by a friend’s house at Kaiaua, awaking to the sweetish smell of silage and distant cajoling whoops as cows were urged into a milking shed.

34.text: The limpid waters of Blue Spring, near Putaruru, are among the clearest, purest in the world; proof that the water flowing across New Zealand—and particularly beneath it—is still relatively unspoiled. Rivers flowing out of conservation lands remain in good health, and trampers can still scoop a handful of healthy water from many streams. We are, after all, an aquatic nation: to be a Kiwi is to be in, on and around water. The fouling of the last quarter century can be halted, even turned around, say water managers. But first, minds must be shifted, new priorities set, and every voice heard.

43.document_title: Government Reveals First Changes to Resource Management Act
43.document_summary: The New Zealand government announced its first changes to the Resource Management Act (RMA), effective May 2024. Minister Chris Bishop outlined five key reforms aimed at reducing regulatory burden on farming, mining, and primary industries: repealing intensive winter grazing regulations, removing low-slope maps from stock exclusion rules, suspending Significant Natural Area identification requirements for three years, removing Te Mana o te Wai hierarchy compliance for resource consents during freshwater policy review, and realigning coal mining consenting with other mining activities. Agriculture Minister Todd McClay emphasized farm-level solutions, while Associate Environment Minister Andrew Hoggard noted concerns about overly restrictive land-use regulations. Federated Farmers and Beef + Lamb New Zealand welcomed the changes as practical relief from complex, unworkable rules. However, Labour and Green Party opposition criticized the reforms as short-sighted, prioritizing profits over environmental protection and waterway health. Local Government New Zealand supported the certainty provided but called for more substantial RMA reform.

44.document_title: Canterbury Dairy Expansion: 32 New Farms as Grain Growers Switch to Milk Production
44.document_summary: Canterbury is experiencing significant dairy farm expansion with 32 new dairy discharge consents approved and 15 more in progress, potentially adding up to 25,000 dairy cows to the region's herd. Low global wheat prices and strong milk payouts are driving arable farmers to convert grain operations to dairy farming. While dairy remains profitable with 81% of surveyed farmers making profit at $9.50/kg milk solids, the arable sector struggles with only 40% profitable. The expansion follows the end of a temporary dairy conversion ban in January 2025. Concerns exist about losing critical mass in the grain industry and its supporting infrastructure. Nationally, dairy cow numbers declined 0.5% to 4.68 million in 2024/25, though milk solids production increased 2.9%.

45.text:
[Page 1] Government's freshwater bill will result in more polluted waterways, critics say ByKate Green Health Correspondent, Niva Chittock WorldWatch Presenter/Producer 2024 06 01 12:06:32+12:00 The Resource Management (Freshwater and Other Matters) Amendment Bill will relax rules for keeping farm animals out of waterways. File photo. A bill changing freshwater protection rules is prompting more accusations of the coalition government prioritising profit over protection. The Resource Management (Freshwater and Other Matters) Amendment Bill will make a series of "targeted changes that can take effect quickly ... while the government develops new legislation to replace the Resource Management Act 1991", according to RMA Reform Minister Chris Bishop. "The bill will also speed up the process for preparing or amending national direction. The current process for making or amending national direction is unnecessarily onerous, costly, and it takes too long." Agriculture Minister Todd McClay said the government was "backing" New Zealand farmers. "Improving primary sector profitability is key to remaining competitive internationally and getting value back into farmers' back pockets." If passed, the bill would mean councils no longer need to abide by the "hierarchy of obligations" (that is, the order of priorities) laid out in the existing legislation when issuing resource consents. It would mean a relaxation of rules for keeping farm animals out of waterways a move the government said would reduce costs for farmers and more permissive rules for intensive winter grazing. It would also suspend requirements for councils to identify areas of precious biodiversity as new Significant Natural Areas (SNAs) and include them in district plans for the next three years, a piece of advice over which Hoggard previously faced criticism. The bill follows the repeal of the Natural and Built Environment Act and the Spatial Planning Act in December, and the introduction of the Fast track Approvals Bill in March, with organisations like Greenpeace dubbing the changes "a war on nature". no caption Could the rule changes affect our drinking water and our health? Greenpeace spokesperson Amanda Larsson said the rule changes would result in more polluted lakes and rivers, and more water species' extinction. It would also likely increase the amount of nitrogen a main component in fertiliser and stock urine entering waterways, which could directly impact the quality of drinking water. "Nitrate contamination of drinking water has been connected to increased risk of health issues such as bowel cancer and pre term birth," she said. GNS Science research found almost 60 percent of freshwater sources analysed had nitrate N concentrations of more than 0.9 milligrams per litre. The current national standard allows for a maximum of 11.3 milligrams per litre, but some overseas studies have suggested it should be as low as 1 milligrams per litre, finding a correlation with colo rectal cancers for anything higher. "We have been finding that even public drinking water supplies in rural Canterbury in particular are approaching levels that are increasing the risk of pre term birth 5 milligrams per litre," Larsson said. "Ecological studies have also shown that above 1.0 mg/L, that the environmental quality of stream habitats are affected and biodiversity begins to decline." Hoggard said it was important to remember that many farmers had already excluded livestock from a "substantial portion" of waterways throughout the country. "I don't believe they get enough recognition for that." He said it would be up to regional councils to determine how winter grazing was managed. "Where there are no local rules, the onus would be on farmers to voluntarily follow good practice." Otago University Wellington research fellow Marnie Prickett said removing priority environmental implications when issuing resource consents was an "alarming trajectory". "It says to regional councils, you don't have to consider will this protect people's drinking water? Will this be consistent with protecting a healthy waterway? "We can read between the lines there and see that it's actually just going to put commercial actions back up the chain and take away that really necessary weight that we've now got to protect people's drinking water sources and the health of their rivers." Ngāi Tahu rūnanga chair Justin Tipa. Removing protection 'unacceptable', iwi says Removing Te Mana o te Wai the from fundamental concept of the Essential Freshwater regulations introduced by the previous government in 2020 was absolutely unacceptable for Ngāi Tahu, rūnanga chair Justin Tipa said. The High Court at Christchurch recently ruled Canterbury Regional Council unlawfully granted an irrigation consent in Ashburton, in part because it failed to properly take into consideration how it would affect the nearby freshwater and coastal waterways. "The [current] hierarchy places the health and well being of the wai, of freshwater first. And that's a critical protection, particularly where freshwater ecosystems are under serious threat," Tipa said. Ngāi Tahu was absolutely supportive of economic development and wanted to see the regions thrive, but not at the expense of the environment, he said. "If we continue to blindly over allocate our freshwater resources and use it in a way that's not sustainable, it's not going to benefit anyone. We can strike a better balance." Freshwater, and the wider natural environment, had been mismanaged for decades, if not centuries, he said. It was time to change that and take a more intergenerational approach, instead of working to three year political cycles. Incentives more helpful than regulation, farmer says A farm owner says farmers are sick of rules being "forced upon us" and want to inspire change. John Burke and his brother Rick own Pukekauri Farm in Katikati in the Western Bay of Plenty. The sheep and beef farm covers 300 hectares. The brothers' environmental restoration journey began 25 years ago. The water quality was poor, running clear through protected land at the top of the catchment, but dirtied by sedimentation as it passed through the farm. "We're farming pastoral land on really steep, erosion prone sites," John Burke said. In the early days, there was "no riparian planting, no wetlands, it was a bit of a mess", he said. Farmers want to inspire change, John Burke says. File photo. "So progressively, over that time, with the assistance of the regional council and specialist advisory services, including ecological input, we've retired what we call the red zone areas of our farm." They planted the edges of waterways and retired some steep areas, instated large setbacks along waterways and restored eight wetlands. These days, the water runs clearer, and deposits far less sediment at the bottom and the brothers are not losing money. "By taking those red zone areas out of our farm, we have not reduced our total pastoral farming profit, we've actually maintained our total profit not profit per hectare, but total profit which tells us that the land we took out was contributing nothing to the bottom line, and in many instances was running at a loss." But farmers needed support to put up that initial cost, and access to knowledge, Burke said. Catchment groups could be a good way to pool knowledge and organise work, but funding was "critical", he said and it needed to start now. "It's taken us over 20 years. The sooner you start, the sooner you finish. "To procrastinate and not get on with it, we're just pushing it out." He said incentives would be more helpful than regulation. "Farmers, people in general, have so much antipathy to regulation, stuff being forced upon us. We want to inspire change." After its first reading, the Resource Management (Freshwater and Other Matters) Amendment Bill will be sent to the primary production select committee for consideration. Bishop said he chose that committee over the environment committee due to the high workload the latter was already facing. The bill would relax rules for keeping farm animals out of waterways, suspend biodiversity protection requirements, and remove the "hierarchy of obligations" that currently prioritizes environmental considerations in resource consents. Critics, including environmental organizations like Greenpeace and indigenous groups such as Ngāi Tahu, warn this will increase water pollution, nitrogen contamination, and health risks including nitrate-related illnesses. [Page 1] Mid Canterbury farmers will be happy the regional council has to stop charging ahead with new freshwater rules, David Acland says. The Federated Farmers Mid Canterbury president said the government's changes around the Resource Management Act will be well received by local farmers. "It's a positive outcome and something Feds and other industry groups have been pushing for." The government's Resource Management (Freshwater and Other Matters) Amendment Bill passed its third reading last week. It restricts councils' ability to notify freshwater plans until the replacement National Policy Statement for Freshwater Management is in place. no metadata Agriculture Minister Todd McClay said the government was taking steps to provide farmers the clarity they need around freshwater management, minimise inefficiencies and duplication for councils, and prevent unnecessary costs for ratepayers. Environment Canterbury was planning on bringing in a new Regional Policy Statement, and a Plan Change to the Land and Water Regional Plan, later this year. Acland said it didn't make sense to introduce new water quality rules at the same time the Government was changing the national direction. ECan should do it once and do it right, and the Government had to make a legislative change "to make the pause button get pushed", he said. ECan chief executive Stefanie Rixecker said the councillors were yet to consider or discuss the changes in the context of the council's current work programmes. "As soon as they have had the opportunity to do so, we will be better placed to make appropriate comment." Acland said the pause on the paperwork isn't about doing nothing and doesn't mean an open season for farmers. Environmental regulation and improvements will continue to implement the Canterbury land and water plan the community signed off on 10 years ago, he said. The RMA Bill also excludes the Te Mana o te Wai hierarchy of obligations from resource consent applicants and pauses work on identifying new Significant Natural Areas. McClay said changes to stock exclusion and winter grazing regulations represent a move to a more risk based, catchment focused approach. "Regulations need to be fit for purpose and not place unnecessary compliance costs on farmers and growers. "The focus is on farm level and regionally suitable solutions." That was music to Acland's ears. "There has been significant change across the plains which has put pressure on it and we do need to improve and adapt. "It's just how we do that, which has to be led by the rural community, not by Wellington." Catchment groups are already popping up across Mid Canterbury and working collaboratively on improving environmental outcomes at a sub regional level, he said. "When they say locally led, we mean these groups who are already implementing change." The government's move hasn't been welcomed by everyone. The Otago Regional Council was blocked from passing its Land & Water Regional plan last week, Newsroom reported. Otago councillor Elliot Weir told Newsroom they had been "cornered" by central government, despite having done "everything we possibly could" to pass the plan. The plan was aimed at increasing freshwater environmental protections and would have set a minimum flow standard for rivers. LDR is local body journalism co funded by RNZ and NZ On Air. Related
