13.fileDescription: This article highlights significant conservation milestones achieved in New Zealand's wildlife in 2024-2025. Key achievements include takahē populations reaching carrying capacity in the Murchison Ranges after 50 years of monitoring, with birds now dispersing to new territories via the Routeburn tramping track. Tokoeka kiwi chick survival rates dramatically improved to 70% following predator control operations. Kiwi populations have expanded from Wellington's Remutaka Ranges to Upper Hutt, with a 55% increase since 2011. The critically endangered Sinbad skink population, found only on a 320-metre vertical cliff face in Milford Sound, faces translocation challenges due to low numbers. Other successes include the first captive breeding of giant wētā in decades, record Northern Albatross breeding seasons, and successful pest control efforts. These milestones demonstrate the effectiveness of long-term conservation efforts and resource management by the Department of Conservation.

chunkHighlights.text: Now, here are some gains for nature you might not have heard about. Original takahē discovery site in the Murchison Ranges reaches full capacity as the population thrives This year was likely the last in which rangers would need to rigorously monitor the population of takahē in the Murchison Ranges, with the population reaching capacity. Glen Greaves, senior ranger in the Department of Conservation's (DOC) takahē recovery team, said the species was rediscovered at this site 76 years ago, and the population had been closely monitored for the past 50. "We think it's around 250, we don't know exactly - it's 50,000 hectares of mountainous terrain, so we have to give it an estimate - but we're pretty

certain its between 220 and 260 birds." That meant the site was at
carrying capacity. It was a huge area, but the usable land was a lot smaller - and takahē needed up to 100 hectares per pair. They still faced challenges, he said. "It's a really tough site, it's not takahē Nirvana. It receives really cold winters, some pretty extreme weather events, its topography is really challenging for the birds as well, we have a lot of misadventure - you know, birds falling off cliffs and drowning in ponds and rivers during flood events." But those challenges meant pests had only just arrived, and that had allowed takahē to thrive. "We think the size of the population means it's quite resilient and we can now take a step back." It had been 20 years of involvement for Greaves, and a labour of love for the team. "We'll miss it, it's definitely the most exciting and rewarding place to go and visit, being such a historically important site for takahē, but it's just an awesome place. "But it's also a big tick in the success box as well, being able to step back means that we can put those resources into new sites." Trampers spotting takahē on the Routeburn In another "massive milestone" for takahē, Greaves said birds from the Greenstone Valley population had begun to disperse outwards in search of new territory, via the popular tramping track, the Routeburn. In 2023, 28 birds were released onto a working station owned by Ngāi Tahu. But in the search for new territory, the birds were taking the path of least resistance. That meant trampers were catching a sighting, with many sending in pictures and reporting what band colours they spotted, which Greaves said was encouraged by DOC. For centuries takahē have only been in the Murchison Mountains and offshore islands, and the Murchison Mountains are closed to the public. "So for the public to be able to see these birds in their natural landscapes, in a place they've been absent for centuries, is huge." Tokoeka kiwi chick survival rate up to 70 percent The Fiordland tokoeka, or Southern Brown kiwi, population at Shy Lake on the remote Wet Jacket peninsula in Fiordland officially reversed its decline with a population growth of about two percent per year. and project lead for tokoeka, Chris Dodd, said two predator control
operations in 2020 and 2023 knocked back stoats and about 20 percent
of kiwi chicks survived for the following two years. This past season,
chick survival spiked to a remarkable 70 percent. And it had been a win

retrieved_chunks.text: [Page 18] “Kākāpō are extinct throughout their natural range,” he began, “and there is no way of returning them there, at least in the short to medium term. If they are to survive in a free living state, then it must be outside their former range. But where? It is fair to expect that the number of kākāpō will steadily, if slowly, increase, and that the small islands where they are being kept will soon reach their holding capacity. What are we going to do then? There aren’t many options, because kākāpō need a lot of space, and a self sustaining population of several hundred birds would require many thousands of hectares. They cannot coexist with predatory mammals, so the mainland is out, and they need a dominant masting plant species in order to breed. We’re looking at all the possi bilities—including the subantarctic.” His eyes had the gleam of a man who sees a prize which is not yet within his grasp. “Campbell?” I asked. “It’s a candidate, and a good one. It is large—over 11,000 hectares—and after last year’s rat eradication project it should now be free of all alien mammals. It has a wide variety of plants, including abundant snow tussock, which could provide the necessary high energy food to enable kākāpō to breed. The climate shouldn’t worry them. I have been in the thick blackness of this southern night for six hours already, waiting for the approaching dawn to silhouette the forest canopy with patches of grey. My only company lies a couple of metres away, in a tangle of rotting rata stumps and roots: a tiny grey chick which looks as cold and disconsolate as I feel. It is H2, a seven day old kakapo and one of the very latest additions to the embattled parrot’s population. While I shiver in layers of expensive polypropylene and synthetic fabrics, H2 has only the finest coating of grey down for warmth and resembles nothing more than a patch of mould on the forest floor. As a volunteer nest minder, I am spending two weeks looking after this fragile addition to the kakapo world while its mother, Heather, forages in the surrounding rimu forest of Codfish Island/Whenua Hou. Fatigued by 10 days of scant and intermittent sleep and up to four hours’ walking on waterlogged tracks each day, I find my biggest challenge is simply to stay awake. It’s rough and it’s raw, but what I’m doing is the reality of conservation in this country. Forget photo opportunities and cuddling one of the world’s rarest birds. At that time, 2002, most of the 86 living kākāpō were clustered on that one island, Whenua Hou. It was the middle of the night, and I was jammed in a tent with two wildlife rangers. Every half an hour or so, we checked the screen of a monitor that was connected to a repurposed domestic security camera stationed 80 metres away, on the island’s summit. The camera was pointed at a shallow depression in the soil—a kākāpō courtship bowl. The bowl was empty. Whenever we turned the monitor on, all we saw were scrubby bushes flailing in the wind, and all we heard was the caterwauling cries of petrels wheeling overhead in the storm. Then, around midnight, we heard what we had been hoping for: the sonorous boom of a kākāpō male. Three hands reached simultaneously for the video button. The screen came to life, and there, pumped up like a rugby ball, was Lionel, singing his basso profundo lovesong to the island’s 21 females. All of whom, apparently, ignored his overtures. response.response_text:
## Kākāpō and Takahē: Two Paths Back from the Brink

New Zealand has produced some of the world's most innovative endangered species recovery work, and the programmes for kākāpō and takahē offer a fascinating study in contrasting — and occasionally converging — conservation philosophies.

![embed-1](embed://1)

## Shared Foundations

Both species share a common starting point: rediscovery after presumed extinction, critically small populations, and the looming threat of introduced predators. Both programmes operate under the Department of Conservation (DOC) and have relied on island sanctuaries, captive breeding, and intensive hands-on management to pull populations back from the edge. [[1]](cite://1/1)[[2]](cite://2/1)

Both species also carry the burden of intensive individual monitoring — every bird checked at least annually. [[3]](cite://3/1)

## The Kākāpō Approach: Total Management on Predator-Free Islands

The kākāpō programme is arguably one of the most intensive wildlife management efforts anywhere in the world. [[4]](cite://4/1) Key features include:

**Predator-free island sanctuaries** — All surviving kākāpō were physically relocated from the mainland and Stewart Island/Rakiura to offshore islands, including Whenua Hou/Codfish Island, Te Hoiere/Maud Island, and Te Kākahu o Tamatea/Chalky Island. Between 1982 and 1992, all 61 surviving Stewart Island kākāpō were transferred. [[2]](cite://2/2)

**Individual monitoring** — Every bird carries a transmitter, and each has a name, a detailed family tree, and a recorded history. As of 2026, there are 235 adult kākāpō alive. [[5]](cite://5/1) Infrared motion sensors and surveillance cameras are installed at all nests, and radio telemetry is used to track females during breeding. [[6]](cite://6/1)

**Breeding intervention** — The programme has used supplementary feeding, egg incubation, artificial insemination, chick hand-rearing, and nest minding (including volunteer nest minders who sit with chicks overnight). [[7]](cite://7/1)[[8]](cite://8/1)[[9]](cite://9/1) Breeding is tightly linked to rimu masting events, which occur every two to four years, and the recovery team monitors rimu fruiting a full year in advance to prepare. [[8]](cite://8/2)

**Hygiene and disease management** — Strict quarantine and hygiene procedures apply on all breeding islands, including freezing supplementary food and ventilating nests, following outbreaks of the fungal disease aspergillosis. [[10]](cite://10/1)

**Private funding** — The programme has attracted significant commercial sponsorship. Between 1990 and 2004, aluminium smelting company Comalco donated $1.6 million towards kākāpō conservation. [[11]](cite://11/1)

![embed-2](embed://2)

## The Takahē Approach: Wild Population Management and Expansion

The takahē recovery programme has taken a somewhat broader geographic approach, combining protection of a wild mainland population with island 'security populations' and active reintroduction to new sites.

**Wild mainland population** — Unlike kākāpō, takahē retained a wild population in the Murchison Mountains, Fiordland, which became a Specially Protected Area with access by permit only. By 2025, this population reached an estimated 220–260 birds — effectively full carrying capacity of around 100 hectares per pair — allowing DOC to step back from intensive monitoring there. [[12]](cite://12/1)

**Burwood Takahē Centre** — In the 1980s, a dedicated captive breeding and chick-rearing facility was established near Te Anau, focused on understanding breeding requirements and reducing chick mortality through egg incubation and captive rearing. [[13]](cite://13/1)[[1]](cite://1/2)

**Island security populations** — As with kākāpō, predator-free offshore islands became refuges, serving as insurance populations in case wild populations failed. Takahē can now be found at Kāpiti Island, Tiritiri Matangi, and Zealandia in Wellington. [[14]](cite://14/1)[[15]](cite://15/1)

**Active reintroduction to new wild sites** — A major point of difference from kākāpō is the takahē programme's push to establish multiple wild populations across different landscapes. Takahē were reintroduced to Kahurangi National Park in 2018, to Ngāi Tahu land at Greenstone Station in the upper Whakatipu in 2023, and to the Rees Valley in 2025. [[13]](cite://13/2) Extensive stoat trap lines must be established before any release. [[13]](cite://13/3)

**Stoat management** — Because takahē are being reintroduced into mainland backcountry environments, ongoing predator control is a central pillar of the programme in ways that island-based kākāpō management doesn't require to the same degree. [[13]](cite://13/4)

By 2023, the total takahē population had reached 500, and as of 2026 stands at around 520. [[15]](cite://15/2)[[13]](cite://13/5)

## A Shared Shift: Stepping Back

Interestingly, both programmes are now moving in a similar direction — away from intensive hands-on management towards greater naturalness.

For kākāpō, 2026 has seen the biggest breeding season on record, with over 90 new chicks alive. The programme is trialling a 'lighter touch' approach: leaving more eggs to hatch in nests rather than incubators, reducing nest checks, and for the first time, leaving some chicks unnamed — a symbolic step towards the ultimate vision of kākāpō wandering wild and nameless through New Zealand's forests. [[5]](cite://5/2)[[4]](cite://4/2)

For takahē, the Murchison Mountains population reaching carrying capacity has allowed DOC to redirect resources to new reintroduction sites, and public sightings of dispersing birds in backcountry areas like the Routeburn track are being celebrated as a milestone. [[12]](cite://12/2)

Both programmes also share aspirations tied to broader predator control — kākāpō supporters look to Predator Free Rakiura as a future wild home, while takahē's expanding backcountry presence depends on sustained stoat trapping. [[16]](cite://16/1)[[13]](cite://13/6)

Would you like to explore more about the role of Ngāi Tahu in either of these recovery programmes?

1.document_title: New Zealand's Threatened Species: Conservation Status, Strategies, and Recovery Efforts
1.document_summary: This comprehensive document provides an overview of New Zealand's threatened species and conservation efforts. It defines threatened species as native plants and animals with critically low populations facing extinction risk, with New Zealand having 2,788 threatened species (37% of birds, 34% of plants). Main causes of decline include habitat destruction, invasive predators like rats and possums, and over-harvesting. New Zealand uses an eight-tier classification system for conservation status based on threats, endemism, vulnerability, and cultural importance. Conservation strategies include island sanctuaries, pest control, captive breeding, and habitat restoration. Notable successes include the black robin recovery (7 to 250 individuals), takahē recovery program, and tuatara reintroduction programs. The document presents case studies of endangered species including the Mahoenui giant wētā, Peraxilla mistletoes, kiwi, and tuatara. About 30% of New Zealand is protected conservation land. Recent efforts have expanded beyond visible species to include freshwater fish and plants, with a shift toward restoring entire habitats. Key challenges include funding limitations, many species poorly understood (1,455 fungi species classified as 'data deficient'), an estimated 50,000 unidentified native species potentially at risk, and preventing 'zombie species' that survive only in cultivation.

2.text:

Project River Recovery was launched in 1991 in partnership with Meridian Energy, restoring some of the Mackenzie Basin habitat by controlling weeds and predators, and digging ponds. This has also benefited other native plants and animals.

The document addresses conservation concerns for endangered species like the Chatham Island oystercatcher and New Zealand dotterel, discussing threats from predators, human activity, and habitat loss. Conservation programs, habitat restoration, predator management, and captive breeding initiatives are emphasized as crucial for species survival. 4.document_summary: Stewart Island/Rakiura is New Zealand's third largest island located south of the South Island. The Māori name "Rakiura" means "glowing skies," referencing the aurora australis, while the English name honors William Stewart, first mate of the sealer Pegasus. Covering 1,680 square kilometers with approximately 85% protected as Rakiura National Park (established 2002), the island features diverse vegetation zones from coastal shrublands to alpine tussock lands, with over half covered by podocarp and hardwood forests. The island supports exceptional biodiversity including 15,000 southern tokoeka (Stewart Island kiwi), kākāpō, three penguin species, fur seals, and sea lions, with 21 endemic alpine plant species. Historically, Polynesians reached the island by the late 1200s, with permanent Māori settlement following primarily around coastal areas for fishing and harvesting tītī (muttonbirds). European contact began with James Cook in 1770, followed by sealers, whalers, and missionaries. Since the 1850s, the island's economy has centered on sheep farming, timber milling, and fishing, with fishing becoming dominant by 2013. Tourism evolved from the 1890s to a major industry attracting 30,000 annual visitors. Key geographic features include Paterson Inlet (8,900 hectares), Mason Bay with 200-metre dunes, Ulva Island (predator-free scenic reserve), Port Pegasus with granite domes, and the Southern Circuit tramping track (71.5 km). Oban (Halfmoon Bay) serves as the main township with 378 residents in 2013.

5.text:
[Page 13] area. Island restoration Some islands are being restored to something resembling their original ecology, with unwanted animals entirely eradicated. Larger browsing animals such as wild cattle and goats are the first to go, followed by smaller predators cats and possums, stoats and weasels, and eventually rats. Existing patches of native vegetation are enlarged, often with the help of planting programmes. Some sparse populations have become abundant once again. Other species were reintroduced to their former homes, while some islands became sanctuaries for animals never previously found there. Kākāpō were once plentiful, but when only a few remained in Fiordland and on Stewart Island (Rakiura), they were moved to Whenua Hou/Codfish, Maud and Little Barrier islands, and in 2003 to Fiordland’s Chalky Island (Te Kākahu o Tamatea). Public sanctuaries Most conservation restrict access to prevent disturbance or the arrival of unwanted pests. But several are open to the public. Kāpiti Island near Wellington and Tiritiri Matangi near Auckland have similar histories. Once cleared for farming, they now have no animal pests, and native forest has been re established over 250,000 native trees were planted on Tiritiri Matangi. Both are refuges for saddlebacks, kōkako, stitchbirds, little spotted kiwi and takahē. Not far from Kāpiti is Mana Island, also a bird sanctuary, and noted for its ‘colony’ of concrete gannets, built to tempt real gannets to breed there. Betty gets her goats In the 1970s the government decided to kill wild goats and sheep on Arapawa Island, in the Marlborough Sounds. Protesters claimed the animals were descendants of those left by James Cook. DNA tests showed some were genetically unique. Many were culled, but others were sent to farms and wildlife parks. Betty Rowe led the rescue campaign and established a sanctuary on Arapawa Island. Marine reserves To create areas where people could not disturb the ocean, seabed and seashore, the Marine Reserves Act was passed in 1971. The first reserve was at Goat Island, north of Auckland (now Cape Rodney Ōkakari Point Marine Reserve). The second was the ocean around the Poor Knights Islands, noted for islands subtropical fish. Others include islands off the Coromandel Peninsula, Tūhua (Mayor Island) in Bay of Plenty, Kāpiti Island, Long Island in the Marlborough Sounds, Tonga Island in Abel Tasman National Park, Elizabeth Island in Fiordland and Ulva Island near Stewart Island.

5.document_title: New Zealand's Nearshore Islands: History, Conservation, and Human Settlement
5.document_summary: This comprehensive document explores New Zealand's over 600 nearshore islands within 50 kilometres of the main islands, covering their geological formation, historical significance, and contemporary conservation status. The islands are distributed around the North Island (Great Barrier, Rangitoto, Bay of Islands) and southern regions (Marlborough Sounds, Fiordland). Historically, Māori utilized these islands for harvesting seafood, birds, and resources like argillite rock, obsidian, and adzite, including tītī (muttonbirds). European contact began in the late 1700s-1800s with sealers, whalers, and explorers like James Cook. Island industries included 19th-century mining, farming, and the world's first regular pigeon airmail service on Great Barrier Island (1897-1908). The document details quarantine facilities on Quarantine Island (Dunedin), Ōtamahua (Christchurch), and Matiu (Wellington), which housed disease victims, leprosy patients, and wartime internees. Today, islands serve as nature reserves hosting endangered species including tuatara, kākāpō, kiwi, and rare plants like Pennantia baylisiana. Conservation efforts began with Resolution Island in 1891 and include successful eradication programs and species reintroduction initiatives.

6.document_title: Native Plants in New Zealand: History, Horticulture, and Commercial Cultivation
6.document_summary: This comprehensive document explores native plants in New Zealand across historical, horticultural, and commercial contexts. It traces native plant use from Māori cultivation of rengarenga lilies and karaka trees through European settlement, highlighting early advocates like Leonard Cockayne and J.G. McKenzie. A pivotal shift occurred in the 1970s-1980s when gardeners like Muriel Fisher and Lawrie Metcalf transformed public perception, demonstrating native plants were attractive and easy to cultivate. The document covers diverse native plant categories including ornamental grasses, tree ferns, alpine species, and specialist plants, with over 800 cultivars of hebes, flax, and mānuka produced through breeding. It emphasizes native garden design principles focusing on form, texture, and foliage. Modern revegetation practices use locally sourced native plants for ecological restoration, with approximately 300 commercial native plant nurseries operating by the late 1990s. Key initiatives include subalpine shrubland, forest revegetation, swamp restoration, and sand dune projects. Commercial applications include historical fiber cultivation of New Zealand flax, pharmaceutical extraction attempts, native food crops like kōkihi, and growing export markets for native foliage plants, particularly Pittosporum, with 1.4 million stems exported in 2003-4.

7.document_title: Canterbury Region: Comprehensive Geography, History, Culture, and Development
7.document_summary: This comprehensive document provides an extensive overview of Canterbury, New Zealand's South Island region, covering geography, history, culture, economy, and governance. Geographically, Canterbury features vast plains, the Southern Alps, braided rivers, and Christchurch, the "garden city." The region's geology was shaped by volcanic activity (Banks Peninsula 15-12 million years ago) and glaciation, with significant seismic activity including devastating earthquakes in 2010-2011 (6.3 magnitude, 185 deaths) and 2016 (7.8 magnitude Kaikōura). Historically, Ngāi Tahu Māori settled the region 600-700 years ago, establishing centers like Kaiapoi. European settlement began with Captain Cook (1770) and intensified after the Treaty of Waitangi (1840), with the Canterbury Association organizing settlement from 1850. The region developed strong agricultural heritage, transitioning from large estates to family farms, with sheep farming dominant (3.15 million head by 1885, 11% of national flock in 2012), supplemented by wheat production (62.5% of national) and expanding dairy operations (115% increase 2002-2012). Major irrigation schemes, including the Rangitātā diversion race (1945) and Central Plains Water scheme (2015), enabled intensive farming. Industrial development centered on farm-related processing and manufacturing, maintaining 11% of national manufacturing employment by 2013. Tourism accounted for 8.4% of jobs in 2010 but was severely impacted by the 2011 earthquake, with recovery underway by 2014. Transport infrastructure evolved significantly with the Lyttelton rail tunnel (1867), road tunnel (1964), Ōtira tunnel (1923), and Christchurch airport (opened 1940, first international airport 1950). Culturally, Canterbury developed a rich artistic heritage with notable figures including Samuel Butler, Denis Glover, Allen Curnow, and Rita Angus. The region has a strong sporting tradition, including rugby (Crusaders), tennis (Anthony Wilding), and hosted the 1974 Commonwealth Games. Governance evolved from provincial abolition (1876) through the Canterbury Regional Council (1989) to the Canterbury Earthquake Recovery Authority (CERA) post-2011. In 2013, Canterbury had 478,623 residents (11.3% of New Zealand's population), predominantly European (86.2%), with recovery efforts including the Christchurch Central Recovery Plan (July 2012) and ongoing reconstruction.

9.document_title: Kaitiakitanga: Māori Guardianship, Environmental Stewardship, and Traditional Conservation Practices
9.document_summary: Kaitiakitanga is a foundational Māori concept of guardianship and environmental stewardship rooted in the worldview that humans are part of nature. A kaitiaki is a guardian recognized by tangata whenua to care for natural areas such as lakes, forests, and waterways. Traditional conservation practices include temporary rāhui (resource restrictions), use of the lunar calendar (maramataka) for planting and harvesting, sustainable hunting and fishing, and blessing of mauri stones by tohunga (priests). Key spiritual concepts include mana (spiritual power), tapu (spiritual restriction), and mauri (life force). Today, kaitiakitanga is experiencing renewal as iwi (tribes) restore ecosystems and apply traditional knowledge in modern contexts. Practical examples include Ngāi Tahu's guardianship of pounamu resources, Ngāti Toa's fishery restoration at Pukerua Bay, and multi-tribal efforts to stop river pollution and protect endangered species. The document outlines challenges in collaborating with non-Māori stakeholders and details legislative frameworks such as the Resource Management Act 1991 and Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004 that incorporate kaitiakitanga principles. Kaitiakitanga offers perspectives on environmental stewardship and kinship with nature, enabling Māori to fulfill ancestral responsibilities while contributing to broader environmental sustainability.

10.document_title: Seaweed: Ecology, Traditional Uses, and Modern Applications in New Zealand
10.document_summary: This comprehensive guide explores seaweed species found in New Zealand, their ecological importance, and diverse applications spanning traditional and modern uses. The document covers three main groups of seaweed classified by color: green, brown, and red seaweeds, with detailed information on their distribution, structure, and life cycles. Green seaweeds thrive in shallow, sunlit waters; brown seaweeds include kelps that form underwater forests over 20 metres tall; red seaweeds grow at greater depths and comprise 550 species in New Zealand. Kelp forests, particularly bladder kelp and common kelp, are vital marine ecosystems supporting numerous species and serving as fundamental food sources and habitats for marine creatures. The document details traditional Māori uses of seaweeds, including karengo as a nutritious food source and bull kelp (rimurapa) for storage in pōhā bags. Modern applications include agar extraction for bacterial cultivation and food preservation, cosmetic thickeners, food seasoning production, shellfish farming support, and potential uses in reducing livestock methane emissions. The document also addresses invasive species like Asian kelp, which threaten native marine habitats, while highlighting New Zealand's abundant seaweed resources and potential for developing a thriving seaweed industry despite current challenges in competing with Asian producers due to labour-intensive harvesting methods.

11.document_title: New Zealand's Threatened Species: Conservation Status, Strategies, and Recovery Efforts
11.document_summary: This comprehensive document provides an overview of New Zealand's threatened species and conservation efforts. It defines threatened species as native plants and animals with critically low populations facing extinction risk, with New Zealand having 2,788 threatened species (37% of birds, 34% of plants). Main causes of decline include habitat destruction, invasive predators like rats and possums, and over-harvesting. New Zealand uses an eight-tier classification system for conservation status based on threats, endemism, vulnerability, and cultural importance. Conservation strategies include island sanctuaries, pest control, captive breeding, and habitat restoration. Notable successes include the black robin recovery (7 to 250 individuals), takahē recovery program, and tuatara reintroduction programs. The document presents case studies of endangered species including the Mahoenui giant wētā, Peraxilla mistletoes, kiwi, and tuatara. About 30% of New Zealand is protected conservation land. Recent efforts have expanded beyond visible species to include freshwater fish and plants, with a shift toward restoring entire habitats. Key challenges include funding limitations, many species poorly understood (1,455 fungi species classified as 'data deficient'), an estimated 50,000 unidentified native species potentially at risk, and preventing 'zombie species' that survive only in cultivation.

14.document_title: Ngā Manu: Birds in Māori Culture, Symbolism, and Tradition
14.document_summary: This comprehensive document explores the multifaceted role of birds in traditional Māori culture, encompassing their practical, spiritual, and symbolic significance in New Zealand indigenous society. Birds served essential functions as food sources (kiwi meat for chiefs), providers of feathers for high-status garments (kahu kiwi cloaks), and indicators of rank and prestige. Specific species held particular importance—huia white-tipped feathers were worn by high-ranking individuals, tūī were trained to speak and recite greetings, and kākā feathers signified high status. The document covers spiritual and predictive dimensions of birds in Māori belief systems, including how certain species signaled weather changes (kārearea falcon calls predicted rain), marked seasonal events (pīpīwharauroa arrival signaled planting time), and carried omens of fortune or misfortune. Birds were associated with death and grieving ceremonies, such as the mātātā used to guide spirits to Hawaiki. The text explores how Māori created sayings and metaphors comparing human characteristics to bird traits, and how birds were named based on their calls, appearance, or behavior. Additional coverage includes specific bird species such as tītiti pounamu (rifleman) and whio (blue duck), detailing their Māori names, habitats, and cultural associations.

15.document_summary: This comprehensive document explores traditional Māori practices of catching, preserving, and harvesting eels (tuna) and lampreys (piharau) in New Zealand. It explains eel weir construction that used fences to guide eels into nets and traps, and describes different hīnaki baskets made from mangemange stems and kiekie roots. The text includes cooking techniques such as wrapping eels in leaves for roasting and packing them in baskets with ferns, as well as karakia (charms) used in eeling practices and the cultural significance of first catches as offerings to the gods. Historical accounts describe seasonal eel migrations (heke tuna) and South Island harvesting practices at locations like Te Waihora and Wairewa.

17.document_title: Step away from the kākāpō
17.document_summary: The 2019 kākāpō breeding season achieved record success but was marred by an aspergillosis fungal disease outbreak on Codfish Island/Whenua Hou, infecting 21 birds and killing nine. Genetic analysis revealed all birds contracted the same fungal strain, likely introduced by humans through supplementary food. The same strain appeared on Anchor Island but caused no illness there. Researchers attribute the outbreak partly to hot, dry summer conditions that coincided with vulnerable chick stages. In response, DOC's recovery programme implemented enhanced biosecurity measures including food freezing, nest ventilation, and reduced direct chick handling. The team is transitioning toward less intensive management with remote monitoring and hands-off breeding sites, recognizing that while intensive management has prevented kākāpō extinction, stepping back represents the future direction for the species' recovery.

18.document_title: Big Birds Fly South: Kakapo Recovery and Breeding Success
18.document_summary: This article documents the kakapo recovery programme in New Zealand, focusing on efforts to save the critically endangered flightless night parrot. With only 58 survivors, the Department of Conservation relocated kakapo from Little Barrier Island to Maud Island and Codfish Island to improve breeding outcomes. A new supplementary feeding strategy based on nutritional cycles has proven effective, triggering successful breeding events. Notable successes include the first breeding on Maud Island and the discovery of previously unknown females. The programme has involved hundreds of volunteers and continues searching for additional birds on Stewart Island to bolster the species' survival prospects.

19.document_title: Feathering the Nest: Restoring Maungatautari
19.document_summary: This article profiles Chris Smuts-Kennedy, an ecologist leading species reintroductions at Maungatautari Ecological Island Trust in New Zealand's Waikato region. The project has enclosed 4,300 hectares with 47 km of predator-proof fencing to restore native wildlife. Recent successes include releasing 79 stitchbirds and 60 whiteheads, with takahe, kaka, and kiwi also reintroduced and breeding. Smuts-Kennedy, with 43 years of experience in New Zealand fauna, aspires to reintroduce kakapo to the mountain, viewing it as an ideal habitat due to its rimu trees and stable fruiting patterns. He discusses potential candidates including Sirocco, a human-raised kakapo ambassador, and other birds unsuitable for breeding. The restoration aims to create a naturally functioning ecosystem, with kakapo reintroduction representing the ultimate achievement for this significant conservation initiative.

20.text: Female kākāpō are devoted mothers, but since they are all solo parents they must leave their eggs and chicks unguarded for long periods each night while they forage. Before the advent of mammalian predators, their absences were of little consequence, but ground-level nests of eggs or chicks are like fast-food outlets to rats and their ilk, and now the only safe place for kākāpō to breed is on predator-free islands. Even in these havens, kākāpō workers take no chances, installing infrared movement sensors and surveillance cameras at all nests. The image shows an infrared movement sensor and surveillance setup in a forest clearing, with a kākāpō egg visible on the ground.

20.document_title: Kākāpō Nest Surveillance

21.text:
[Page 1] It is four in the morning, and I am sitting alone on the rain soaked soil of an island at the edge of Foveaux Strait, hunched against the pre dawn cold and endless southwesterlies. I have been in the thick blackness of this southern night for six hours already, waiting for the approaching dawn to silhouette the forest canopy with patches of grey. My only company lies a couple of metres away, in a tangle of rotting rata stumps and roots: a tiny grey chick which looks as cold and disconsolate as I feel. It is H2, a seven day old kakapo and one of the very latest additions to the embattled parrot’s population. While I shiver in layers of expensive polypropylene and synthetic fabrics, H2 has only the finest coating of grey down for warmth and resembles nothing more than a patch of mould on the forest floor. As a volunteer nest minder, I am spending two weeks looking after this fragile addition to the kakapo world while its mother, Heather, forages in the surrounding rimu forest of Codfish Island/Whenua Hou. Fatigued by 10 days of scant and intermittent sleep and up to four hours’ walking on waterlogged tracks each day, I find my biggest challenge is simply to stay awake. It’s rough and it’s raw, but what I’m doing is the reality of conservation in this country. Forget photo opportunities and cuddling one of the world’s rarest birds. Saving this species requires patience, sturdy boots and getting used to rivulets of water trickling down your neck. Nest minders, including the author (viewing a video monitor connected to an infrared camera at the nest). The cables, batteries and electronic gadgetry involved in the project had to be kept operational in the demanding outdoor conditions by Kakapo Recovery Programme scientist Graeme Elliott.

21.document_title: Minders: The Kakapo Caregivers of Codfish Island - Conservation and Intensive Management
21.document_summary: This comprehensive document chronicles the extraordinary kakapo conservation efforts on Codfish Island/Whenua Hou, focusing on the landmark 2002 breeding season. Over 100 volunteer nest minders from around the world participated in intensive 24-hour surveillance of 24 nests, resulting in 26 chicks hatching with 24 surviving—a 39% increase in the world kakapo population from 62 to 86 birds. The nest minders maintained constant vigilance, acted as surrogate parents during female foraging periods, and used innovative equipment like heat pads and infrared monitoring systems. The Department of Conservation-led intervention programme involved detailed monitoring, video surveillance, nightly chick weighing, and hand-rearing of struggling chicks. Despite harsh conditions—steep boggy tracks, cold nights, and minimal sleep—volunteers found the opportunity invaluable. The document profiles individual kakapo mothers (Heather, Ruth, Nora, Flossie) and their distinct parenting behaviors. A 1999 aerial poison drop eradicated rats, dramatically improving nesting success. With a chick mortality rate of just 8%, the 2002 season represented the most significant breakthrough for kakapo recovery since their rediscovery in 1977, demonstrating that intensive human intervention can successfully secure this endangered species' survival.

22.text:
[Page 9] Feral cats had developed a taste for kākāpō, and within five years these bushwise and feisty predators halved the remaining kākāpō population. Just as in Fiordland, searchers realised they were riding a bow wave of extinction. This time, however, they would take more radical measures. Between 1982 and 1992, all 61 surviving Stewart Island kākāpō were caught and transferred to safe island sanctuaries: Whenua Hou, Te Hoiere/Maud Island and Hauturu/Little Barrier Island, in the Hauraki Gulf . The kākāpō’s wild days were over. From now on, constant inter island transfers and airlifts out of trouble would become the norm in kākāpō life. While a long term solution to their predicament was being sought, the birds would remain refugees in their own homeland. One evening in early April 1999, as the seasons were turning and winter storms were edging in from the Southern Ocean, I walked with photographer Rod Morris through wet rimu forest down from the summit of Whenua Hou. We each carried a plastic cat box housing a kākāpō. The boxes were heavy, and every few hundred metres we stopped to swap hands and to catch a glimpse of the birds: a youngster named Sirocco in Morris’s cage, a female called Hoki in mine. The birds had just been ferried in from Pearl Island—at the entrance of Port Pegasus, on the eastern side of Stewart Island—their temporary home while 1396 hectare Whenua Hou Nature Reserve was being purged of any remaining vermin. Back in the mid 1980s, possums had been eradicated from Whenua Hou, and even egg stealing weka removed, and now, having been blitzed with 22 air dropped tonnes of poison pellets, the island had been declared a predator free “kākāpōrium”—the safest haven the birds would ever know. At the release site I opened the grille door of my cage and Hoki stomped out angrily, dragging her brown tail like a hand baggage trolley, and vanished in the undergrowth. Hoki was the star of several media appearances in the early 1990s when, rescued as a starving chick from Whenua Hou, she became the first ever kākāpō to be successfully hand reared. (She also featured on the cover of Issue 15 of New Zealand Geographic.) She is a free agent now, and tends to shun human company.

22.document_title: Kākāpō: Bird on the Brink - Conservation Efforts and Recovery Success
22.document_summary: This comprehensive document chronicles the remarkable conservation journey of the kākāpō, New Zealand's critically endangered flightless nocturnal parrot. Once abundant throughout New Zealand's islands, the species declined dramatically to just 18 males in Fiordland by the 1980s, with only 62 birds remaining by the early 2000s due to introduced predators and historical human hunting. The breakthrough came with the discovery of a 200-strong population on Stewart Island in 1977, including the first identified female since the early 1900s. The recovery program involved relocating all surviving kākāpō to predator-free island sanctuaries including Whenua Hou, Maud Island, and Little Barrier Island between 1982-1992. Key conservation innovations include helicopter access to remote populations, hand-rearing of chicks, inter-island transfers, electronic surveillance systems, and supplementary feeding programs. The species' unique lekking courtship behavior, where males inflate and boom low-frequency calls from elaborately maintained bowl-shaped arenas, was crucial to understanding their breeding patterns. Despite their appearance as ecological relics, kākāpō demonstrate adaptability and have become marathon survivors with lifespans potentially exceeding 60 years. The dedicated recovery team has achieved significant breeding successes, transforming wild kākāpō into managed refugees in their own homeland. The long-term vision includes establishing free-living, self-sustaining populations on subantarctic islands like Campbell Island, representing an unprecedented turning point in the species' survival.

23.text:
[Page 13] Female kākāpō are devoted mothers, but since they are all solo parents they must leave their eggs and chicks unguarded for long periods each night while they forage. Before the advent of mammalian predators, their absences were of little consequence, but ground level nests of eggs or chicks are like fast food outlets to rats and their ilk, and now the only safe place for kākāpō to breed is on predator free islands. Even in these havens, kākāpō workers take no chances, installing infrared movement sensors and surveillance cameras at all nests.

24.text:
[Page 13] Creating a stoat proof enclave for kiwi was a priority for McLennan, and he chose Puketukutuku because, like a fortress, it could be easily defended. Across the narrow neck of the peninsula he ran a double trapline, and then, with the help of a professional hunter, eradicated all the stoats inside the enclosure. He thus effectively turned the peninsula into a predator free island, a kiwi haven. In 1998, all of his chicks survived. [chapter break] The concept of island sanctuaries is not new. In 1894, Richard Henry masterminded the transfer of some 750 kiwi and kakapo to Resolution Island, in Fiordland. But he underestimated the enemy. Stoats swam across from the mainland, and 14 years of work was undone. Despite that setback, many of our offshore islands have now been turned into refuges for species that elsewhere are either extinct or extremely rare. Some of them were natural sanctuaries on account of their distance from the mainland or their inaccessibility, and only needed to have landings strictly controlled. Others, in the fashion of McLennan’s peninsula, have had to be restored through painstaking trapping of noxious animals and subsequent vigilance against reinvasion. Whatever their past, these islands now serve as insular aviaries, genetic safe houses which offer endangered species an evolutionary second chance, the opportunity of an assisted comeback. For kiwi, there is no more telling example than Kapiti, a sliver of mountainous, rain soused land lying off the west coast north of Wellington. Former home of Te Rauparaha, then the site of a whaling station, then a ne’er do well sheep farm, in 1897 the island was turned into a wildlife sanctuary. The cleared forest slowly grew back, and the resident caretakers methodically eradicated the vermin. Between 1980 and 1986, 22,500 possums were removed from this 2000 ha island, and a week before my visit the reserve was officially declared rat free.

24.document_title: Kiwi Conservation in New Zealand: Endangered Species, Predators, and Recovery Initiatives
24.document_summary: This comprehensive document examines the critical conservation challenges facing New Zealand's iconic kiwi bird and efforts to ensure its survival. The kiwi, once abundant with an estimated 12 million birds 1200 years ago, has declined to approximately 70,000 by 1995-96, declining at six percent annually. Key threats include introduced predators, particularly stoats (introduced in the 1880s), which are highly efficient hunters. Young kiwi face extreme vulnerability, with only 5% of chicks surviving their first few months until reaching 1200g at approximately 40 weeks. Conservation strategies encompass predator-free island sanctuaries (exemplified by Kapiti Island hosting over 1000 little spotted kiwi), mainland predator control grids targeting rats, mustelids, and feral cats, Operation Nest Egg captive breeding programs, and community-driven initiatives. Successful examples include Trounson Forest (over 200 kiwi since 1996) and Project Kiwi on the Coromandel Peninsula (improving chick survival from 5% to 87%). The document emphasizes ecosystem restoration over single-species protection, highlighting the resilience of North Island brown kiwi and the potential for coexistence between kiwi and human populations through targeted conservation strategies and public awareness campaigns.

It was later found that both had died of acute respiratory problems caused by the inhalation of food particles—a problem to which hand reared birds are very susceptible. The death of BJ saddened and frustrated everyone. Many hours were spent going back over their records, puzzling over where they might have gone wrong. “We’ve always been very, very cautious about the health of the chicks,” Sibley says. “Any rare species you take into captivity is a learning time. It’s sad to lose some, but it’s the only way to find out about them. All we can do is document their progress and have that on hand, should this exercise be repeated.” Those sentiments are echoed by Don Merton. “Events this year on Codfish Island, though tragic, have had a massive, positive impact on the recovery programme. We now have a better understanding of the pivotal role that an abundant, dependable food supply throughout the 10 12 month breeding cycle plays in successful breeding, and this has helped crystallise for me and others what we must do to save kakapo from extinction. The zoo has given us valuable new knowledge about the development of kakapo chicks, and has demonstrated that these birds can be hand reared.” The Department of Conservation has now accepted that intervention and monitoring are vital if the kakapo is to survive. The goals of the recovery programme are to boost the bird’s ultra slow reproductive rate and to enhance the survival of the young. Because Hoki has been hand reared she is the first kakapo to be comfortable in close proximity to humans. Says Don Merton, “We can watch her at close quarters and handle her without causing stress. She therefore provides opportunities for study which we have never had before. But, since she was raised to five weeks by kakapo on Codfish Island and was subsequently in the company of the other two chicks, her level of imprinting on humans is unlikely to compromise her ability to breed.” Supplementary feeding of kakapo on the four islands on which they are now found—Little Barrier, Maud, Mana and Codfish—will continue, and the department will support the females and their broods by controlling kiore and protecting the nests from natural disasters such as flooding. It will also redistribute the chicks if necessary—exactly the same management strategy applied so successfully to the last five black robins. But what of the zoo’s third chick? The good news is that this bird survived, and three weeks after Ks death was fit and healthy enough to be moved to her new home. On July 6, three months old and weighing 1.3kg, she was flown to Maud Island in the Marlborough Sounds to join two other female and three male kakapo. There she is being closely monitored in a 50 metre radius aviary in order to gain much needed information on behaviour and nutrition. When she reaches breeding age (in five to eight years) it is hoped she will form the nucleus of a captive population—a “safety net” should the wild populations fail. She may well be a deciding factor in saving the species, much as Old Blue, the Chatham Islands black robin, saved her species in the 1980s by being the only female to breed successfully during a critical four year period. Don Merton had nicknamed this bird Gale, after her grandmother Nora, the north wind, and her mother Zephyr, a gentle breeze.

25.document_title: The Kakapo of Codfish Island: Conservation, Hand-Rearing, and Species Recovery
25.document_summary: This comprehensive document chronicles critical conservation efforts to save the kakapo, one of the world's rarest parrots, from extinction. In March 1992, with only 50 kakapo remaining and just 15 known females, the Department of Conservation launched a rescue mission on Codfish Island after El Niño-driven gales threatened chick survival. Don Merton coordinated the transfer of critically underweight chicks to Auckland Zoo for artificial rearing, including a challenging rescue of two chicks from an inaccessible nest beneath a boulder. At Auckland Zoo, Curator Mick Sibley supervised intensive hand-rearing of three chicks—Alf, BJ, and Nora's foster chick—providing round-the-clock care with specialized feeding every two hours using soya bean-based porridge. The programme achieved remarkable success in raising multiple chicks together but faced tragic setbacks, including deaths from acute respiratory problems caused by food particle inhalation. The surviving chick Hoki was successfully transferred to Maud Island, serving as a crucial research subject and potential nucleus for a captive breeding population. The recovery programme gained invaluable insights into kakapo development and breeding requirements, with the Department of Conservation recognizing that intervention, monitoring, supplementary feeding, and nest protection are essential for species survival. This conservation effort mirrors successful strategies used with black robins, offering hope that kakapo can return from the brink of extinction.

26.document_title: Kākāpō get busy
26.document_summary: On Whenua Hou island sanctuary, kākāpō breeding is triggered by rimu tree masting events. Scientists predict masting based on temperature patterns and fruit development on branch tips. In autumn, 47% of rimu branch tips bore fruit, signaling a record-breaking 2019 breeding season. Ripe red fruit carpeted the ground, and kākāpō mothers fed it to their chicks, which grew faster than usual. Nearly every nest contained two or three chicks—unprecedented in observations. This mega-mega-mast event is exceptionally rare, combining simultaneous beech and rimu masting with unusually widespread distribution, resulting in almost every kākāpō bird breeding.

Fiordland is considered the prototype of community driven marine protection. Developed over 10 years, the Fiordland marine conservation strategy became enshrined in legislation in 2005. [sidebar 1] One of the principles developed by Fiordland was the ‘egg’ organisational model, in which local interests (tourism, fishing, conservation, runanga) form the central decision making yolk, while statutory agencies (councils, ministries, wider iwi, the Department of Conservation) occupy a supporting role as the surrounding white. This structure puts the stewardship responsibility squarely on the community. Another Fiordland principle bequeathed to Te Korowai was the idea of gifts and gains. Each interest group gives concessions in order to gain a desired outcome, expressed in Te Korowai’s vision of “a flourishing, rich and healthy environment where opportunities abound”—a.k.a. “more fish”. In Fiordland, commercial lobster fishers agreed to stop setting pots in the inner fjords and recreational fishers conceded lower bag limits. Perhaps the most important piece of advice Fiordland’s guardians gave the Kaikoura group was that to get buy in, you have to consult widely, listen carefully and not impose a time frame on the process. Nine years on, Kaikoura has the most innovative combination of marine protections anywhere in the country. [Chapter Break] It also has the strangest shaped marine reserve. It looks like an AK47 with its muzzle resting on State Highway 1, just north of Goose Bay.

27.document_title: Sea Change: Marine Management and Conservation in Aotearoa New Zealand
27.document_summary: This comprehensive collection examines New Zealand's marine resource management, conservation, and governance challenges. Key topics include Kaikoura's successful community engagement process resulting in marine protection legislation (2014) with whale and seal sanctuaries; Te Korowai and no-take reserves effectiveness; collaborative community-based management in Otago through taiapure customary areas; and marine biosecurity challenges from invasive species like Undaria seaweed and Mediterranean fanworms. The collection addresses the global fishing crisis where 75-85% of world fisheries are fully exploited or depleted, analyzing New Zealand's Quota Management System as a rare success with unintended consequences. Case studies illustrate how building trust across Māori, Pākehā, and tourism operators through shared dialogue enables sustainable coastal management. The documents emphasize New Zealand's fragmented marine governance (18 statutes, 14 agencies, six strategies) and advocate for integrated ocean policy, positioning ocean management as a defining environmental challenge.

28.document_title: The Lost Tribe of Fiordland: Māori History, Archaeology, and the Challenge to Colonial Narratives
28.document_summary: This comprehensive document explores the century-old legend of a "lost tribe" of Māori living in Fiordland, New Zealand, challenging colonial narratives through historical research, archaeological evidence, and indigenous perspectives. The narrative begins with a vivid reimagining of a Māori family's encounter with Captain Cook's Resolution in Tamatea/Dusky Sound in 1773, followed by European accounts of mysterious sightings and abandoned campsites. The document traces complex tribal dynamics between Kāi Tahu, Kāti Mamoe, and Waitaha peoples, including the legendary story of Tarewai, a Kāi Tahu warrior who survived inter-tribal conflicts and orchestrated a daring recovery of his whalebone patu. Through interviews with Kāi Tahu leaders and historians, the text argues that Māori groups in Fiordland were not isolated or lost, but rather engaged in long-standing hunting and harvesting traditions. Archaeological evidence—including rock shelters on Lee Island, tōtara baskets, bird-hunting implements, and abundant food remains—reveals thriving seasonal and semi-permanent communities with sophisticated material culture spanning centuries. The document challenges the "lost tribe" narrative, presenting instead resourceful Māori communities with access to abundant resources. It explains how sealing conflicts in the late 1700s and early 1800s created wariness of unknown boats. Fiordland remained an integral part of the southern Māori domain, with contemporary Kāi Tahu maintaining active kaitiaki (guardianship) roles and cultural connections to the region.

29.document_title: A Stitch in Time: Hihi Conservation, Nesting Behavior, and Management Strategies
29.document_summary: This comprehensive article explores the stitchbird (hihi), a rare endemic New Zealand honeyeater species that nearly went extinct. Once widespread in North Island forests, hihi disappeared from mainland New Zealand by 1883 due to forest clearance, introduced predators, and disease, surviving only on Little Barrier Island until conservation efforts began in the 1980s. The article details hihi characteristics including sexual dimorphism with striking males featuring black heads and yellow markings, and describes their unique behaviors: simple songs, cavity nesting, and flexible mating systems. Research reveals hihi can form conventional pairs or breeding groups and adjust social structures based on sex ratios. The article examines nesting behavior in detail, describing the male's role in prospecting nest sites and the female's 10-day nest construction using twigs, moss, and feathers. Females lay 3-5 eggs and incubate them for 14 days before chicks hatch. Conservation programs have translocated hihi to predator-free islands including Kapiti, Tiritiri Matangi, and Mokoia Island. Key management strategies include artificial feeders, artificial nest boxes, cross-fostering of clutches, mite control, and bird banding for population tracking. These interventions have proven effective in maintaining the hihi population, demonstrating that dedicated conservation efforts can ensure this species remains viable in New Zealand's biodiversity.

31.text:
[Page 1] If we’re serious about Predator Free 2050—about ridding New Zealand of every last rat, stoat and possum—then Fiordland poses its sternest backcountry test. If we can pull it off here, we can pull it off in any of our national parks. What makes this land so difficult—and so important? Lining up a limb, DOC biodiversity ranger Bex Jackson readies to fire a lead sinker into the canopy of a beech tree, site of a long tailed bat roost in the Iris Burn. Behind her, senior ranger Emmanuel Oyston holds the fishing line the pair will use to haul a climbing rope up to the roost. Since DOC began rodent control in 2014, this bat colony at Rocky Point has doubled in size. Looking at this part of the country, I’m not so sure. Fiordland National Park—12,600 square kilometres, barely scratched by road or track, suffering some of the planet’s foulest meteorology. It will be raining here for more than half the year—eight metres of rain disembogues annually over Milford Sound. Chill southerlies mean the forest is defeated at just 1000 metres of altitude: above is gaunt granite, some of the oldest rock in the land. The single biggest problem with pests in this park is getting to them. Glaciers have carved a confusing coastline—is that a passage or a peninsula? An island or an isthmus? You’ll need a boat, a good one—or a helicopter, and lots of fuel. Any endeavour here has to plan for immensity, hindrance, contingency and the consent of that funereal firmament.

31.document_title: Predator Free 2050 in Fiordland: Conservation Strategies and Wildlife Recovery in New Zealand
31.document_summary: This comprehensive document chronicles New Zealand's ambitious Predator Free 2050 initiative, with Fiordland National Park serving as the ultimate test case for eliminating invasive predators including rats, stoats, and possums. The narrative follows DOC rangers conducting fieldwork across challenging terrain, documenting conservation successes in long-tailed bat monitoring, whio (blue duck) recovery, and wildlife protection efforts. Despite receiving less than 1% of DOC's budget while occupying 15% of the conservation estate, Fiordland has achieved measurable results through aerial 1080 drops, sustained rat trapping, and innovative pest management strategies. Key programs include Andrew Smart's whio recovery programme using trained detection dogs, Lindsay Wilson's stoat and rat control operations across 65,000+ hectares using Goodnature A24 traps, and the Zero Invasive Predators (ZIP) initiative's "remove and protect" strategy. Success stories include doubled bat populations at Rocky Point (2014-2017) and increased kākā populations following aerial drops in Waitutu Forest. The document emphasizes that success depends on community support, social license, and local commitment alongside technological innovation, arguing that if conservation goals can be achieved in Fiordland's harsh conditions, they can succeed anywhere in New Zealand.

32.text:
[Page 1] Backyard explorers By discoveryexpeditions.co.nz Within our New Zealand bubble are some of the most dramatic, breathtaking landscapes in the world. Fiordland and Rakiura/Stewart Island offer an insight into the world as it once was: raw, pristine, largely uninhabited. Recognised by UNESCO World Heritage status, Fiordland National Park is characterised by steep, jumbled topography, a rugged coastline, dense rainforest and a dynamic climate. Further south, most of Rakiura/Stewart Island is part of Rakiura National Park, with settlement confined mainly to Oban, the only township. The island’s densely forested hills, tiny population and untouched coastline of rocky outcrops and golden sand beaches make it a natural refuge for marine and bird life. Few people venture to these isolated parts of the deep south, but leading tourism operator Real Journeys explores Fiordland and Rakiura/Stewart Island on Discovery Expeditions, sea voyages ranging from four to seven days. Some expeditions retrace Captain James Cook’s 1773 voyage around the Fiordland coastline and visit Māori and European historical sites that have played a part in New Zealand’s history. On Fiordland voyages, passengers have the opportunity to catch glimpses of the region’s abundant wildlife: bottlenose dolphins, Fiordland crested penguins and the occasional whale. Each voyage offers plenty of opportunities to disembark the vessel with daily nature hikes, kayaking, or tender craft activities. Throughout the trip, on board nature guides, who are experts on southern New Zealand, share knowledge of the flora, fauna and history of these regions. Travel in these parts is never predictable: the elements shape each trip, but being flexible yields rewards. Days are spent in isolated wilderness, taking in the sights and wildlife along the way.

33.document_title: Kaka Recovery in Fiordland
33.document_summary: This article documents the successful recovery efforts of South Island kaka, a native New Zealand forest parrot, in Fiordland National Park's Eglinton Valley. Historically abundant across New Zealand, kaka populations declined dramatically after stoats were introduced in the 1800s to control rabbits. Young kaka are particularly vulnerable to stoat predation during their three-month nesting period and first week after fledging. A low-cost stoat-control trial using egg-baited traps began in 1997, proving highly effective. During the severe "stoat plague summers" of 1999/2000 and 2000/2001, 15 pairs of kaka successfully reared 26 chicks with only two females killed by stoats, exceeding expectations. This demonstrates that targeted predator management can effectively protect kaka populations, offering hope for the species' future despite their current numbers being reduced to fewer than 100,000 from historical abundance.

34.document_title: Travels in a Wilderness: Fiordland's Untamed History and Modern Exploration
34.document_summary: This comprehensive collection explores Fiordland National Park in New Zealand through multiple interconnected narratives spanning historical settlement, wilderness survival, and contemporary tourism. The work chronicles the region's dramatic transformation from a frontier of dreams to a tourist destination, weaving together accounts of 19th-century pioneers like Dan and Alice McKenzie, Donald Sutherland, and the failed Jamestown settlement with modern-day experiences of travelers and conservationists. The narratives detail the harsh realities faced by early settlers—extreme weather, isolation, and devastating losses—contrasted against contemporary infrastructure developments including the Homer Tunnel and hydroelectric power generation. Key themes include the famous Milford Track (described as "The Finest Walk in the World"), conservation efforts such as rat eradication on Breaksea Island, and encounters with unique wildlife including Fiordland crested penguins, fur seals, and keas. The collection captures Fiordland's distinctive ecosystem—moss gardens, hydroponic forests, and tree avalanches—while exploring the tension between human ambition and nature's unforgiving terrain. Through vivid travel narratives and historical accounts, the work celebrates the resilience of those who inhabit this extraordinary landscape, from hermits and fishermen to modern trampers and tourists, ultimately portraying Fiordland as a place that has tested human determination across centuries.

35.document_title: Finding a Place for Wapiti in the Wild
35.document_summary: This article explores the century-long conflict between hunters and conservationists over wapiti (elk) management in New Zealand's Fiordland National Park. President Theodore Roosevelt gifted wapiti to New Zealand in 1905, but their presence has sparked ongoing debate. The article traces the wapiti's history: early legal protection, interbreeding with red deer, culling operations, and the dramatic "deer wars" of the 1970s involving helicopter hunters. A 1981 government relocation attempt and subsequent decision to keep the Crown Wapiti Herd in captivity disappointed hunters. Currently, the Fiordland Wapiti Foundation proposes a novel compromise: selective removal of red deer while protecting wapiti as a sport-hunting resource. This initiative represents a significant shift in the hunting lobby's approach and may offer a path toward reconciling conservation and hunting interests in managing Fiordland's ecosystem.

46.document_title: Four Kākāpō Move to New Home Off Fiordland
46.document_summary: Four male kākāpō have been relocated to Coal Island (Te Puka-Hereka) off Fiordland as part of the DOC Kākāpō Recovery Programme to address habitat shortage. The transfer aims to test whether the island can support a larger population ahead of a predicted 2026 breeding season. Only males were introduced due to the presence of stoats on the island. Coal Island was selected for its similar habitat and proximity to existing breeding islands. The Coal Island Trust has spent 20 years removing predators to create a haven for native species. This trial will help assess the island's viability for future kākāpō breeding and potentially open doors to additional sites. The programme is supported by Meridian Energy since 2016.

47.text:
[Page 1] Our Changing World: Looking to a wild future for kākāpō ByClaire Concannon Producer 2026 05 12 20:05:17+12:00 [wk_audio]738d77e3 14ff 48fa ba00 910b0b7242e8 Follow Follow Changing World on Apple, Spotify, iHeartRadio or wherever you listen to your podcasts There are 235 adult kākāpō alive today each of them has a name, a detailed family tree, a backstory, and a high tech transmitter that logs their activity. It's fun and it makes it easier for people to engage with these charismatic parrots. To talk about You Tube star Rakiura, and cliff top nesting adrenaline junkie mum Rimu and of course, the famously named Attenborough the kākāpō. But that's not the ultimate goal of the kākāpō recovery programme, says operations manager Deirdre Vercoe. "Our vision is to restore the mauri of the kākāpō, or the life force of the kākāpō. And that vision is to have kākāpō nameless, wandering through our forests, booming from the mountains and the hilltops around our cities and towns. Not to have a transmitter on, not to have a name and a well known history." Deidre Vercoe does a nighttime kākāpō chick check So this year, for the first time in the programme's 31 year history, which began when there were just 51 birds alive, some of the new kākāpō chicks will not be named. Normally naming happens when a chick has fledged and has passed the 150 day mark since they hatched. It's then that they get added to the adult kākāpō tally. Currently there are 92 new chicks alive. They may not all make it but there is hope that the population will reach over 300 birds by the end of this year. The next question is where to put them. Home birds or wanderers? Dr Andrew Digby sits in front of a laptop in a side small room off the large hut on Whenua Hou / Codfish island. On the screen in front of him is a map of the island populated with different coloured dots. Each represents an individual kākāpō, and movements around it's home range. And there are no gaps left. When it comes to how much space a kākāpō needs the estimate ranges between about 15 and 50 hectares says Andrew. Plus different kākāpō will have different requirements depending on the context a breeding female will need a different space than a juvenile, for example. Dr Andrew Digby it's prepares DNA samples in the Whenua Hou hut It's this sort of detail that Our Andrew is hoping to learn about through an ongoing study in which GPS loggers have been added to some birds' transmitters to get precise location data from different kākāpō across the seasons. Tracking kākāpō using their existing transmitters had given them some idea of their movements, but the GPS data is a whole new level of detail says Andrew. And it is resulting in a few surprises. The birds move around a lot more than they thought, and there seems to be an unexpected seasonal variation in the movements. The same GPS loggers were added to male birds released into the fenced ecosanctuary Sanctuary Mountain Maungatautari in July 2023. Some of those birds surprised everyone with their wanderlust, with a few making it out over the fence and into the surrounding farmland and roads. Fenced mainland sites like Sanctuary Mountain Maungatautari could be an option for future kākāpō habitat It was unexpected that they would travel so far, alarming to those caring for them, and it also pointed to one of the key questions Andrew would like answered. "One thing we don't know anything about, because we've always had kākāpō on islands, is what do they do when they get to big landscapes and how far can they move?...They could go massive distances. We just have no idea." As they move towards that future, that would present a monitoring challenge too, says Andrew. Currently the birds sport radio transmitters which log their activity and allow them to be tracked down. The breeding birds live on three islands with information networks and monitoring stations at every nest to keep real time tabs on the mums' movements. As the population grows, and they expand into new habitat, it's not feasible that the programme will be able to maintain this scale of monitoring. They will have to find another way to keep an eye on the birds, says Andrew, whether that could be eDNA monitoring, acoustic methods, or thermal drones. The kākāpō challenges The issue of where to put them is increasingly becoming an urgent challenge. Flightless, smelly and with a freezing threat response, they are particularly vulnerable to predation by introduced mammals. But, says Deirdre Vercoe, the programme has run out of "really high quality predator free island sites". Their likely next move will be to islands that have low densities of stoats or rats, while continuing investigations of fenced sites, mainland efforts like Predator Free South Westland, and always with an ever hopeful eye on Predator Free Rakiura efforts. Could a Predator Free Rakiura be a future home for kākāpō? A dearth of good quality habitat is not the only challenge that kākāpō face. The fertility rate of the birds is only about 50%, and disease is a constant threat. The team has learned that there are some management choices that can help with fertility, and Dr Andrew Digby hopes that ongoing investigations of the genome sequences of each kākāpō will tease out more answers too. It's the reason why, although the shift to kākāpō living truly wild has already begun, it will be a long transition says Deirdre Vercoe. "If you think about that number, even if we do get to 300 this year, there's still less kākāpō in the world than there are children at my daughter's school. You know, it's such a small number. So they are still vulnerable. We can't walk away just yet. We do have quite a long path to go. But we have made some really good progress." Sign up to the Our Changing World monthly newsletter for episode backstories, science analysis and more. Related

Despite progress toward a target of 300+ birds by year-end, the population remains vulnerable, necessitating continued intensive management.

49.document_title: Looking to a Wild Future for Kakapo
49.document_summary: This article discusses the kakapo recovery programme and its vision for the future of this endangered New Zealand parrot species. Currently, kakapo breed on three remote islands where each bird is equipped with a transmitter and closely monitored. The ultimate goal of the recovery programme is to restore the mauri (spiritual essence) of the kakapo by reintroducing them to forests as wild, unnamed birds. The article explores the steps needed to achieve this transition and examines how science can support kakapo safety during the reintroduction process.

50.text:
[Page 1] ByAlexia Russell Producer of The Detail 2025 11 20 06:42:08+13:00 Next year 2026 could be the year that the kākāpō breeding programme takes such a big leap forward that conservationists can finally take a step [wk_audio]aca70a6e 44d5 4344 8c1b b24cd9c093e0 Kākāpō numbers are so thin that all 237 of them have a name and a transmitter. The funny little tree climbing, owl like parrot has had intensive management over the last several decades, and its numbers have come back from the brink to give conservationists hope. And after a four year wait, they're preparing for what could be the biggest boom in kākāpō chicks yet, because next year is a mast year. That means rimu trees on the predator free islands where the birds live are about to burst with seeds, the bumper year that kākāpō wait for. "You have to wait around to get a good thing from kākāpō, but this year all the stars are in alignment," says Alison Ballance, who will be continuing her Kākāpō Files podcast series from December 16. It will also mark the first time that conservationists take a step back from such intensive methods of rescuing the critically endangered population. Those methods are resource heavy and not sustainable. So instead of incubating every egg, encouraging the females to lay more than one clutch, and providing supplementary feed, attention is turning to making sure the birds have enough room to spread their wings. The ultimate prize would be to turn Stewart Island/Rakiura into a pest free haven. "That's why we're looking with great interest at the Predator Free Rakiura programme," says Ballance, "where the community down there alongside DoC, and Zero Invasive Predators and Ngāi Tahu are starting to begin a programme where [they're asking] can they get rid of things like feral cats and rats on Stewart Island. "And if that was the case, then we could move kākāpō back to Rakiura and just stand back and let them be kākāpō in their own time frame, without the risk of predation." Conservationists know that back the risk of taking their eye off every egg and chick means they may lose more than they have in the past. They say while it's nerve wracking, it's essential. There will be fewer chick checks this season, more eggs hatching in nests rather than in incubators, and generally a move towards minimal intervention. The last mast years were in 2019 and 2022, so the big crop of chicks that arrived in 2019 will now be ready to breed. The females start from age five but it's possible some four year olds may also lay eggs. "There should be lots of new, young female kākāpō trying to breed this year which will be really exciting. The Department of Conservation's kākāpō recovery team tell me there's a bit of a wild card. There's 24 young females who are four years old and basically they [DoC] haven't had experience in the last 30 years of intensive kākāpō management of a breeding season that was four years apart. "So they're wondering ... maybe some of those precocious four year olds ... will they breed?" Thirty years ago there were 51 known kākāpō; 21 female and 30 male. Now we've got 84 females of breeding age, so that's about a 400 percent increase in potential chicks. Kākāpō are a long lived species, although we don't know exactly how long lived. There are definitely some birds in their late 40s and early 50s and there's speculation they could live up to 80 or even 100 and they keep laying until the end. Check out how to listen to and follow The Detail here. You can also stay up to date by liking us on Facebook or following us on Twitter.
