19.document_title: Eyes in the Land: Dune Lakes, Wetlands, and Indigenous Stewardship in Northland
19.document_summary: This comprehensive collection explores New Zealand's dune lakes and wetlands in Northland, examining their ecological significance and cultural importance to iwi communities. The articles document indigenous stewardship and scientific conservation efforts, featuring Lake Ngatu and NIWA scientist Paul Champion's research on unique flora including kuta sedge and tuatara plants. Key threats include invasive species such as hornwort, Egeria densa, Gambusia affinis, and grass carp. The collection emphasizes kaitiakitanga (environmental stewardship) as the foundation for restoration, incorporating ecological and cultural dimensions. Monitoring strategies using the LakeSPI bio-assessment tool are detailed, alongside management approaches including herbicide applications and freshwater mussel restoration. The narrative incorporates the Māori proverb "Te roto tāpokopoko, he wai whakahuihui, he pukenga ora" (a dune lake is an oasis that gathers and grows life) and explores te mana o te repo (the mana of wetlands) as intermediaries between Tāne (forests) and Tangaroa (seas). Community engagement initiatives like "Get to Know Your Dune Lake" days link lake conservation to Māori traditions and reconnect communities with their ancestral lands.

20.text:
[Page 9] If everyone foraged, would we strip the land? Wellington author Johanna Knox (Ngāti Tukorehe, Ngāti Raukawa ki te Tonga, Ngāti Ranginui, Tangata Tiriti), who wrote the book on foraging in New Zealand, thinks that eating the environment is a pretty good way of reconnecting with it. She reckons foraging could resurrect the idea of the commons—not just the tragedy of it. It could bring back the concept of places that are used and maintained by people for each other—and for future generations. That idea has been largely lost from the Pākehā world, but it’s remained intact in te ao Māori. Despite the destruction of traditional food gathering areas, despite the theft of land, the depletion of resources, and the loss of kōrero about how different species are prepared—despite all of that, the philosophy of how to gather food sustainably remains intact. It’s the concept of kaitiakitanga. “A big difference between Western environmentalism and Māori kaitiakitanga is how they see humans in the environment,” says Knox. “So in Pākehā conservation, it’s like, ‘We must keep these areas pristine. Nobody can take anything from here,’ but in te ao Māori it’s like, ‘People are part of the landscape. It’s a reciprocal relationship, so of course we’re taking stuff.’ McKenzie and Mikhail Shatura, head chef at downtown Auckland restaurant Ahi, taste the morning’s foraging. Shatura assembles a dish of quail, chickweed, huruhuru whenua and ureure. Foraged ingredients don’t form the bulk of a dish, says McKenzie, but they bring the flavours of a place onto the plate. “These are supporting characters,” he says. “So I come at foraging from the perspective that if you get right out there and involve yourself in the landscape—which means taking what you can, but respectfully and sustainably and at the same time giving back—that’s just a really good way to do things.” Raglan ecologist and rongoā practitioner Mahuru Wilcox (Ngāti Awa, Ngāti Ranginui) echoes Knox. She forages native plants traditionally used for medicinal purposes for her small business, Hau Botanicals. “How can you teach people to value something if you can’t connect to it?” she asks. “These [plants] are valued because they were important as kai or as rongoā or they were important as ancestors, as tūpuna. If you’re really thinking of our world around us as our tūpuna, as our ancestors, how would you respect your tūpuna? So using those principles for how you connect.” Even in the most densely populated parts of the city, plants move through the cycles of the year. Retreating into their roots to conserve water, springing forth with new shoots. Exploding into colour for a week or two. “It’s such a reminder in your daily life as a human that everything has a season,” says Wilcox. Over time, you start to see it: the living calendar, the shifts in weather and sunlight reflected in the plants changing, day by day, in all the gaps between the fixed and immobile parts of the city.

20.document_title: The Weed Eaters: Urban and Rural Foraging in New Zealand
20.document_summary: This comprehensive article explores the growing practice of foraging in New Zealand, examining both urban and rural contexts. The piece follows multiple narratives: in Auckland, forager Bella Burgess leads a Facebook community group on Maungawhau/Mount Eden, teaching participants to identify and harvest edible wild plants including vetch, wild brassica, pūhā, nasturtium, oxalis, and onion weed while emphasizing ethical foraging practices. In Canterbury, Peter Langlands scouts for elderflower and wild parsnips for restaurants, demonstrating how roadsides and berms provide abundant biodiversity and foraged ingredients. The article features interviews with professional foragers like Nate McKenzie and Rico Birndt who maintain sustainable harvesting practices. It highlights the cultural and philosophical dimensions of foraging, connecting it to Māori philosophy of kaitiakitanga—a reciprocal relationship with the environment—and contrasting this with Western conservation approaches. The piece explores the underlying human desire for self-reliance and independence from modern systems, noting how the surge in foraging interest during COVID-19 lockdowns reflects deeper needs for connection and resilience. The article showcases how edible plants grow abundantly in plain sight throughout New Zealand's towns and cities, challenging cultural hesitation about harvesting from public spaces while advocating for sustainable practices and "feral parks" instead of manicured lawns.

It is not so much owned as occupied, an assessment which fosters a sense guardianship—kaitiakitanga—on behalf of future generations. The land is to be used, but not abused. Above all, its living essence is to be respected. of

21.document_title: Between a Rock and a Hard Place
21.document_summary: This article examines the contentious Denniston Plateau mining debate, which pits resource extraction against environmental preservation. With 6.1 million tonnes of bituminous coal beneath a 150-hectare site, the proposed open-cast mine would generate 14 million tonnes of CO2 emissions when burned—equivalent to New Zealand's annual dairy herd emissions. The article explores the tension between economic benefits ($46 million in salaries for a struggling West Coast region) and environmental costs, including mercury, selenium, arsenic emissions, and climate change contributions. It presents three perspectives: exploitation versus preservation, and a Māori concept of land as taonga (treasure and resource), emphasizing guardianship (kaitiakitanga) and respect for the land's living essence. The author questions whether this traditional approach might offer a less-destructive path to prosperity.

22.text:
[Page 2] These are among the challenging terms of reference for the panel deciding the fate of stewardship land. Should it be entirely protected—no use permitted—or entirely exploited? Other voices, predominantly Māori ones, are pointing out that perhaps this all or nothing approach isn’t necessary, and that, historically, the concept of kaitiakitanga allowed for both protection and utility, even commerce. You could have your birds and eat them, too.

22.document_title: The Art of Weaving
22.document_summary: This essay explores the tension between environmental protection and resource exploitation in New Zealand. The author argues that the traditional binary approach of designating areas for total protection or total exploitation is outdated. Drawing on Māori concepts of kaitiakitanga (stewardship), the piece advocates for a balanced approach that allows both protection and sustainable use of natural resources. The author acknowledges that reducing humanity's environmental footprint requires difficult choices and collective action, emphasizing the need for respectful dialogue and integration of diverse knowledge systems to develop a more sustainable approach to living in Aotearoa (New Zealand).

23.text:
[Page 4] Ngāti Kuri, another iwi from the Far North, has been on a similar journey of restoration. Wayne Petera, Ngāti Kuri’s coordinator for wai māori (freshwater), tells me that his people are awakening to the importance of the dune lakes in their rohe, and to their role as kaitiaki. Petera says the kaitiaki responsibility is an ancestral mantle laid on the shoulders of each generation. “We have no choice in the matter,” he says. “Mana requires that we act.” On the basis that Ngāti Kuri has existed for close to a thousand years, Petera says the iwi has decided it must have a thousand year vision for itself and its environment, lakes included. “We recognise that if we are the people we say we are, then we have a deep responsibility to ensure the life and well being of all of these ecological gems,” he says.

24.document_title: Blue Carbon in New Zealand: Fiords, Coastal Wetlands, and Seagrass Restoration
24.document_summary: This comprehensive collection examines New Zealand's blue carbon ecosystems and their role in climate regulation. New Zealand's fiords, particularly Doubtful Sound and Dusky Sound, store approximately 2.24 billion tonnes of carbon—about one percent of the world's seabed carbon. These fiords bury organic carbon faster than similar ecosystems worldwide due to unique geography, steep valleys, heavy rainfall, and anaerobic mud conditions. Scientists at the Cawthron Institute are pioneering seed-based seagrass restoration methods, discovering that Zostera muelleri flowers more frequently than previously believed. Seagrass ecosystems capture carbon 55 times faster than tropical rainforests and store four times more carbon per hectare in soils. Coastal wetland restoration projects like Te Wahapū o Waihī integrate mātauranga Māori with coastal ecology, with five iwi collaborating on restoration efforts. Seaweed research reveals varying decomposition rates in deep-sea environments, though scientists raise concerns about accurately measuring seaweed's carbon removal potential. The research emphasizes protecting natural carbon sinks while addressing legal complexities involving Māori rights and rangatiratanga, highlighting kaitiakitanga (stewardship) and cultural significance of coastal ecosystem restoration.

25.text:
[Page 16] [Chapter Break] On an autumn afternoon in early March, I pull off State Highway 6 just south of Hokitika, into the carpark at Mananui Bush. Powerlines stretch overhead, curving north across fields of fodder beet. Lake Mahinapua lies across the highway to the east, hidden by thick coastal bush. Through the open window, in the quiet after I switch off the engine, I hear the faint boom and hiss of Te Tai o Rehua, the Tasman Sea. A group of Pākehā men and women stand waiting in the small clearing beneath a fierce sun. Between the laughter and the bags of kai lined up in the back of a nearby van, they could be friends on a package tour except for the hefty spiral bound books in their hands and the two huge maps spread on the ground. Clifton is kneeling on the ground, pointing at the map. The others, ranged in a semicircle, are conservation ecologist Bill Lee, veteran conservation leader Jo Breese, archaeologist Katharine Watson and landscape architect Philip Blakely. COVID related work disruptions have kept mātauranga expert Marama Muru Lanning (Waikato, Ngāti Maniapoto, Ngāti Whātua) in Auckland today. On paper their depth of experience is intimidating; in person they’re attentive and intelligent, though a little fatigued. It’s their final day together in the field—they’ve visited around 90 per cent of the stewardship land parcels, and flown over those too big to take in on foot. They’ve travelled from southern Kohaihai in Kahurangi right down to Fiordland. I ask how it’s been. “Intense,” several say at once. “Bill is our resident scientist,” Breeze says, “and he’s been recording our entrances and exits to vehicles. Our record is 54 movements in a day.” “Be careful how you phrase that,” Lee says to me, straight faced. The grazed area in the photograph above is stewardship land, at the mouth of the Karamea River, at Māori Point. It’s blocks like these that are potential candidates for an assessment of low or no conservation values, which could lead to their sale. Climate advocates argue such blocks should be reforested instead. That intensity has largely come from the volume of complex information. “We rely heavily on these,” Neil says, brandishing his Conservation Value Report for the area: a compendium of DOC’s information about each block, grouped into sections such as mātauranga, ecology, landscape, recreation and heritage. Depending on the dominant values in a block, different experts have taken the lead, as the group analyses the values against what they find on the ground, debates the merits of different classifications, talks the issues through with local DOC rangers. I ask how it worked if they needed more information.

25.document_title: Stewardship Land Reclassification in New Zealand: Conservation, Māori Rights, and the Old Ghost Road
25.document_summary: This comprehensive document collection examines New Zealand's stewardship land—nine percent of Aotearoa's total land area—through interconnected narratives spanning conservation policy, indigenous rights, and economic development. The collection begins with the Old Ghost Road project in the Mokihinui Gorge, illustrating how stewardship land's lower protection status both threatened and enabled conservation initiatives, ultimately generating $4 million annually for local communities after Meridian Energy abandoned its proposed dam project. The documents trace the government's 2021 fast-tracked reclassification process, which proposed appointing expert panels to assess stewardship land within eight months. This initiative sparked significant controversy, particularly from Ngāi Tahu iwi, who filed urgent High Court proceedings citing consultation breaches and Treaty of Waitangi violations. The historical context reveals how the Crown's 1859 acquisition of the West Coast from Poutini Ngāi Tahu for £300 left the iwi with only 4,000 hectares despite claiming 151,757 hectares, with 87% of their territory now managed by DOC with minimal iwi input. The collection explores the tension between traditional conservation frameworks and contemporary approaches that integrate mātauranga (Māori knowledge) and recognize Māori cultural values extending beyond preservation to include economic and commercial use on ancestral land. Through case studies such as Lake Mahinapua, the documents examine how mana whenua and national assessment panels are collaboratively developing integrated conservation models that respect rangatiratanga while addressing concerns about mining interests and the Stockton Coal Mine on Denniston Plateau.

29.text: When the family house was washed away by a flood in the Waimana River, Maui Te Pou built a whare high on the side of the Matahi valley, which is now a sleep-out for his 12-year-old granddaughter Taonga Freedom Teaonui. The girl—whose first name means ‘treasure’—is being raised in the whāngai tradition, in which children are informally adopted by other whānau members, often grandparents, who instil in them Tūhoe values and beliefs known as tikanga. “Our total tikanga boils down to one word: respect,” says Te Pou.“You respect me, I respect you—we’re off to a good start.”

It is the whakataukī (Māori proverb) that means most to Māori data, AI and technology ethicist Dr Karaitiana Taiuru (Ngāi Tahu, Ngāti Kahungunu, Ngāti Toa). Translated to English, it means "the ability to create and control our destiny for generations to come". It links in well with his work and family life, Taiuru told RNZ Nights. For his work, it reminded Taiuru why he still does what he does and that there was a new generation of children who will not know life without AI and it was "our role to create the new normal for them". Taiuru applies a te ao Māori perspective to AI. https://www.rnz.co.nz/national/programmes/nig hts/audio/2018930609/whakatauki of the week with karaitiana taiuru Listen to the full interview on Nights "We already know that internationally, there's bias against minority peoples so what I do, in conjunction with international best practices with artificial intelligence and other technologies, is bring that Māori voice and Te Tiriti o Waitangi considerations to play." There were "a number" of cultural values that needed to be considered in terms of AI, he said. Many Māori have moko (facial tattoos) so understanding how that was considered with facial technologies was a big factor. In his personal life, the whakataukī applied to his whānau. [Page 1] 2024 01 29 21:53:12+13:00 Anton Matthews is the director of Hustle Group, a company operating a bunch of restaurants and catering companies in Ōtautahi Christchurch. He's also a big advocate for people learning te reo Māori, also running online course Normalising Te Reo Māori. In the next in a weekly series, he shares a favourite whakataukī, or traditional Māori aphorism, with Emile Donovan. Ko te amorangi ki mua, ko te hāpai ō ki muri The leader at the front and the workers behind the scenes This simple whakataukī, or Māori proverb, is a multi layered favourite of Matthews. While he was fortunate to grow up immersed in te ao Māori, including being educated at kohanga reo and kura kaupapa, Matthews tells Nights anyone exposed to a lot of te reo Māori quickly learns that it’s a language rich in metaphor. “There’s the literal meaning of whatever has been said, but it often takes a couple of years (sometimes it never actually dawns on us), but there is a hidden meaning there as well. “That’s what I love about whakataukī is that yep, there's that kind of surface layer literally, what is the person saying? But what's the hidden meaning? What are they really trying to explain or what sort of message or idea are they trying to convey when they use the whakataukī? That's the beauty of language, not just te reo Māori, but any language has those kinds of beautiful nuances, I think.” Matthews says he loves all sorts of different whakataukī for different reasons and occasions, but his favourite is particularly appropriate to his work in the hospitality sector. Ko te amorangi ki mua, ko te hāpai ō ki muri has two parts to it, Matthews says. Amorangi is a term that refers to recognised iwi leaders, the ones who are front and centre when leading a pōwhiri, or welcome, onto the marae. “These are the familiar faces that everyone kind of knows… these people are highly respected. They have a lot of mana. We look to them when we need guidance.” Te hāpai ō referred to in the second part of the whakataukī is the complete opposite, Matthews says.

This multi-layered aphorism illustrates the duality and balance fundamental to te ao Māori. The amorangi represents recognized iwi leaders at the front, while te hāpai ō (food carriers) work behind the scenes. 45.text:
[Page 1] Historically, Māori did not have a sole leader over all the people, says historian Vincent O'Malley. O'Malley, who has just released a new book The Invasion of Waikato, Te Riri ki Tainui, spoke to Saturday Morning about the history of the Kiingitanga after its seventh monarch, Kiingi Tuheitia Pootatau Te Wherowhero, died early on Friday. After a number of Māori went to England and met Queen Victoria, they advocated for a Māori monarch, he said. "In Māori culture, there wasn't really this notion of a single leader. You saw that in some other Pacific cultures you know, Tonga, Hawaii and so on but it was something entirely new here." https://www.rnz.co.nz/national/programmes/saturday/audio/2018 953559/vincent o malley reflects on kiingi tuuheitia The Māori monarch was not set up to take away power from Queen Victoria, but rather to complement her, said O'Malley. But the wider context was that in the 1850s, settler numbers in Aotearoa were surging. In 1854, the first Parliament convened in Auckland with no Māori members, and very few Māori men were eligible to vote at the time. Members of Parliament had to own property from the Crown, and while Māori owned land, very few had a piece of paper from the Crown declaring they were the land owners, he explained. "Tainui at this time [were] developing a very prosperous economy based on feeding the settlers in Auckland, even exporting wheat to Australia, California and elsewhere," said O'Malley. But that way of life was under threat because of the exclusion of Māori from Parliament. "So that's really the context in which the kiingitanga is established in 1858. Pootatau Te Wherowhero is raised up as the first Māori King and Tuheitia is, of course, a direct descendant and the seventh Māori monarch," he said. In the beginning, the kiingitanga was seen as a "positive development" by some Pākehā. In fact, Tainui were seen as the most loyal iwi in the country and it was "inconceivable" that Tainui would be seen as rebels. "They were regarded as extremely loyal, in terms of their relationship with the Crown and with settlers," said O'Malley. But by 1858, Māori were being outnumbered by the settlers for the first time, setting the scene for the invasion of Waikato in 1863. "You had a huge number of British imperial troops arrive in the country and the context here is that in the 1860s, Britain is the world's sole superpower so Māori are fighting this great power that has the latest weapons and technology," he said. "Māori have none of that ... the British have armoured plated steamers and Māori have wooden canoes and really, this should have been no contest. "So this is what Māori [were] up against during the New Zealand Wars in the 1860s." Related

45.document_title: Monarchy a 'new' idea for Māori, historian says
45.document_summary: Historian Vincent O'Malley discusses the establishment of the Kiingitanga (Māori monarchy) in 1858, explaining that monarchy was a novel concept for Māori who historically lacked a single leader. The institution was created following Māori delegations to England and meetings with Queen Victoria, designed to complement rather than challenge Crown authority. Established during a period of rapid European settlement and Māori political exclusion—the 1854 Parliament had no Māori members—the Kiingitanga represented a response to threats to Māori prosperity and autonomy. Initially viewed positively by some Pākehā, particularly regarding Tainui's loyalty, the institution emerged amid growing settler dominance. By 1858, settlers outnumbered Māori for the first time, setting the stage for the 1863 Waikato invasion, where Māori faced British imperial forces with superior weaponry and technology.

1.fileDescription: Kaitiakitanga is a foundational Māori concept of guardianship and environmental stewardship rooted in the worldview that humans are part of nature. A kaitiaki is a guardian recognized by tangata whenua to care for natural areas such as lakes, forests, and waterways. Traditional conservation practices include temporary rāhui (resource restrictions), use of the lunar calendar (maramataka) for planting and harvesting, sustainable hunting and fishing, and blessing of mauri stones by tohunga (priests). Key spiritual concepts include mana (spiritual power), tapu (spiritual restriction), and mauri (life force). Today, kaitiakitanga is experiencing renewal as iwi (tribes) restore ecosystems and apply traditional knowledge in modern contexts. Practical examples include Ngāi Tahu's guardianship of pounamu resources, Ngāti Toa's fishery restoration at Pukerua Bay, and multi-tribal efforts to stop river pollution and protect endangered species. The document outlines challenges in collaborating with non-Māori stakeholders and details legislative frameworks such as the Resource Management Act 1991 and Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004 that incorporate kaitiakitanga principles. Kaitiakitanga offers perspectives on environmental stewardship and kinship with nature, enabling Māori to fulfill ancestral responsibilities while contributing to broader environmental sustainability.

chunkHighlights.text: By Te Ahukaramū Charles Royal

Understanding kaitiakitanga Kaitiakitanga means guardianship and
protection. It is a way of managing the environment, based on the Māori world view. A kaitiaki is a guardian. This can be a person or group that cares for an area such as a lake or forest. They are given that role by the local iwi . Māori world view In the Māori world view, people are closely connected to the land and nature. Kaitiakitanga is based on this idea of humans as part of the natural world. Traditional practices In the past, people followed traditional practices when they were hunting, fishing, growing or finding food. These helped them to care for the environment. They included: temporary bans (rāhui) on taking food from an area using the lunar calendar (maramataka) to decide when to plant and harvest taking only what was needed hunting and fishing only for food, not as sport using bird snares at the right time – for example, not when the birds were breeding. Mana, tapu and mauri Mana means spiritual power. If a forest has mana , it will have plenty of flowers, fruit and birds. Tapu can mean spiritual restriction. Sometimes rāhui (restrictions) are needed to help the mana of the forest. A rāhui might stop people taking birds, fish or fruit from a certain area, or at a certain time. Mauri means life force. This must be protected in forests, rivers, gardens, lakes and the sea. Special mauri stones, which tohunga (priests) said prayers over, were used to preserve this force. Kaitiakitanga today Today there is growing interest in kaitiakitanga. Iwi are restoring their environment and culture, and using traditional ideas in the modern world. Ngāi Tahu are guardians of pounamu (greenstone) in the South Island. Te Āti Awa ki Taranaki made a claim to the government to stop pollution in their fishing areas. Four iwi (Ngāti Kahungunu, Rangitāne, Muaūpoko and Ngāti Raukawa) have come together to stop the Manawatū River being polluted. The Te Rarawa people are working to save the kūkupa (New Zealand pigeon). Kaitiakitanga has also been included in some laws,
such as the Resource Management Act 1991.
Kaitiakitanga means guardianship, protection, preservation or sheltering. It is a way of managing the environment, based on the traditional Māori world view.

chunkHighlights.text: Tiaki

The word tiaki is the basis of the longer word kaitiakitanga. Tiaki means to guard. It also means to preserve, foster, protect and shelter. So, notions of care and protection are at the heart of kaitiakitanga, and give

chunkHighlights.text: Legislation

Kaitiakitanga has been included in some legislation. The Resource Management Act 1991 aims to enable sustainable management of environmental resources. It states that people managing resources under the act must take kaitiakitanga into account.

The act defines kaitiakitanga as ‘the exercise of guardianship by the tangata whenua of an area in accordance with tikanga Māori in relation to natural and physical resources; and includes the ethic of stewardship’.
Kaitiakitanga was also included in the Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004, where it has the same meaning.

Kaitiakitanga allows Māori today to feel they are meeting the responsibilities and hopes of their ancestors. It also allows non-Māori to reflect on the notion of kinship with nature, and how this idea might be useful in an environmentally threatened world.

[Page 1] In traditional Māori society, children were seen as belonging to, and being the responsibility of, the wider whānau and hapū . Children quickly learnt to identify with their hapū community. The natural parents were not the sole caregivers child raising involved grandparents, uncles, aunts, great uncles and great aunts. This collective responsibility and these kinship ties ensured the safety and welfare of children, who were seen as representing the future heritage of the tribe. This principle was conveyed in the proverb: ‘He kai poutaka me kinikini atu, he kai poutaka me horehore atu, mā te tamaiti te iho’ (pinch off a bit of the potted bird, peel off a bit of the potted bird, but the inside is for the child save the best for the child).

She reckons foraging could resurrect the idea of the commons—not just the tragedy of it. It could bring back the concept of places that are used and maintained by people for each other—and for future generations. That idea has been largely lost from the Pākehā world, but it’s remained intact in te ao Māori. But what's the hidden meaning? What are they really trying to explain or what sort of message or idea are they trying to convey when they use the whakataukī? That's the beauty of language, not just te reo Māori, but any language has those kinds of beautiful nuances, I think.” Matthews says he loves all sorts of different whakataukī for different reasons and occasions, but his favourite is particularly appropriate to his work in the hospitality sector. After a number of Māori went to England and met Queen Victoria, they advocated for a Māori monarch, he said. "In Māori culture, there wasn't really this notion of a single leader. You saw that in some other Pacific cultures you know, Tonga, Hawaii and so on but it was something entirely new here." https://www.rnz.co.nz/national/programmes/saturday/audio/2018 953559/vincent o malley reflects on kiingi tuuheitia The Māori monarch was not set up to take away power from Queen Victoria, but rather to complement her, said O'Malley. But the wider context was that in the 1850s, settler numbers in Aotearoa were surging. In 1854, the first Parliament convened in Auckland with no Māori members, and very few Māori men were eligible to vote at the time. Members of Parliament had to own property from the Crown, and while Māori owned land, very few had a piece of paper from the Crown declaring they were the land owners, he explained. "Tainui at this time [were] developing a very prosperous economy based on feeding the settlers in Auckland, even exporting wheat to Australia, California and elsewhere," said O'Malley. But that way of life was under threat because of the exclusion of Māori from Parliament. "So that's really the context in which the kiingitanga is established in 1858. ## Te Tikanga o Kaitiakitanga

Ko 'kaitiakitanga' tētahi kupu Māori whakahirahira. I roto i te reo Pākehā, ko te tikanga: **guardianship, protection, preservation, and stewardship** — arā, te tiaki i te taiao me ngā taonga katoa.

### Ōna Pūtake — The Word's Roots

Ko te puna o tēnei kupu ko te kupu **'tiaki'**, arā: to guard, to preserve, to foster, to protect, and to shelter. Ko te **'kai-'** he tāhuhu e tohu ana i tētahi tangata e mahi ana i taua mahi. Nō reira, ko te **kaitiaki** he tangata, he rōpū rānei e tiaki ana i tētahi wāhi, tētahi taonga rānei [[1]](cite://1/1).

### He Tirohanga Māori — The Māori World View

E ai ki ngā kōrero, ko te tūāhuatanga o kaitiakitanga ko te hononga hōhonu o te tangata ki te whenua me te taiao [[2]](cite://2/1). I roto i te ao Māori, ehara te tangata i te kaiwhakahaere o te taiao — engari he wāhanga o te taiao tonu ia [[3]](cite://3/1).

Ko ngā atua o te ao tūroa ngā kaitiaki tuatahi rawa. Ko Tāne, arā, ko ia te atua o te ngahere, ōna kaitiaki tuatahi. Nō reira, ko ngā hapū me ngā whānau e tiaki ana i ō rātou wāhi, e whai ana i taua tauira [[4]](cite://4/1).

### Ngā Tikanga o Mua — Traditional Practices

I ngā rā o mua, i mahi ngā tūpuna i ēnei tikanga hei tiaki i te taiao:

- **Rāhui** — he aukati mō ētahi wāhi, ētahi wā hoki, kia hou anō te ora o taua wāhi [[3]](cite://3/2)
- **Maramataka** — he maramataka lunar e ārahina ana ngā mahi māra, hī ika, me ērā atu [[3]](cite://3/3)
- **Mauri** — ko te mauri o ngā ngahere, awa, roto me te moana me tiaki, me ārahina rānei e ngā tohunga [[3]](cite://3/4)
- Ko te tango noa iho i ngā rawa kia ōrite ki ngā hiahia, kaua te rawa katoa [[3]](cite://3/5)

### Kaitiakitanga i Ēnei Rā — Today

E kīia ana e Kennedy Warne, he "stewardship far deeper than resource management" — he mea tiaki, he mea whakanui i te ao [[5]](cite://5/1). He rereke tēnei i te tiaki taiao ā-Pākehā, i te mea ko te tangata Māori he wāhanga o te taiao, ā, he hononga tauutuutu tō rāua [[6]](cite://6/1).

Kua whakaurua hoki a kaitiakitanga ki roto i ngā ture o Aotearoa. I raro i te **Resource Management Act 1991**, ko tōna tikanga whaimana: *"the exercise of guardianship by the tangata whenua of an area in accordance with tikanga Māori in relation to natural and physical resources; and includes the ethic of stewardship"* [[7]](cite://7/1).

### He Mea Whānui — Broader than the Environment

Ehara a kaitiakitanga i te tiaki taiao anake. Ka taea hoki te tono ki ngā taonga tūturu pēnei i ngā korowai, ngā mere pounamu, ngā pukapuka whakapapa hoki. Ko te kaitiaki e tiaki ana i ēnei mō te katoa o ōna uri [[8]](cite://8/1).

Nō reira, ko kaitiakitanga he ara whakaaro me he ara mahi — he mea tiaki, he mea whakanui, he mea haumaru i ngā taonga katoa mō ngā uri whakatipu [[9]](cite://9/1).

He pātai āu: E hiahia ana koe ki te mōhio ake mō ngā tikanga o mua (traditional practices) i whakamahia hei tiaki i te taiao?

1.text:
[Page 1] By Te Ahukaramū Charles Royal Understanding kaitiakitanga Kaitiakitanga means guardianship and protection. It is a way of managing the environment, based on the Māori world view. A kaitiaki is a guardian. This can be a person or group that cares for an area such as a lake or forest. They are given that role by the local iwi . Māori world view In the Māori world view, people are closely connected to the land and nature. Kaitiakitanga is based on this idea of humans as part of the natural world. Traditional practices In the past, people followed traditional practices when they were hunting, fishing, growing or finding food. These helped them to care for the environment. They included: temporary bans (rāhui) on taking food from an area using the lunar calendar (maramataka) to decide when to plant and harvest taking only what was needed hunting and fishing only for food, not as sport using bird snares at the right time for example, not when the birds were breeding. Mana, tapu and mauri Mana means spiritual power. If a forest has mana , it will have plenty of flowers, fruit and birds. Tapu can mean spiritual restriction. Sometimes rāhui (restrictions) are needed to help the mana of the forest. A rāhui might stop people taking birds, fish or fruit from a certain area, or at a certain time. Mauri means life force. This must be protected in forests, rivers, gardens, lakes and the sea. Special mauri stones, which tohunga (priests) said prayers over, were used to preserve this force. Kaitiakitanga today Today there is growing interest in kaitiakitanga. Iwi are restoring their environment and culture, and using traditional ideas in the modern world. Ngāi Tahu are guardians of pounamu (greenstone) in the South Island. Te Āti Awa ki Taranaki made a claim to the government to stop pollution in their fishing areas. Four iwi (Ngāti Kahungunu, Rangitāne, Muaūpoko and Ngāti Raukawa) have come together to stop the Manawatū River being polluted. The Te Rarawa people are working to save the kūkupa (New Zealand pigeon). Kaitiakitanga has also been included in some laws, such as the Resource Management Act 1991. Kaitiakitanga means guardianship, protection, preservation or sheltering. It is a way of managing the environment, based on the traditional Māori world view.

1.document_title: Kaitiakitanga: Māori Guardianship, Environmental Stewardship, and Traditional Conservation Practices
1.document_summary: Kaitiakitanga is a foundational Māori concept of guardianship and environmental stewardship rooted in the worldview that humans are part of nature. A kaitiaki is a guardian recognized by tangata whenua to care for natural areas such as lakes, forests, and waterways. Traditional conservation practices include temporary rāhui (resource restrictions), use of the lunar calendar (maramataka) for planting and harvesting, sustainable hunting and fishing, and blessing of mauri stones by tohunga (priests). Key spiritual concepts include mana (spiritual power), tapu (spiritual restriction), and mauri (life force). Today, kaitiakitanga is experiencing renewal as iwi (tribes) restore ecosystems and apply traditional knowledge in modern contexts. Practical examples include Ngāi Tahu's guardianship of pounamu resources, Ngāti Toa's fishery restoration at Pukerua Bay, and multi-tribal efforts to stop river pollution and protect endangered species. The document outlines challenges in collaborating with non-Māori stakeholders and details legislative frameworks such as the Resource Management Act 1991 and Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004 that incorporate kaitiakitanga principles. Kaitiakitanga offers perspectives on environmental stewardship and kinship with nature, enabling Māori to fulfill ancestral responsibilities while contributing to broader environmental sustainability.

[Page 11] Legislation Kaitiakitanga has been included in some legislation. The Resource Management Act 1991 aims to enable sustainable management of environmental resources. It states that people managing resources under the act must take kaitiakitanga into account. The act defines kaitiakitanga as ‘the exercise of guardianship by the tangata whenua of an area in accordance with tikanga Māori in relation to natural and physical resources; and includes the ethic of stewardship’. Kaitiakitanga was also included in the Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004, where it has the same meaning.

13.document_title: New Zealand Rivers: Comprehensive Guide to Geography, Ecology, Culture, and Conservation
13.document_summary:
This comprehensive document explores New Zealand's extensive river systems across both the North and South Islands, covering over 180,000 kilometres of mapped rivers including the Waikato (425 km) and Clutha (largest by volume). It details river formation through high rainfall, glacial activity, and geological processes, describing distinct river types: deep, fast-flowing rivers in the North Island hills and wide, braided rivers in the South Island's east.

The document emphasizes the profound cultural significance of rivers to Māori people, including their roles in exploration, transportation, food sources, and spiritual traditions involving taniwha (river spirits). It documents European settlement impacts including military conquest, transport use, 19th-century gold rushes, and industrial/agricultural pollution.

The content examines ecological transformations over two centuries, detailing how introduced species like rainbow trout, brown trout, and salmon impacted native fish populations. It describes the creation of eight artificial lakes along the Waikato River through hydroelectric dams (1945-1970s) and habitat loss through forest clearance. Conservation efforts are discussed, from late 19th-century catchment protection through the 1941 Soil Conservation Act to the 1981 Wild and Scenic Rivers Amendment protecting 12 rivers.

Modern challenges including invasive species like didymo, dairy farming impacts on water quality, and off-road vehicle use are addressed. The document highlights Māori guardianship cases involving the Waikato and Whanganui rivers, explores rivers' cultural significance through 19th and 20th-century art, literature, and film, and examines contemporary management practices including jet boat tourism, riparian protection through native tree planting, and regional council monitoring.

15.document_title: Taranaki Region: Comprehensive Geography, History, Geology, Economy, and Cultural Heritage
15.document_summary: This comprehensive document provides an extensive overview of New Zealand's Taranaki region. The region is dominated by Taranaki Maunga (Mt. Egmont), a 2,518-metre cone-shaped volcano with significant spiritual importance to Māori. Geologically, the area features a complex volcanic history spanning 20 million years with four major volcanic centers and diverse fossil fauna from the Pliocene period. Māori settlement dates to 1250-1300 CE, with eight iwi developing distinctive wood-carving traditions. European settlement began in 1841 with the Plymouth Company, leading to the Taranaki Wars (1860-1881) that resulted in over 700 deaths. The region's economy has been built on dairy farming since the 1880s, with Fonterra processing 14 million litres daily, supplemented by oil and gas production from the 1960s onward. Taranaki is renowned as "the garden of New Zealand" due to its fertile volcanic soils supporting agriculture and horticulture. The region features diverse ecosystems with unique native species, though environmental transformation has reduced original forests to 30% by the 2010s. Cultural heritage includes notable arts institutions, a vibrant music scene, strong sporting traditions, and significant historical landmarks. Current demographics show a population of approximately 109,608 with distinctive employment patterns emphasizing agriculture, manufacturing, and energy sectors.

[Page 3] For Māori, shifting kōura around was about more than shoring up the food supply; it was part of kaitiakitanga, stewardship of the land and the species they shared it with. When, for example, Māori found waterways that had been overfished or cleaned out by a flood, they’d top them up again with kōura from elsewhere in the catchment.

16.document_title: Kōura: Māori Stewardship, Conservation, and Freshwater Ecosystem Restoration in Aotearoa New Zealand
16.document_summary: This comprehensive document collection explores the ecological, cultural, and conservation significance of kōura (New Zealand freshwater crayfish) through multiple interconnected narratives. It traces the historical role of kōura in Māori diet and culture, documenting how Māori ancestors practiced kaitiakitanga (environmental stewardship) by translocating crayfish across the country for centuries to ensure food security. The document examines kōura's ecological importance as ecosystem engineers that control invasive species and restore waterway health. It details the dramatic decline of kōura populations due to trout predation, forest clearing, invasive species (particularly brown bullhead catfish and marron), and water quality degradation, with some populations experiencing up to 99% decline. The collection highlights contemporary restoration efforts led by iwi and freshwater biologists using adapted traditional harvesting methods like the tau kōura technique. It features innovative approaches including John Hollows' professional kōura farming operations in Southland wetlands, which demonstrate sustainable aquaculture, and Kāti Huirapa rūnanga's initiatives to reconnect whānau with traditional food sources. The document emphasizes that mātauranga (Māori knowledge) remains essential for freshwater conservation and advocates for transferring ecosystem management responsibility back to indigenous communities.

17.document_title: Between a Rock and a Hard Place
17.document_summary: This article examines the contentious Denniston Plateau mining debate, which pits resource extraction against environmental preservation. With 6.1 million tonnes of bituminous coal beneath a 150-hectare site, the proposed open-cast mine would generate 14 million tonnes of CO2 emissions when burned—equivalent to New Zealand's annual dairy herd emissions. The article explores the tension between economic benefits ($46 million in salaries for a struggling West Coast region) and environmental costs, including mercury, selenium, arsenic emissions, and climate change contributions. It presents three perspectives: exploitation versus preservation, and a Māori concept of land as taonga (treasure and resource), emphasizing guardianship (kaitiakitanga) and respect for the land's living essence. The author questions whether this traditional approach might offer a less-destructive path to prosperity.

18.text:
[Page 9] Step up one more level on Maslow’s pyramid and you breathe the necessary air of esteem. Recognition from others, knowing one’s worth, a sense of mana—these are as essential to human wholeness as food, security and companionship, the previous three. Kearns gave Maslow’s category a further spin, speaking of the mutual esteem that grows between people and place. He spoke of how repeated engagements lead to pride and care of a space, further creating a sense of belonging. In time, an ethic of kaitiakitanga, or guardianship, develops. Of all nights to hear that message—only an hour earlier I had thrown in my lot with the Friends, paid my membership and offered my services. I could see a direct cause and effect at work. As fondness, indeed almost reliance, on the creek had grown, I had felt keenly a desire to assist its protection. At the time, that was no idle concern. There was still a possibility that the space could be compromised by the Auckland motorway extension. The direct threat of the reserve’s being sacrificed for an above ground road had been averted; the connection between New Windsor and Waterview was to be by way of a tunnel. But the details of how the construction would be managed with ecological sensitivity were still being negotiated. It was a good time to be thinking about kaitiakitanga.

18.document_title: Pilgrim at Oakley Creek: Urban Nature, Memory, and Human Flourishing
18.document_summary: This comprehensive collection of interconnected essays by Kennedy Warne explores the transformative power of Oakley Creek (Te Auaunga) in Auckland, New Zealand, examining it through multiple lenses: personal pilgrimage, human psychology, historical memory, and place attachment. The work chronicles Warne's six-month photographic journey from winter to summer solstice, inspired by contemplative writers and Zen philosophy, demonstrating how mindful observation of urban nature fosters deep ecological connection. The essays apply Maslow's hierarchy of needs to show how urban green spaces fulfill fundamental human requirements—from physiological exercise and emotional security to social belonging and self-actualization—while highlighting the critical importance of preserving these spaces as Auckland's open space availability declines. Through archival research and personal narrative, Warne traces the layered histories converging at Oakley Creek, including indigenous Māori heritage, colonial discoveries, the legacy of Carrington Psychiatric Hospital, and the story of patient Rolfe Hattaway whose artistic vision inspired modernist artists. The collection advocates for kaitiakitanga (guardianship) and "locaphilia"—binding oneself to place through loving attention, storytelling, and ceremonial engagement—demonstrating how individuals can expand a place's narrative and experience meaningful homecoming through relationship-based environmental engagement.

19.document_title: Eyes in the Land: Dune Lakes, Wetlands, and Indigenous Stewardship in Northland
19.document_summary: This comprehensive collection explores New Zealand's dune lakes and wetlands in Northland, examining their ecological significance and cultural importance to iwi communities. The articles document indigenous stewardship and scientific conservation efforts, featuring Lake Ngatu and NIWA scientist Paul Champion's research on unique flora including kuta sedge and tuatara plants. Key threats include invasive species such as hornwort, Egeria densa, Gambusia affinis, and grass carp. The collection emphasizes kaitiakitanga (environmental stewardship) as the foundation for restoration, incorporating ecological and cultural dimensions. Monitoring strategies using the LakeSPI bio-assessment tool are detailed, alongside management approaches including herbicide applications and freshwater mussel restoration. The narrative incorporates the Māori proverb "Te roto tāpokopoko, he wai whakahuihui, he pukenga ora" (a dune lake is an oasis that gathers and grows life) and explores te mana o te repo (the mana of wetlands) as intermediaries between Tāne (forests) and Tangaroa (seas). Community engagement initiatives like "Get to Know Your Dune Lake" days link lake conservation to Māori traditions and reconnect communities with their ancestral lands.

20.document_title: A Gulf in my Thinking
20.document_summary: Kennedy Warne reflects on his deep personal connection to the Hauraki Gulf in New Zealand, tracing memories from childhood through his grandfather's swordfishing boat. He explores the concept of guardianship and stewardship through the Inuit legend of the mother of the sea—a story about how people's disrespect for the ocean causes the sea's bounty to disappear until a shaman restores harmony by combing her hair. Warne connects this ancient wisdom to the Māori concept of kaitiakitanga, arguing it represents a profound stewardship that goes beyond mere resource management. He observes a growing movement of individuals taking environmental responsibility into their own hands, becoming "ministers of the environment" by caring for wetlands, forests, and oceans. The essay emphasizes humanity's forgotten relationship with the sea and calls for a return to reverence and respect for the natural world.

21.text:
[Page 4] Ngāti Kuri, another iwi from the Far North, has been on a similar journey of restoration. Wayne Petera, Ngāti Kuri’s coordinator for wai māori (freshwater), tells me that his people are awakening to the importance of the dune lakes in their rohe, and to their role as kaitiaki. Petera says the kaitiaki responsibility is an ancestral mantle laid on the shoulders of each generation. “We have no choice in the matter,” he says. “Mana requires that we act.” On the basis that Ngāti Kuri has existed for close to a thousand years, Petera says the iwi has decided it must have a thousand year vision for itself and its environment, lakes included. “We recognise that if we are the people we say we are, then we have a deep responsibility to ensure the life and well being of all of these ecological gems,” he says.

22.document_title: The Art of Weaving
22.document_summary: This essay explores the tension between environmental protection and resource exploitation in New Zealand. The author argues that the traditional binary approach of designating areas for total protection or total exploitation is outdated. Drawing on Māori concepts of kaitiakitanga (stewardship), the piece advocates for a balanced approach that allows both protection and sustainable use of natural resources. The author acknowledges that reducing humanity's environmental footprint requires difficult choices and collective action, emphasizing the need for respectful dialogue and integration of diverse knowledge systems to develop a more sustainable approach to living in Aotearoa (New Zealand).

23.document_title: Morepork: New Zealand's Native Owl - Adaptations, Behavior, and Conservation
23.document_summary: This comprehensive document collection explores the morepork (ruru), New Zealand's native nocturnal owl. The first section provides personal observations of morepork hunting behavior, detailing their diet of insects, small birds, mice, and geckos through pellet analysis, with regional variations across different islands. Moreporks inhabit diverse environments including native bush, pine forests, and suburban areas, maintaining 3-5 hectare territories and navigating by memory. The second section examines remarkable sensory and behavioral adaptations enabling nocturnal hunting, including specialized night vision with rod-cell-dominated retinas 100 times more sensitive than pigeons' eyes, asymmetrical skull structures for precise sound localization, and silent flight through specialized feather structures. Research suggests moreporks may detect infrared light to locate warm-blooded prey. The third section details the complete life cycle, focusing on chick development from fledging through independence and territorial behavior. The collection highlights a significant conservation success story involving a nearly-extinct Norfolk Island boobook successfully bred with New Zealand moreporks, resulting in a growing population with potential reintroduction to Lord Howe Island. Additionally, the collection addresses Māori cultural perspectives, where moreporks held spiritual significance as ancestral guardians and messengers.

24.document_title: Blue Carbon in New Zealand: Fiords, Coastal Wetlands, and Seagrass Restoration
24.document_summary: This comprehensive collection examines New Zealand's blue carbon ecosystems and their role in climate regulation. New Zealand's fiords, particularly Doubtful Sound and Dusky Sound, store approximately 2.24 billion tonnes of carbon—about one percent of the world's seabed carbon. These fiords bury organic carbon faster than similar ecosystems worldwide due to unique geography, steep valleys, heavy rainfall, and anaerobic mud conditions. Scientists at the Cawthron Institute are pioneering seed-based seagrass restoration methods, discovering that Zostera muelleri flowers more frequently than previously believed. Seagrass ecosystems capture carbon 55 times faster than tropical rainforests and store four times more carbon per hectare in soils. Coastal wetland restoration projects like Te Wahapū o Waihī integrate mātauranga Māori with coastal ecology, with five iwi collaborating on restoration efforts. Seaweed research reveals varying decomposition rates in deep-sea environments, though scientists raise concerns about accurately measuring seaweed's carbon removal potential. The research emphasizes protecting natural carbon sinks while addressing legal complexities involving Māori rights and rangatiratanga, highlighting kaitiakitanga (stewardship) and cultural significance of coastal ecosystem restoration.

25.text:
[Page 9] If everyone foraged, would we strip the land? Wellington author Johanna Knox (Ngāti Tukorehe, Ngāti Raukawa ki te Tonga, Ngāti Ranginui, Tangata Tiriti), who wrote the book on foraging in New Zealand, thinks that eating the environment is a pretty good way of reconnecting with it. She reckons foraging could resurrect the idea of the commons—not just the tragedy of it. It could bring back the concept of places that are used and maintained by people for each other—and for future generations. That idea has been largely lost from the Pākehā world, but it’s remained intact in te ao Māori. Despite the destruction of traditional food gathering areas, despite the theft of land, the depletion of resources, and the loss of kōrero about how different species are prepared—despite all of that, the philosophy of how to gather food sustainably remains intact. It’s the concept of kaitiakitanga. “A big difference between Western environmentalism and Māori kaitiakitanga is how they see humans in the environment,” says Knox. “So in Pākehā conservation, it’s like, ‘We must keep these areas pristine. Nobody can take anything from here,’ but in te ao Māori it’s like, ‘People are part of the landscape. It’s a reciprocal relationship, so of course we’re taking stuff.’ McKenzie and Mikhail Shatura, head chef at downtown Auckland restaurant Ahi, taste the morning’s foraging. Shatura assembles a dish of quail, chickweed, huruhuru whenua and ureure. Foraged ingredients don’t form the bulk of a dish, says McKenzie, but they bring the flavours of a place onto the plate. “These are supporting characters,” he says. “So I come at foraging from the perspective that if you get right out there and involve yourself in the landscape—which means taking what you can, but respectfully and sustainably and at the same time giving back—that’s just a really good way to do things.” Raglan ecologist and rongoā practitioner Mahuru Wilcox (Ngāti Awa, Ngāti Ranginui) echoes Knox. She forages native plants traditionally used for medicinal purposes for her small business, Hau Botanicals. “How can you teach people to value something if you can’t connect to it?” she asks. “These [plants] are valued because they were important as kai or as rongoā or they were important as ancestors, as tūpuna. If you’re really thinking of our world around us as our tūpuna, as our ancestors, how would you respect your tūpuna? So using those principles for how you connect.” Even in the most densely populated parts of the city, plants move through the cycles of the year. Retreating into their roots to conserve water, springing forth with new shoots. Exploding into colour for a week or two. “It’s such a reminder in your daily life as a human that everything has a season,” says Wilcox. Over time, you start to see it: the living calendar, the shifts in weather and sunlight reflected in the plants changing, day by day, in all the gaps between the fixed and immobile parts of the city.

25.document_title: The Weed Eaters: Urban and Rural Foraging in New Zealand
25.document_summary: This comprehensive article explores the growing practice of foraging in New Zealand, examining both urban and rural contexts. The piece follows multiple narratives: in Auckland, forager Bella Burgess leads a Facebook community group on Maungawhau/Mount Eden, teaching participants to identify and harvest edible wild plants including vetch, wild brassica, pūhā, nasturtium, oxalis, and onion weed while emphasizing ethical foraging practices. In Canterbury, Peter Langlands scouts for elderflower and wild parsnips for restaurants, demonstrating how roadsides and berms provide abundant biodiversity and foraged ingredients. The article features interviews with professional foragers like Nate McKenzie and Rico Birndt who maintain sustainable harvesting practices. It highlights the cultural and philosophical dimensions of foraging, connecting it to Māori philosophy of kaitiakitanga—a reciprocal relationship with the environment—and contrasting this with Western conservation approaches. The piece explores the underlying human desire for self-reliance and independence from modern systems, noting how the surge in foraging interest during COVID-19 lockdowns reflects deeper needs for connection and resilience. The article showcases how edible plants grow abundantly in plain sight throughout New Zealand's towns and cities, challenging cultural hesitation about harvesting from public spaces while advocating for sustainable practices and "feral parks" instead of manicured lawns.

[Page 1] Māori AI expert Dr Karaitiana Taiuru shares his favourite whakataukī 2024 03 18 22:44:07+13:00 Dr Karaitiana Taiuru. Tino rangatiratanga: mō tātou, ā, mō kā uri ā muri ake nei. It is the whakataukī (Māori proverb) that means most to Māori data, AI and technology ethicist Dr Karaitiana Taiuru (Ngāi Tahu, Ngāti Kahungunu, Ngāti Toa). Translated to English, it means "the ability to create and control our destiny for generations to come". It links in well with his work and family life, Taiuru told RNZ Nights. For his work, it reminded Taiuru why he still does what he does and that there was a new generation of children who will not know life without AI and it was "our role to create the new normal for them". Taiuru applies a te ao Māori perspective to AI. https://www.rnz.co.nz/national/programmes/nig new generation of children who will not know life without AI and it was "our role to create the new normal for them". Taiuru applies a te ao Māori perspective to AI. https://www.rnz.co.nz/national/programmes/nig hts/audio/2018930609/whakatauki of the week with karaitiana taiuru Listen to the full interview on Nights "We already know that internationally, there's bias against minority peoples so what I do, in conjunction with international best practices with artificial intelligence and other technologies, is bring that Māori voice and Te Tiriti o Waitangi considerations to play." There were "a number" of cultural values that needed to be considered in terms of AI, he said. Many Māori have moko (facial tattoos) so understanding how that was considered with facial technologies was a big factor. In his personal life, the whakataukī applied to his whānau. "For me, I consider that I have an opportunity to create wealth and opportunities for my children and also for my grandchildren. "I live by that rule. I make that sure my children have the opportunities that I didn't always have, make sure they have access to education, financial resources, a home, and part of my planning in life is that my grandchildren will also have the same access and all going well in life, I should see my great grandchildren and maybe great great grandchildren whom I will also ensure that they have equal access. "And I know my children also that they consider the same sort of philosophies in life where they want to protect their whānau as well for the future." Taiuru said the whakataukī came out of working groups around the South Island when Ngāi Tahu was trying to identify a new tribal vision that would be carried into the future. 37.document_title: Māori Landowners Take Crown to High Court Over Freshwater Rights
37.document_summary: Approximately 60 Māori Land Trusts, representing over 150,000 landowners, hapū, and iwi have filed proceedings in the High Court against the Crown over freshwater rights. The claimants argue the Crown has broken promises and failed to uphold Te Tiriti o Waitangi obligations regarding Māori proprietary and kaitiaki rights in freshwater and geothermal resources. They seek immediate action to stop water degradation, recognition of tikanga Māori rights, and a fair water allocation system enabling Māori to exercise kaitiakitanga. The case follows over a decade of Crown inaction despite 2012-2013 acknowledgments of Māori rights. The claimants criticize the current "first-in, first-served" allocation system and the dismantling of Te Mana o te Wai framework. Kingi Smiler, representing the claimant group, emphasizes the urgency of restoring balance and protecting waterways for future generations. The legal process is expected to take two to three years.

[Page 1] By5am 2025 01 31 16:12:25+13:00 Nicola Toki. The head of a conservation society says she is deeply concerned about politicians misrepresenting the value of stewardship land. Forest and Bird chief executive Nicola Toki told First Up that according to the law, stewardship land was actually public conservation land. She was responding to comments made by Minister of Economic Growth Nicola Willis who told First Up about the possibility of mining on conservation land. "DOC (Department of Conservation) actually manages a huge amount of other land, sometimes referred to as stewardship land, which is not these pristine environments often it's just scrubby land," Willis said. https://www.rnz.co.nz/national/programm es/first up/audio/2018972876/stewardship land is valuable land forest a nd bird Toki said many areas were in fact pristine and of immense value, and were home to threatened birds. "There's a bit of alternative facts going on, I think, with respect to stewardship land. It's… really naughty of the ministers, particularly senior ministers who should know better, because it's important that the public are aware of the facts." Comment has been requested from Shane Jones' and Nicola Willis' offices. Toki said stewardship land "belongs to New Zealand". "It just got caught up in this terrible kind of bureaucratic limbo back in the '80s [and] '90s and never really got properly gazetted into the requisite categories for example, national park, conservation park, all of that kind of thing. It just hasn't been filed in the right drawer, basically." She said stewardship land made up about one third of DOC administered land. Toki told First Up a few years ago, a robust review was carried of 644,000 hectares of stewardship land on the West Coast of the South Island. "They found only 0.01 percent was recommended for disposal. That's the scrubby land that that senior ministers keep trying to tell the public, is fine for digging up for mining. Well, we know that's not true. "I'm pretty growly about the way they're telling the story." Minister for Resources Shane Jones. All stewardship land is administered by the Department of Conservation, she said, and iwi also had a "fairly high interest". "It is classified under the Conservation Act, it is looked after by DOC". Toki said she had heard Minister for Resources Shane Jones and others talk about it not being owned by DOC. "I want the public to be aware that there's a bit of wool being pulled over eyes, here." She said last week, in his state of the nation address, Prime Minister Christopher Luxon focused on growth. "He's saying mining on conservation land is going to be one of the ways that we're going to do that. And then following that, we've had ministers say 'don't worry, it's only stewardship land'." "It kind of gives the impression that these are just these waste pits or scrub." Toki said the statements alleviated the public's concerns. "They say, 'Oh, it's not so bad, is it?' It is bad, it's really bad because you might have one foot on a conservation park or a national park and one foot in some beautiful mountainous environment, one foot on what is classified as stewardship land in exactly the same place." "It's just… bureaucratic slow down that has led to this beautiful places kind of living in limbo. It doesn't mean they're any less valuable." Appearing later on Morning Report, Jones said his plan was to marginalise "the gatekeepers hiding behind the Wildlife Act, the people trying to turn DOC into some sort of preservationist state and deny New Zealand as a livelihood". He also said experts in "geology minerals engineering" would be making the decisions, not "insect ecologists". 42.document_summary: Conservation Minister Tama Potaka has reclassified significant stewardship land on New Zealand's West Coast, marking the most substantial reclassification since the Department of Conservation's inception in 1987. The changes include 6 proposals for national park additions (4,298 hectares), 63 disposal investigations (3,352 hectares), 151 Reserves Act protections (192,973 hectares), and 157 Conservation Act protections. A notable 181,000-hectare Tarahanga e Toru Historic Reserve recognizes Poutini Ngāi Tahu's cultural significance. Potaka used an 'order in council' process bypassing Cabinet approval. ACT leader David Seymour supports the changes, noting alignment with Ngāi Tahu settlement provisions and treaty obligations.

[Page 1] Dozens of cameras installed on the Kaitake Range in Taranaki are revealing the success stemming from five years of intensive predator control. The western most of three mountain ranges Papa Kura o Taranaki, Kaitake is the focus for a joint predator control programme involving the Department of Conservation, Taranaki Maunga Project, iwi, and other community collaborators. DOC biodiversity ranger Brandon Kingi said a comparison of images captured by the trail cameras dotted across the Kaitake showed a dramatic decrease in predators such as possums, stoats and feral cats and a notable increase in protected native species like kiwi, which had been successfully reintroduced to the area. "We've seen a big fall in the number of feral cats caught on our cameras, which shows the 1080 operation has effectively controlled them," said Kingi. "Immediately after the operation in November last year, the number of cats detected dropped almost overnight from about 95 percent of the cameras showing feral cats, to about 1 percent. "There was a similar result for stoats they were seen on our cameras before the operation, then they had almost vanished when we checked the cameras afterwards." The predator control methods used at Kaitake also included bait stations and leg hold possum traps. Kingi said keeping predator numbers down required hard physical labour, carried out by staff from DOC and Taranaki Maunga Project, as well as volunteers and paid staff from iwi and community groups. "The community collaborators contributing to Kaitake working to protect biodiversity on the maunga have also helped control rats and mustelids." Kingi said the measured reduction of predators at Kaitake demonstrated how a trapping network extended the benefits from aerial operations by reducing predator reinvasion. There were also anecdotal observations of more birdlife across the range and a healthier forest. Taranaki Maunga Project pou whakahaere taurua/co project director, Sean Zieltjes, said the camera data was another tangible measure that the hard work by kaimahi and volunteers removing predators and reintroducing kiwi was paying off. "We're really in Te stoked, mate there. Our latest round of camera data from Kaitake is showing more images of kiwi than possums up there at the moment. We're really psyched with this and some ways we can't believe it. But it certainly gives us a shot in the arm and a steer that we're on the on the right track up there, that's for sure." Zieltjes said it showed the power of community involvement to really make a difference in driving biodiversity improvements. Kaitake didn't have a particular focus for Taranaki Mounga Project when it started nearly a decade ago, but community support for it changed that. "Relationships fostered with Ngā Mahanga a Tāiri, the Kaitake Conservation Ranges Trust, schools, landowners, and other groups and agencies, have snowballed into achieving much more than we could ever have done working separately." Zieltjes said invasive species were putting immense pressure on New Zealand's ecosystems and at 4000 Aotearoa had one of the highest rates of threatened species in the world. "Once our unique native species are gone, they are gone for good. The results at Kaitake demonstrate a small but important success in protecting native species." Organisations contributing to predator control and species protection at Kaitake include Ngā Mahanga a Tāiri hapū, Kaitake Conservation Ranges Trust, environmental educators Te Ara Taio, and numerous schools. Taranaki Kiwi Trust, Sanctuary Mountain Maungatautari, Ngāti Koroki Kahukura, and Save the Kiwi had all contributed to the return of kiwi to the maunga. 1.fileDescription: Kaitiakitanga is a foundational Māori concept of guardianship and environmental stewardship rooted in the worldview that humans are part of nature. A kaitiaki is a guardian recognized by tangata whenua to care for natural areas such as lakes, forests, and waterways. Traditional conservation practices include temporary rāhui (resource restrictions), use of the lunar calendar (maramataka) for planting and harvesting, sustainable hunting and fishing, and blessing of mauri stones by tohunga (priests). Key spiritual concepts include mana (spiritual power), tapu (spiritual restriction), and mauri (life force). Today, kaitiakitanga is experiencing renewal as iwi (tribes) restore ecosystems and apply traditional knowledge in modern contexts. Practical examples include Ngāi Tahu's guardianship of pounamu resources, Ngāti Toa's fishery restoration at Pukerua Bay, and multi-tribal efforts to stop river pollution and protect endangered species. The document outlines challenges in collaborating with non-Māori stakeholders and details legislative frameworks such as the Resource Management Act 1991 and Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004 that incorporate kaitiakitanga principles. Kaitiakitanga offers perspectives on environmental stewardship and kinship with nature, enabling Māori to fulfill ancestral responsibilities while contributing to broader environmental sustainability.

chunkHighlights.text: Tiaki

The word tiaki is the basis of the longer word kaitiakitanga. Tiaki means to guard. It also means to preserve, foster, protect and shelter. So, notions of care and protection are at the heart of kaitiakitanga, and give
it its conservation ethic.

chunkHighlights.text: By Te Ahukaramū Charles Royal

Understanding kaitiakitanga Kaitiakitanga means guardianship and
protection. It is a way of managing the environment, based on the Māori world view. A kaitiaki is a guardian. This can be a person or group that cares for an area such as a lake or forest. They are given that role by the local iwi . Māori world view In the Māori world view, people are closely connected to the land and nature. Kaitiakitanga is based on this idea of humans as part of the natural world. Traditional practices In the past, people followed traditional practices when they were hunting, fishing, growing or finding food. These helped them to care for the environment. They included: temporary bans (rāhui) on taking food from an area using the lunar calendar (maramataka) to decide when to plant and harvest taking only what was needed hunting and fishing only for food, not as sport using bird snares at the right time – for example, not when the birds were breeding. Mana, tapu and mauri Mana means spiritual power. If a forest has mana , it will have plenty of flowers, fruit and birds. Tapu can mean spiritual restriction. Sometimes rāhui (restrictions) are needed to help the mana of the forest. A rāhui might stop people taking birds, fish or fruit from a certain area, or at a certain time. Mauri means life force. This must be protected in forests, rivers, gardens, lakes and the sea. Special mauri stones, which tohunga (priests) said prayers over, were used to preserve this force. Kaitiakitanga today Today there is growing interest in kaitiakitanga. Iwi are restoring their environment and culture, and using traditional ideas in the modern world. Ngāi Tahu are guardians of pounamu (greenstone) in the South Island. Te Āti Awa ki Taranaki made a claim to the government to stop pollution in their fishing areas. 5.fileDescription: Kennedy Warne reflects on his deep personal connection to the Hauraki Gulf in New Zealand, tracing memories from childhood through his grandfather's swordfishing boat. He explores the concept of guardianship and stewardship through the Inuit legend of the mother of the sea—a story about how people's disrespect for the ocean causes the sea's bounty to disappear until a shaman restores harmony by combing her hair. Warne connects this ancient wisdom to the Māori concept of kaitiakitanga, arguing it represents a profound stewardship that goes beyond mere resource management. He observes a growing movement of individuals taking environmental responsibility into their own hands, becoming "ministers of the environment" by caring for wetlands, forests, and oceans. The essay emphasizes humanity's forgotten relationship with the sea and calls for a return to reverence and respect for the natural world.

6.fileDescription: This comprehensive article explores the growing practice of foraging in New Zealand, examining both urban and rural contexts. The piece follows multiple narratives: in Auckland, forager Bella Burgess leads a Facebook community group on Maungawhau/Mount Eden, teaching participants to identify and harvest edible wild plants including vetch, wild brassica, pūhā, nasturtium, oxalis, and onion weed while emphasizing ethical foraging practices. In Canterbury, Peter Langlands scouts for elderflower and wild parsnips for restaurants, demonstrating how roadsides and berms provide abundant biodiversity and foraged ingredients. The article features interviews with professional foragers like Nate McKenzie and Rico Birndt who maintain sustainable harvesting practices. It highlights the cultural and philosophical dimensions of foraging, connecting it to Māori philosophy of kaitiakitanga—a reciprocal relationship with the environment—and contrasting this with Western conservation approaches. The piece explores the underlying human desire for self-reliance and independence from modern systems, noting how the surge in foraging interest during COVID-19 lockdowns reflects deeper needs for connection and resilience. The article showcases how edible plants grow abundantly in plain sight throughout New Zealand's towns and cities, challenging cultural hesitation about harvesting from public spaces while advocating for sustainable practices and "feral parks" instead of manicured lawns.

chunkHighlights.text: If everyone foraged, would we strip the land? Wellington author Johanna Knox (Ngāti Tukorehe, Ngāti Raukawa ki te Tonga, Ngāti Ranginui, Tangata Tiriti), who wrote the book on foraging in New Zealand, thinks that eating the environment is a pretty good way of reconnecting with it. She reckons foraging could resurrect the idea of the commons—not just the tragedy of it. It could bring back the concept of places that are used and maintained by people for each other—and for future generations.

That idea has been largely lost from the Pākehā world, but it’s remained intact in te ao Māori. Despite the destruction of traditional food-gathering areas, despite the theft of land, the depletion of resources, and the loss of kōrero about how different species are prepared—despite all of that, the philosophy of how to gather food sustainably remains intact. It’s the concept of kaitiakitanga.

“A big difference between Western environmentalism and Māori kaitiakitanga is how they see humans in the environment,” says Knox. “So in Pākehā conservation, it’s like, ‘We must keep these areas pristine. Nobody can take anything from here,’ but in te ao Māori it’s like, ‘People are part of the landscape. It’s a reciprocal relationship, so of course we’re taking stuff.’

McKenzie and Mikhail Shatura, head chef at downtown Auckland restaurant Ahi, taste the morning’s foraging. Shatura assembles a dish of quail, chickweed, huruhuru whenua and ureure. Foraged ingredients don’t form the bulk of a dish, says McKenzie, but they bring the flavours of a place onto the plate. “These are supporting characters,” he says.

“So I come at foraging from the perspective that if you get right out there and involve yourself in the landscape—which means taking what you can, but respectfully and sustainably and at the same time giving back—that’s just a really good way to do things.”

Raglan ecologist and rongoā practitioner Mahuru Wilcox (Ngāti Awa, Ngāti Ranginui) echoes Knox. She forages native plants traditionally used for medicinal purposes for her small business, Hau Botanicals.

“How can you teach people to value something if you can’t connect to it?” she asks. “These [plants] are valued because they were important as kai or as rongoā or they were important as ancestors, as tūpuna. If you’re really thinking of our world around us as our tūpuna, as our ancestors, how would you respect your tūpuna? So using those principles for how you connect.”

Even in the most densely populated parts of the city, plants move through the cycles of the year. Retreating into their roots to conserve water, springing forth with new shoots. Exploding into colour for a week or two.
“It’s such a reminder in your daily life as a human that everything has a season,” says Wilcox.
Over time, you start to see it: the living calendar, the shifts in weather and sunlight reflected in the plants changing, day by day, in all the gaps between the fixed and immobile parts of the city.
