9.fileDescription: This article examines the contentious Denniston Plateau mining debate, which pits resource extraction against environmental preservation. With 6.1 million tonnes of bituminous coal beneath a 150-hectare site, the proposed open-cast mine would generate 14 million tonnes of CO2 emissions when burned—equivalent to New Zealand's annual dairy herd emissions. The article explores the tension between economic benefits ($46 million in salaries for a struggling West Coast region) and environmental costs, including mercury, selenium, arsenic emissions, and climate change contributions. It presents three perspectives: exploitation versus preservation, and a Māori concept of land as taonga (treasure and resource), emphasizing guardianship (kaitiakitanga) and respect for the land's living essence. The author questions whether this traditional approach might offer a less-destructive path to prosperity.

response.response_text:
## Te Tikanga o 'Kaitiakitanga'

Ko 'kaitiakitanga' tētahi kupu Māori e whakaahua ana i te tiaki, i te manaaki, i te ārai hoki i te taiao — ā, i ngā taonga katoa o te ao Māori. I roto i te reo Pākehā, ko te tikanga ko *guardianship*, *protection*, *preservation*, me *stewardship*. [[1]](cite://1/1)

He mea hanga tēnei tikanga i runga i te tirohanga Māori ki te ao — arā, he hononga tōtika tō te tangata ki te whenua, ki te taiao hoki. [[2]](cite://2/1)

## Ko Wai te Kaitiaki?

Ko te kupu 'kai' he tohu mō tē nāna e mahi ana tētahi mahi. Nō reira, ko te 'kaitiaki' ko tērā e tiaki ana, e manaaki ana, e ārai ana i tētahi mea. [[3]](cite://3/1) Ko te kaitiaki he tangata, he rōpū rānei e whakaaetia ana e ngā tangata whenua o tētahi wāhi — hei tiaki i tētahi roto, i tētahi ngahere, i tētahi awa rānei. [[4]](cite://4/1)

I te tīmatanga, ko ngā atua o te ao tūāhuru ngā kaitiaki tuatahi — hei tauira, ko Tāne, ko ia te kaitiaki o te ngahere. Ka whai atu ngā kaitiaki katoa i tēnā tauira. [[3]](cite://3/2)

## Kaitiakitanga me te Taiao

E kī ana ngā kōrero tuku iho, he hononga pūmau tō te tangata ki tōna taiao — ā, ko te hauora o te hapū, he āhua ōrite ki te hauora o tōna taiao. Ki tauira, ki kino, ki paru ngā awa, ko tērā tohu he raruraru kei roto i te hapū. [[5]](cite://5/1)

Ko ētahi tikanga i whāia e ngā tīpuna hei tiaki i te taiao:

- **Rāhui** — he aukati wā, kia kaua ai e tangohia ngā kai o tētahi wāhi [[1]](cite://1/2)
- **Maramataka** — ko te maramataka Māori hei arahi i ngā wā tōtika ki te māra, ki te hauhake [[1]](cite://1/3)
- Ko te tango anake i ērā mea e hiahiatia ana [[1]](cite://1/4)
- Ko te hī ika, ko te hao manu mō te kai anake, kaua mō te hākinakina [[1]](cite://1/5)

He mea nui hoki ngā tikanga e toru nei:

- **Mana** — ko te mana o te ngahere, ka kitea ki ōna hua, ki ōna manu [[1]](cite://1/6)
- **Tapu** — he ārai wairua; ko te rāhui tētahi āhua o te tapu [[1]](cite://1/7)
- **Mauri** — ko te mauri o ngā ngahere, o ngā awa, o ngā moana me tiakina [[1]](cite://1/8)

## Kaitiakitanga mō ngā Taonga

Ehara i te taiao anake te kaupeka o kaitiakitanga — ka taea hoki te tāpiri ki ngā taonga tuku iho, pēnei i ngā korowai, i ngā mere pounamu, i ngā pukapuka whakapapa. Ko ēnei taonga, nō tētahi tīpuna i mua, ka noho hei taonga mō ngā uri katoa, ā, ka tiakina e tētahi kaitiaki mō te katoa o te whānau. [[6]](cite://6/1)

## Kaitiakitanga i Ēnii Rā

Kei roto hoki ko kaitiakitanga i ētahi ture o Aotearoa — ko te Resource Management Act 1991 (RMA) tētahi, e taea ai te kaitiakitanga hei ārahitanga ki ngā kaiwhakahaere rauemi. E kī ana te RMA: ko kaitiakitanga ko *'the exercise of guardianship by the tangata whenua of an area in accordance with tikanga Māori in relation to natural and physical resources; and includes the ethic of stewardship.'* [[7]](cite://7/1)

E ai ki tētahi tuhinga, ko kaitiakitanga he momo tiakitanga kei tua atu i te whakahaere rauemi noa iho — he mea hōhonu ake, ko te whakamana i te ao, ko te aroha ki ēnā taonga katoa. [[8]](cite://8/1)

Ka āhei hoki ngā tāngata kore-Māori ki te whakaaro mō tō rātou hononga ki te ao tūāhuru mā tēnei kaupeka — he āhuatanga e hiahiatia ana i ēnei rā o te taiao kino. [[9]](cite://9/1)

Ka pātai atu au — he hiahia āu ki te mōhio ake ki ētahi iwi e mahi ana i ngā kaupeka kaitiakitanga i Aotearoa i ēnei rā?

1.text:
[Page 1] By Te Ahukaramū Charles Royal Understanding kaitiakitanga Kaitiakitanga means guardianship and protection. It is a way of managing the environment, based on the Māori world view. A kaitiaki is a guardian. This can be a person or group that cares for an area such as a lake or forest. They are given that role by the local iwi . Māori world view In the Māori world view, people are closely connected to the land and nature. Kaitiakitanga is based on this idea of humans as part of the natural world. Traditional practices In the past, people followed traditional practices when they were hunting, fishing, growing or finding food. These helped them to care for the environment. They included: temporary bans (rāhui) on taking food from an area using the lunar calendar (maramataka) to decide when to plant and harvest taking only what was needed hunting and fishing only for food, not as sport using bird snares at the right time for example, not when the birds were breeding. Mana, tapu and mauri Mana means spiritual power. If a forest has mana , it will have plenty of flowers, fruit and birds. Tapu can mean spiritual restriction. Sometimes rāhui (restrictions) are needed to help the mana of the forest. A rāhui might stop people taking birds, fish or fruit from a certain area, or at a certain time. Mauri means life force. This must be protected in forests, rivers, gardens, lakes and the sea. Special mauri stones, which tohunga (priests) said prayers over, were used to preserve this force. Kaitiakitanga today Today there is growing interest in kaitiakitanga. Iwi are restoring their environment and culture, and using traditional ideas in the modern world. Ngāi Tahu are guardians of pounamu (greenstone) in the South Island. Te Āti Awa ki Taranaki made a claim to the government to stop pollution in their fishing areas. Four iwi (Ngāti Kahungunu, Rangitāne, Muaūpoko and Ngāti Raukawa) have come together to stop the Manawatū River being polluted. The Te Rarawa people are working to save the kūkupa (New Zealand pigeon). Kaitiakitanga has also been included in some laws, such as the Resource Management Act 1991. Kaitiakitanga means guardianship, protection, preservation or sheltering. It is a way of managing the environment, based on the traditional Māori world view.

1.document_title: Kaitiakitanga: Māori Guardianship, Environmental Stewardship, and Traditional Conservation Practices
1.document_summary: Kaitiakitanga is a foundational Māori concept of guardianship and environmental stewardship rooted in the worldview that humans are part of nature. A kaitiaki is a guardian recognized by tangata whenua to care for natural areas such as lakes, forests, and waterways. Traditional conservation practices include temporary rāhui (resource restrictions), use of the lunar calendar (maramataka) for planting and harvesting, sustainable hunting and fishing, and blessing of mauri stones by tohunga (priests). Key spiritual concepts include mana (spiritual power), tapu (spiritual restriction), and mauri (life force). Today, kaitiakitanga is experiencing renewal as iwi (tribes) restore ecosystems and apply traditional knowledge in modern contexts. 12.document_title: Māori Housing in New Zealand: Historical Evolution, Challenges, and Contemporary Solutions
12.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of Māori housing from pre-colonial times through the early 21st century in New Zealand. Traditionally, Māori lived in family-based kāinga (villages) with rectangular wharepuni (sleeping houses) constructed from natural materials. European settlers introduced European-style housing from the early 1800s, though most Māori initially maintained traditional dwellings. From the late 1800s, poor sanitary conditions—including inadequate water, sewerage, and overcrowding—led to disease outbreaks, prompting government intervention that resulted in the demolition of 1,256 houses and construction of 2,103 cottages by 1909. The 1918 influenza epidemic devastated Māori communities and prompted new housing initiatives including the Native Housing Act 1935. Post-WWII urbanization saw Māori migrate to cities like Auckland and Wellington, facing discrimination from landlords and living in overcrowded subdivided apartments. State housing policies effectively excluded Māori through discriminatory practices until 1944, while housing designs ignored Māori cultural values (tikanga), contributing to assimilation policies. By the 1980s-90s, Māori home ownership remained significantly lower than the general population (29-49% vs. 50-73%). Persistent problems in the early 21st century included substandard, cold, damp housing; overcrowding (23% of Māori in 2006 vs. 4% for Europeans); and poor health outcomes. Modern solutions emerged through iwi-led initiatives including papakāinga schemes, rural housing programs, and the government's Whānau Ora scheme (2010), which combines housing with health, education, and legal support, representing a shift toward Māori self-determination.

14.document_title: Kōrero taiao: Māori Sayings and Proverbs from the Natural World
14.document_summary: This document explores traditional Māori sayings and proverbs (whakataukī) derived from nature, reflecting the deep connection between Māori culture and the natural world. It covers how the sky, sea, and land were used to convey meanings about human qualities and social behavior. The stars, particularly Matariki (Pleiades), signaled seasonal changes crucial for agriculture and fishing. The sea was gendered—gentle East Coast waters called "Te Tai Tamawahine" (female sea) and rough West Coast waters "Te Tai Tamatāne" (male sea). Land's importance was captured in the proverb about food providing blood and land providing health. The document details how natural imagery described beauty (white shells for teeth, full moon for eyes, spider webs for intricate weaving), good qualities (persistence compared to boulders and bellbirds), and negative traits (laziness likened to cuckoos, greed to kahawai fish). Tribal society's communal nature meant lazy and greedy individuals were particularly despised, as group effort was essential for survival.

15.document_title: Pilgrim at Oakley Creek: Urban Nature, Memory, and Human Flourishing
15.document_summary: This comprehensive collection of interconnected essays by Kennedy Warne explores the transformative power of Oakley Creek (Te Auaunga) in Auckland, New Zealand, examining it through multiple lenses: personal pilgrimage, human psychology, historical memory, and place attachment. The work chronicles Warne's six-month photographic journey from winter to summer solstice, inspired by contemplative writers and Zen philosophy, demonstrating how mindful observation of urban nature fosters deep ecological connection. The essays apply Maslow's hierarchy of needs to show how urban green spaces fulfill fundamental human requirements—from physiological exercise and emotional security to social belonging and self-actualization—while highlighting the critical importance of preserving these spaces as Auckland's open space availability declines. Through archival research and personal narrative, Warne traces the layered histories converging at Oakley Creek, including indigenous Māori heritage, colonial discoveries, the legacy of Carrington Psychiatric Hospital, and the story of patient Rolfe Hattaway whose artistic vision inspired modernist artists. The collection advocates for kaitiakitanga (guardianship) and "locaphilia"—binding oneself to place through loving attention, storytelling, and ceremonial engagement—demonstrating how individuals can expand a place's narrative and experience meaningful homecoming through relationship-based environmental engagement.

[Page 9] If everyone foraged, would we strip the land? Wellington author Johanna Knox (Ngāti Tukorehe, Ngāti Raukawa ki te Tonga, Ngāti Ranginui, Tangata Tiriti), who wrote the book on foraging in New Zealand, thinks that eating the environment is a pretty good way of reconnecting with it. She reckons foraging could resurrect the idea of the commons—not just the tragedy of it. It could bring back the concept of places that are used and maintained by people for each other—and for future generations. That idea has been largely lost from the Pākehā world, but it’s remained intact in te ao Māori. Despite the destruction of traditional food gathering areas, despite the theft of land, the depletion of resources, and the loss of kōrero about how different species are prepared—despite all of that, the philosophy of how to gather food sustainably remains intact. It’s the concept of kaitiakitanga. “A big difference between Western environmentalism and Māori kaitiakitanga is how they see humans in the environment,” says Knox. “So in Pākehā conservation, it’s like, ‘We must keep these areas pristine. Nobody can take anything from here,’ but in te ao Māori it’s like, ‘People are part of the landscape. It’s a reciprocal relationship, so of course we’re taking stuff.’ McKenzie and Mikhail Shatura, head chef at downtown Auckland restaurant Ahi, taste the morning’s foraging. Shatura assembles a dish of quail, chickweed, huruhuru whenua and ureure. Foraged ingredients don’t form the bulk of a dish, says McKenzie, but they bring the flavours of a place onto the plate. “These are supporting characters,” he says. “So I come at foraging from the perspective that if you get right out there and involve yourself in the landscape—which means taking what you can, but respectfully and sustainably and at the same time giving back—that’s just a really good way to do things.” Raglan ecologist and rongoā practitioner Mahuru Wilcox (Ngāti Awa, Ngāti Ranginui) echoes Knox. She forages native plants traditionally used for medicinal purposes for her small business, Hau Botanicals. “How can you teach people to value something if you can’t connect to it?” she asks. “These [plants] are valued because they were important as kai or as rongoā or they were important as ancestors, as tūpuna. If you’re really thinking of our world around us as our tūpuna, as our ancestors, how would you respect your tūpuna? So using those principles for how you connect.” Even in the most densely populated parts of the city, plants move through the cycles of the year. Retreating into their roots to conserve water, springing forth with new shoots. Exploding into colour for a week or two. “It’s such a reminder in your daily life as a human that everything has a season,” says Wilcox. Over time, you start to see it: the living calendar, the shifts in weather and sunlight reflected in the plants changing, day by day, in all the gaps between the fixed and immobile parts of the city.

Key threats include invasive species such as hornwort, Egeria densa, Gambusia affinis, and grass carp. The collection emphasizes kaitiakitanga (environmental stewardship) as the foundation for restoration, incorporating ecological and cultural dimensions. Monitoring strategies using the LakeSPI bio-assessment tool are detailed, alongside management approaches including herbicide applications and freshwater mussel restoration. The narrative incorporates the Māori proverb "Te roto tāpokopoko, he wai whakahuihui, he pukenga ora" (a dune lake is an oasis that gathers and grows life) and explores te mana o te repo (the mana of wetlands) as intermediaries between Tāne (forests) and Tangaroa (seas). Community engagement initiatives like "Get to Know Your Dune Lake" days link lake conservation to Māori traditions and reconnect communities with their ancestral lands.

18.document_title: Blue Carbon in New Zealand: Fiords, Coastal Wetlands, and Seagrass Restoration
18.document_summary: This comprehensive collection examines New Zealand's blue carbon ecosystems and their role in climate regulation. New Zealand's fiords, particularly Doubtful Sound and Dusky Sound, store approximately 2.24 billion tonnes of carbon—about one percent of the world's seabed carbon. These fiords bury organic carbon faster than similar ecosystems worldwide due to unique geography, steep valleys, heavy rainfall, and anaerobic mud conditions. Scientists at the Cawthron Institute are pioneering seed-based seagrass restoration methods, discovering that Zostera muelleri flowers more frequently than previously believed. Seagrass ecosystems capture carbon 55 times faster than tropical rainforests and store four times more carbon per hectare in soils. Coastal wetland restoration projects like Te Wahapū o Waihī integrate mātauranga Māori with coastal ecology, with five iwi collaborating on restoration efforts. Seaweed research reveals varying decomposition rates in deep-sea environments, though scientists raise concerns about accurately measuring seaweed's carbon removal potential. The research emphasizes protecting natural carbon sinks while addressing legal complexities involving Māori rights and rangatiratanga, highlighting kaitiakitanga (stewardship) and cultural significance of coastal ecosystem restoration.

19.document_title: Kōura: Māori Stewardship, Conservation, and Freshwater Ecosystem Restoration in Aotearoa New Zealand

The document examines kōura's ecological importance as ecosystem engineers that control invasive species and restore waterway health. It details the dramatic decline of kōura populations due to trout predation, forest clearing, invasive species (particularly brown bullhead catfish and marron), and water quality degradation, with some populations experiencing up to 99% decline. The collection highlights contemporary restoration efforts led by iwi and freshwater biologists using adapted traditional harvesting methods like the tau kōura technique. It features innovative approaches including John Hollows' professional kōura farming operations in Southland wetlands, which demonstrate sustainable aquaculture, and Kāti Huirapa rūnanga's initiatives to reconnect whānau with traditional food sources. The document emphasizes that mātauranga (Māori knowledge) remains essential for freshwater conservation and advocates for transferring ecosystem management responsibility back to indigenous communities.

20.document_title: Between a Rock and a Hard Place
20.document_summary: This article examines the contentious Denniston Plateau mining debate, which pits resource extraction against environmental preservation. With 6.1 million tonnes of bituminous coal beneath a 150-hectare site, the proposed open-cast mine would generate 14 million tonnes of CO2 emissions when burned—equivalent to New Zealand's annual dairy herd emissions. The article explores the tension between economic benefits ($46 million in salaries for a struggling West Coast region) and environmental costs, including mercury, selenium, arsenic emissions, and climate change contributions. It presents three perspectives: exploitation versus preservation, and a Māori concept of land as taonga (treasure and resource), emphasizing guardianship (kaitiakitanga) and respect for the land's living essence. The author questions whether this traditional approach might offer a less-destructive path to prosperity.

21.document_title: Morepork: New Zealand's Native Owl - Adaptations, Behavior, and Conservation
21.document_summary: This comprehensive document collection explores the morepork (ruru), New Zealand's native nocturnal owl. The first section provides personal observations of morepork hunting behavior, detailing their diet of insects, small birds, mice, and geckos through pellet analysis, with regional variations across different islands. Moreporks inhabit diverse environments including native bush, pine forests, and suburban areas, maintaining 3-5 hectare territories and navigating by memory. The second section examines remarkable sensory and behavioral adaptations enabling nocturnal hunting, including specialized night vision with rod-cell-dominated retinas 100 times more sensitive than pigeons' eyes, asymmetrical skull structures for precise sound localization, and silent flight through specialized feather structures. Research suggests moreporks may detect infrared light to locate warm-blooded prey. The third section details the complete life cycle, focusing on chick development from fledging through independence and territorial behavior. The collection highlights a significant conservation success story involving a nearly-extinct Norfolk Island boobook successfully bred with New Zealand moreporks, resulting in a growing population with potential reintroduction to Lord Howe Island. Additionally, the collection addresses Māori cultural perspectives, where moreporks held spiritual significance as ancestral guardians and messengers.

22.text:
[Page 14] Rangatiratanga—that vexing word, promised in Te Tiriti and, Maori would say, never kept. Erimana Taniora traced its origins in his testimony at Panguru. ‘Raranga’ means to bind or weave; ‘tira’ is a group, such as a hapu. A rangatira is one whose role is to lead and unite a hapu and maintain its mana, and rangatiratanga is the process by which that happens. Rangatiratanga releases human potential—and for Taniora, this was a crucial point. If you are prevented from exercising your function in life, what chance do you have to flourish as a human being? The Waitangi Tribunal has heard this line of argument before, and has spoken strongly in its favour. In its report on the Wai 262 claim concerning Maori traditional knowledge, the tribunal wrote about the failure of governing structures in New Zealand to recognise the iwi role of guardianship or kaitiakitanga, one of the functions of rangatiratanga. The tribunal wrote: “If iwi and hapu are unable to exercise their kaitiaki obligations, they are deprived of a core aspect of their culture… Without kaitiakitanga, Maori are lost.” In his covering letter for the Wai 262 report, then chairman of the Waitangi Tribunal Justice Joe Williams laid down a gauntlet when he wrote: “ What we saw and heard in sittings over many years left us in no doubt that unless it is accepted that New Zealand has two founding cultures, not one; unless Maori culture and identity are valued in everything government says and does; and unless they are welcomed into the very centre of the way we do things in this country, nothing will change. Maori will continue to be perceived, and know they are perceived, as an alien and resented minority, a problem to be managed with a seemingly endless stream of taxpayer funded programmes, but never solved.” Solving the problem, say Ngapuhi, involves a question of honour. In 2010, when the Wai 1040 claim began, the fiery Ngapuhi matriarch Titewhai Harawira told the Waitangi Tribunal that her tupuna were bound by rules of ‘kupu mana’—your word is your bond—and they signed Te Tiriti believing the Crown would honour its word, too. “The Crown, however, has acted with deceit and dishonour, seeking to suppress us and take what it wanted, even those things we agreed to share,” she said. “We don’t want to stand here and argue about which Crown or what Government. We don’t need to. Every single one of them has been part of a lie that festers within our history.” [sidebar 1] If those words sound like anti Pakeha fanaticism, consider this statement made in 1847, a mere seven years after the Treaty was signed, in a letter to the British Colonial Office: “I am grieved beyond the power of expression at the attempted violation of the Treaty, and must never again plead the honour and integrity of Her Majesty’s Government. This appears to have been lost or never to have been possessed.” Who wrote those words of damning disappointment? The Rev Henry Williams, the missionary who translated the Treaty into Maori, explained it to the Ngapuhi chiefs, and acted as the Crown’s intermediary in persuading the chiefs to sign. [Chapter break] At this moment , New Zealand is in the midst of a constitutional review. Unlike most countries, we do not have a single constitutional document, but several, of which the Treaty of Waitangi is considered foundational. Ngapuhi assert that the country picked the wrong foundation, and that it is He Whakaputanga, not the English language Treaty with assumption of ceded sovereignty, that should be the constitutional footing on which this country rests. its To write this story, I needed to go back to the north, to the place where the foundations were laid. I suspect that to resolve the sovereignty question will require us all to ‘go back’ in some way—anathema though that is for many non Maori, whose mantra is to “put the past behind us” and who, by those words, align themselves with the discarders of history. The view from the other side of the Treaty page is, “Ma te tika te he ka tika”—we need to right the wrong. What would it mean if the tribunal were to find in favour of Ngapuhi’s claim? I cannot begin to guess, but I suspect that things would look very different in Waitangi at dawn on Independence Day. The post A Sovereign Act appeared first on New Zealand Geographic .

22.document_title: Ngapuhi Sovereignty: He Whakaputanga, the Declaration of Independence, and Constitutional Foundations of New Zealand
22.document_summary: This comprehensive document collection examines Ngapuhi's assertion of sovereignty and their claim that Māori never ceded sovereignty to Britain. The materials trace Ngapuhi's political development in the early 19th century, focusing on their diplomatic engagement with European powers and the formation of Te Whakaminenga (a confederation) around 1807. Central to the narrative is He Whakaputanga (the Declaration of Independence), signed in 1835 by 34 rangatira with British Resident James Busby's facilitation, which the authors argue should serve as New Zealand's constitutional foundation rather than the Treaty of Waitangi. The documents explore the cultural and political significance of these declarations, drawing parallels to Scotland's Declaration of Arbroath, and emphasize that Ngapuhi's whakaputanga was a manifesto of self-determination asserting independence while seeking external protection. The collection includes discussion of Ngapuhi's 2010 Waitangi Tribunal claim (Wai 1040) questioning the government's authority to govern, the sacred nature of moko marks as royal seals, and the concept of rangatiratanga (chieftainship authority) as essential for Māori flourishing. It also features Rev Henry Williams' 1847 letter expressing disappointment in the Crown's violation of the Treaty, and argues that the Crown's historical dismissal of the Treaty covenant has caused 170 years of suffering.

It’s a model that may point a direction to a new future for the management of wilderness areas, one that recognises the Māori worldview and strikes the fine balance between protection and flexibility. The model may provide some insights into the biggest questions facing New Zealand’s wilderness system. Will it grow any bigger, and if so, how? A purist approach to what constitutes wilderness will ensure that authorities will not add to the current number, while being too flexible undermines the very purpose of the areas. A greater recognition of the Māori worldview could be key to striking this fine balance, and even promote a truly indigenous wilderness policy.

23.document_title: Hunt for the Wilder Places: New Zealand's Wilderness Areas, Policy, and Indigenous Land Management
23.document_summary: This comprehensive document explores New Zealand's wilderness areas through historical, philosophical, and policy perspectives. It traces how American conservation philosophy, particularly through Olaus Murie's 1949 visit, influenced the establishment of New Zealand's 11 official wilderness areas. Key milestones include the National Parks Act 1952, the first wilderness area at Otehake in 1955, and the 1981 Rotoiti conference. New Zealand adopted stricter wilderness criteria than the US, requiring minimum sizes of at least two days' foot travel with no huts, tracks, bridges, or aerial access. The document examines wilderness as both a historical construct and personal concept—a "state of mind and heart" rather than objective designation. It addresses tensions between resource development and conservation, overuse challenges, and the evolution from seven wilderness areas in 1981 to 11 by 2006. A critical focus is recognizing Māori perspectives on wilderness management, challenging Western concepts that render Indigenous homes invisible. Te Urewera National Park's 2014 settlement with Tūhoe represents a transformative model where land is recognized as a legal entity with mana and mauri, with Tūhoe as guardians and governors. This approach offers solutions for balancing protection and flexibility while incorporating Indigenous worldviews into New Zealand's conservation policy.

24.text:
[Page 5] It’s 11am on Saturday 30 March 2008 and dozens of buses and cars fill the parking lot. Hundreds of people, dressed mostly in black, have been welcomed on to Te Tokonganuianoho Marae for this poukai. Dozens of guests; speakers, kaumatua and kuia, sit under a marquee with its walls removed so they may catch any breeze on this hot day. Others brave the sun while many find relief from the heat in the shade of trees, verandahs and the sides of buildings. King Tuheitia and about 75 relations from his extended whanau sit in their own marquee, Whare o te Kahuiariki (House of the Royal Family). Over the lawn from him, the host speakers sit on the paepae. They briefly break the speeches, which have been going for an hour, to welcome on more guests, including some from Whanganui. A few walk directly to the wharenui, where they join others who have lost whanau over the last 12 months. They recline on mattresses and pillows in the porch, clutching photos of those who have passed on. The speeches soon resume (although the monarch does not speak at poukai) and, until lunch, are mainly concerned with sharing greetings. Kuia listening to whaikorero take shelter from the hot Te Kuiti sun. After lunch however, the content changes. This is where one poukai will be noticeably different from the next. Koro Wetere, who sits on this marae’s kaumatua council, explains, “Generally debate ties back to the raupatu. They want to know how the grants are going.” Tiwha Bell, chair of the committee, adds, “But there are bigger things than just grants; the political side, the relationship with different tribes, the economics and all of those things.” I ask if anyone can stand up and speak. Hinekahukura Tuti Aranui, or Aunty Tuti, says, “Yes—but anybody has to be somebody. They have to have some standing in the community.” Although the poukai committee has a pretty good idea who will come and speak, there can be the unexpected. “Jokers come here wanting to push a barrow on the day of the poukai,” Bell explains, “but I soon put a stop to that nonsense.” [Chapter Break] Under the trees at the sunny end of the wharekai, people are taking time out from the speeches; drinking tea, smoking cigarettes and invariably starting conversations with something like, “Hey, auntie, good to see you! Kei te pehea koe?” Catching up with whanau has long been a feature of poukai but, for those like Kingi Turner, it can go deeper than that. Down from Te Awamutu for his fourth poukai this year, this proud father of two and grandfather of six tells me, “[Poukai] means I get a chance to come back home to Te Tokonganuianoho in Te Kuiti to reconnect with my whanau, my marae, my waahi tapu (sacred ground) around here. It gives me a chance to reconnect the strands that I know are very strong—from our Maniapoto people to the Kingitanga—and it reconnects me to those people who are no longer with us.” Is it a matter of identity as well? “Oh yes. We live in mainstream New Zealand life where another culture predominates.

24.document_title: King's Tour: The Poukai Tradition and the Maori Kingitanga Movement
24.document_summary: This comprehensive document explores the poukai tradition, the travelling court of the Maori King Tuheitia, which celebrates 150 years of the Kingitanga movement. Originating as solace for Waikato Maori during 19th-century land confiscations, poukai gatherings unite Maori communities to feast, grieve, share news, and bring concerns to the King. The document details a 2008 poukai at Te Tokonganuianoho Marae in Te Kuiti, describing the elaborate feasts, ceremonial welcomes, formal speeches, and substantive discussions on topics including land grants, tribal relations, and economics. It traces the historical context: King Tawhiao established poukai after the 1863 British invasion of Waikato and subsequent raupatu (land seizure) that displaced thousands. The tradition represents resilience and mana, serving bereaved families and the destitute post-war. The poukai operates independently under Maori leadership with minimal external influence, running from 10am to 4pm to accommodate travelers. Participants reconnect with whanau (family), share kai (food), and maintain cultural traditions passed down through generations, emphasizing Maori sovereignty, identity, and manaaki (hospitality). The document includes historical perspectives from 1882 when Kerry-Nicholls visited King Tawhiao to discuss raupatu settlement, highlighting the King's determination to maintain Maori sovereignty and traditions.

25.document_title: Sea Change: Marine Management and Conservation in Aotearoa New Zealand
25.document_summary: This comprehensive collection examines New Zealand's marine resource management, conservation, and governance challenges. Key topics include Kaikoura's successful community engagement process resulting in marine protection legislation (2014) with whale and seal sanctuaries; Te Korowai and no-take reserves effectiveness; collaborative community-based management in Otago through taiapure customary areas; and marine biosecurity challenges from invasive species like Undaria seaweed and Mediterranean fanworms. 26.document_title: A Gulf in my Thinking
26.document_summary: Kennedy Warne reflects on his deep personal connection to the Hauraki Gulf in New Zealand, tracing memories from childhood through his grandfather's swordfishing boat. He explores the concept of guardianship and stewardship through the Inuit legend of the mother of the sea—a story about how people's disrespect for the ocean causes the sea's bounty to disappear until a shaman restores harmony by combing her hair. Warne connects this ancient wisdom to the Māori concept of kaitiakitanga, arguing it represents a profound stewardship that goes beyond mere resource management. He observes a growing movement of individuals taking environmental responsibility into their own hands, becoming "ministers of the environment" by caring for wetlands, forests, and oceans. The essay emphasizes humanity's forgotten relationship with the sea and calls for a return to reverence and respect for the natural world.

27.text:
[Page 8] interests, if the stewardship land process is an opportunity to ensure access to our lake bed, then we should certainly take advantage of that.” Zoom out from Mahinapua to the long green sweep of Te Tai Poutini/the West Coast, and there are many other such ancient places with contemporary significance on stewardship land. Pull back again to take in stewardship land nationwide, and you’ll find myriad similar sites: part of a deeper geography that lives on in the place names, practices and memories of local hapū. An increasingly vocal, self resourced Māori world is seeking to haul such places back into the light, and is asserting its right to have a say in how they’re managed. Given the vast majority of stewardship land is in Ngāi Tahu’s takiwā, and the majority of that is on Te Tai Poutini, it’s not surprising the iwi’s local and central leadership was paying close attention when reclassification process was announced. But to truly understand why they picked up the phone to call their lawyers, you have to go back even further. the [Chapter Break] In 1859, young Nelson settler and Crown agent James Mackay Jr was paddling the Māwhera when he upset his canoe. The river, also known as the Grey, is significant to Poutini Ngāi Tahu. The river’s path to the sea was forged by Aoraki’s nephew, Tūterakiwhānoa, to drain the wrecked hull of his uncle’s island sized waka. Later, in the time of mortals, the river was a trade and travel route. The principal kāinga of Ngāti Waewae was then at the river’s mouth. So it’s interesting that when Mackay had his mishap, among the items the river soaked was the freshly signed deed of sale for the entire West Coast. The signatures could still be read, but in places the ink had faded and bled. The history of outsiders making unilateral decisions about Poutini Ngāi Tahu’s territory had begun two years earlier, when Mackay first visited. He told one of the senior chiefs, Tarapuhi, that the government had already bought their territory from arch rivals Ngāti Toa in 1853 for £5000. The Crown had paid this and other amounts to various northern iwi for parts of Te Waipounamu, including portions of the Coast, without bothering to ascertain who actually owned the land. Tarapuhi and the other chiefs asserted their legitimate ownership. Stewardship land designations are at times nonsensically small and isolated. At Woodpecker Bay, a small comma shaped parcel of forest at the centre of the picture is stewardship land, while the remainder of the area behind the ridgeline is part of Paparoa National Park. Mackay then returned in 1858 with authorisation to purchase the entire West Coast from them for £200, and to leave the iwi with 200 hectares in reserves. His offer was met with the contempt it deserved. Chief Werita Tainui dismissed it as the price of a horse. When Mackay returned with a marginally better offer, he was well aware of the value of the land: there was significant demand for it, and the possibility of goldfields. Under Te Tiriti o Waitangi, the Crown had a duty to act in good faith, and had committed to actively protecting the chiefs’ ability to exercise chieftainship over their lands. As the Crown’s agent, if Mackay was aware of this conflict of interest, he didn’t let on. He made the Crown’s final offer: £300. The chiefs agreed—in part to assert their mana over the land in the face of Ngāti Toa’s claims. The price might not have mattered if Poutini Ngāi Tahu had been able to reserve from sale whatever lands they chose—a right guaranteed under Te Tiriti. The 151,757 hectares they wished to keep would have protected rights to pounamu and provided an economic base for future generations. But with few Māori on the Coast at the time and the balance of power tipped firmly in favour of settlers, the chiefs settled for a little more than 4000 hectares scattered across 58 reserves. (The Crown later described this allocation as “the bare minimum”, with “scant consideration” for future needs.) The chiefs did manage to insist on reserves at Māwhera (which later became Greymouth) and the banks of the Arahura, and secured ownership of the Arahura riverbed up to its source. Despite its dunking in the river, the Arahura Deed stood. The Crown acquired and then began to sell the land. Goldfields, mining, farming and logging built towns and a measure of prosperity for Pākehā. Meanwhile, many of the reserves, including the one at Māwhera, were taken from the iwi’s control and administered by government trustees. The trustees made some leases perpetual without the owners’ consent, and later fixed rents. Some land was sold off against the owners’ will. Parts of the Arahura Reserve were taken for roading and the railway line without compensation, because until well into the 20th century, the law didn’t require compensation to be paid when taking Māori land for public works. Other ancestral landscapes, such as Kaniere and Mahinapua, were put into scenic reserves. Today, 87 per cent of Poutini Ngāi Tahu’s takiwā is managed by DOC. Ngāi Tahu had little, if any, say in any of this. Ngāi Tahu is now in a position to insist on its rights. Socially and politically, there are signs of change as well. The law is now clear on the need for DOC to work with iwi as Treaty partners: section 4 of the Conservation Act requires DOC to give effect to the Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi—the strongest incorporation of the Treaty into any of New Zealand’s laws. A landmark Supreme Court case, Ngāi Tai ki Tāmaki v Minister of Conservation , affirmed DOC’s Treaty responsibilities in 2018. 27.document_title: Stewardship Land Reclassification in New Zealand: Conservation, Māori Rights, and the Old Ghost Road
27.document_summary: This comprehensive document collection examines New Zealand's stewardship land—nine percent of Aotearoa's total land area—through interconnected narratives spanning conservation policy, indigenous rights, and economic development. The collection begins with the Old Ghost Road project in the Mokihinui Gorge, illustrating how stewardship land's lower protection status both threatened and enabled conservation initiatives, ultimately generating $4 million annually for local communities after Meridian Energy abandoned its proposed dam project. The documents trace the government's 2021 fast-tracked reclassification process, which proposed appointing expert panels to assess stewardship land within eight months. This initiative sparked significant controversy, particularly from Ngāi Tahu iwi, who filed urgent High Court proceedings citing consultation breaches and Treaty of Waitangi violations. The historical context reveals how the Crown's 1859 acquisition of the West Coast from Poutini Ngāi Tahu for £300 left the iwi with only 4,000 hectares despite claiming 151,757 hectares, with 87% of their territory now managed by DOC with minimal iwi input. The collection explores the tension between traditional conservation frameworks and contemporary approaches that integrate mātauranga (Māori knowledge) and recognize Māori cultural values extending beyond preservation to include economic and commercial use on ancestral land. Through case studies such as Lake Mahinapua, the documents examine how mana whenua and national assessment panels are collaboratively developing integrated conservation models that respect rangatiratanga while addressing concerns about mining interests and the Stockton Coal Mine on Denniston Plateau.

28.text:
[Page 9] Flack is tangata tiaki, a local guardian or trustee of this coastline, and the chair of the East Otago Taiāpure committee. Taiāpure, coastal patches, are one of the tools Māori have been using to manage their customary fisheries and exercise their rangatiratanga, or chieftainship, since the Fisheries Settlement. For 24 years, Flack’s hapū, Kāti Huirapa ki Puketeraki, have looked after this area with other locals and fishers. We can see parts of the taiāpure from here. To the south, beyond a sloped headland, cliffs, points and estuaries stretch for 22 kilometres. It’s not technically a marine protected area, and would not count towards the United Nations convention, because commercial fishing is still allowed. But the committee have banned set netting here, protected native kelp from harvest, restricted commercial cockle fishing, removed invasive seaweeds, and in 2010 placed an enduring rāhui on collecting pāua around one hard hit peninsula.

28.document_title: Marine Protection and Indigenous Rights in New Zealand: Conservation, Treaty Rights, and Sustainable Governance
28.document_summary: This comprehensive collection examines New Zealand's marine conservation challenges and the intersection of environmental protection with indigenous rights and Treaty of Waitangi obligations. The documents trace marine reserves from Goat Island's pioneering success to current proposals for expanded protection in the Hauraki Gulf and Kermadec Ocean Sanctuary. New Zealand currently has less than 0.5% of its waters fully protected, falling short of the 30% protection target by 2030. Key tensions exist between conservation goals and Māori rights, particularly regarding the outdated Marine Reserves Act and the Fisheries Settlement, which converted Māori fishing rights into tradeable quota divorced from geographic connection to rohe. Case studies include the proposed Te Umu Koau Marine Reserve in Otago and the contentious Kermadec Ocean Sanctuary, where iwi rejected the Crown's initial offer due to Treaty rights concerns. The articles showcase successful ecosystem restoration through well-designed reserves and Māori-led management alternatives like taiāpure and mātaitai, which combine conservation with cultural practices. Proposed legislation aims to increase protected areas from 0.28% to nearly 5% through 12 new high-protection zones while incorporating Treaty principles allowing limited customary harvesting by iwi and hapū according to tikanga and kaitiakitanga. The collection emphasizes the need for genuine partnership, respect for indigenous sovereignty and rangatiratanga, and innovative solutions reconciling marine conservation with Māori settlement rights.

30.document_title: Stewardship Land Reclassification in New Zealand: Conservation, Māori Rights, and the Old Ghost Road
30.document_summary: This comprehensive document collection examines New Zealand's stewardship land—nine percent of Aotearoa's total land area—through interconnected narratives spanning conservation policy, indigenous rights, and economic development. The collection begins with the Old Ghost Road project in the Mokihinui Gorge, illustrating how stewardship land's lower protection status both threatened and enabled conservation initiatives, ultimately generating $4 million annually for local communities after Meridian Energy abandoned its proposed dam project. The documents trace the government's 2021 fast-tracked reclassification process, which proposed appointing expert panels to assess stewardship land within eight months. This initiative sparked significant controversy, particularly from Ngāi Tahu iwi, who filed urgent High Court proceedings citing consultation breaches and Treaty of Waitangi violations. The historical context reveals how the Crown's 1859 acquisition of the West Coast from Poutini Ngāi Tahu for £300 left the iwi with only 4,000 hectares despite claiming 151,757 hectares, with 87% of their territory now managed by DOC with minimal iwi input. The collection explores the tension between traditional conservation frameworks and contemporary approaches that integrate mātauranga (Māori knowledge) and recognize Māori cultural values extending beyond preservation to include economic and commercial use on ancestral land. Through case studies such as Lake Mahinapua, the documents examine how mana whenua and national assessment panels are collaboratively developing integrated conservation models that respect rangatiratanga while addressing concerns about mining interests and the Stockton Coal Mine on Denniston Plateau.

31.document_title: Far North: Tail of the Fish - New Zealand's Remote Peninsula: Economic Development, Māori Heritage, and Environmental Transformation
31.document_summary: This comprehensive document explores New Zealand's remote Far North region, specifically the Aupouri Peninsula (Te Hiku-o-te-Ika), known as the "Tail of the Fish." It traces the peninsula's geological history, including its formation through sand tombolos and ancient kauri forests buried 30,000-50,000 years ago. The work details Māori settlement and spiritual significance, particularly the journey of spirits along Ninety Mile Beach to Cape Reinga. A major focus is the kauri gum industry (1840s-1940s), which generated approximately $50 million in revenue and attracted international workers, including Croatians from Dalmatia. The document chronicles the region's transformation from a sand-devastated wasteland into productive land through strategic reforestation beginning in 1959, when the New Zealand Forest Service established Pinus radiata forests that stabilized dunes and provided employment for Māori communities. Today, the region's economy is sustained by diverse industries including ancient kauri timber processing, avocado horticulture (producing 13-20% of the national crop), and pine forests that employ 280 people and inject $12.6 million annually into the local economy. The text addresses ongoing Māori land and fishing rights issues, including the Muriwhenua fishing claim and emerging aquaculture ventures like oyster farming. Despite its sparse amenities and harsh landscape, the region attracts hundreds of thousands of tourists annually and represents a fragile but economically significant way of life with unique biodiversity and cultural heritage.

It is the whakataukī (Māori proverb) that means most to Māori data, AI and technology ethicist Dr Karaitiana Taiuru (Ngāi Tahu, Ngāti Kahungunu, Ngāti Toa). Translated to English, it means "the ability to create and control our destiny for generations to come". It links in well with his work and family life, Taiuru told RNZ Nights. For his work, it reminded Taiuru why he still does what he does and that there was a new generation of children who will not know life without AI and it was "our role to create the new normal for them". Taiuru applies a te ao Māori perspective to AI. https://www.rnz.co.nz/national/programmes/nig new generation of children who will not know life without AI and it was "our role to create the new normal for them". Taiuru applies a te ao Māori perspective to AI. https://www.rnz.co.nz/national/programmes/nig hts/audio/2018930609/whakatauki of the week with karaitiana taiuru Listen to the full interview on Nights "We already know that internationally, there's bias against minority peoples so what I do, in conjunction with international best practices with artificial intelligence and other technologies, is bring that Māori voice and Te Tiriti o Waitangi considerations to play." There were "a number" of cultural values that needed to be considered in terms of AI, he said. Many Māori have moko (facial tattoos) so understanding how that was considered with facial technologies was a big factor. In his personal life, the whakataukī applied to his whānau. "For me, I consider that I have an opportunity to create wealth and opportunities for my children and also for my grandchildren. "I live by that rule. I make that sure my children have the opportunities that I didn't always have, make sure they have access to education, financial resources, a home, and part of my planning in life is that my grandchildren will also have the same access and all going well in life, I should see my great grandchildren and maybe great great grandchildren whom I will also ensure that they have equal access. "And I know my children also that they consider the same sort of philosophies in life where they want to protect their whānau as well for the future." Taiuru said the whakataukī came out of working groups around the South Island when Ngāi Tahu was trying to identify a new tribal vision that would be carried into the future. It came after settlements with the Crown in 1996. "That whakataukī was the key whakataukī that came out of those hui." Related

Whakataukī (Māori proverbs) are a fun and powerful way to help rangatahi develop their own voices and find grounding in the "continuum of whakapapa", Dr Hinemoa Elder says. The child psychiatrist and author weaves observations from her professional life into the new book Dear Moko a child centred reshaping of her beloved 2020 whakataukī collection. https://www.rnz.co.nz/nation professional life into the new book Dear Moko a child centred reshaping of her beloved 2020 whakataukī collection. https://www.rnz.co.nz/nation al/programmes/saturday/audio/2018961498/hinemoa elder dear moko The idea that children should be "seen and not heard" first introduced to Aotearoa by Pākehā settlers is one that Elder challenges in Dear Moko. Although this "older, more colonised" message about the place of young people still prevails in New Zealand culture, it is critical that whānau seek to understand young people's actual lived experience, she says, as they did in generations past. "I'm constantly trying to tune into a tūpuna [ancestral] voice in thinking about their struggles and trying to retain at least some of the older kōrero." Most young people are just trying to please their families, she says, and are "exquisitely attuned" to how their whānau receives them. "I'm often saying to parents 'Hey, our teenagers, our rangatahi get a bit of a bad rap but actually they're very caring because they've been keeping their pain private in order to protect your feelings and they pay a big price for that'." [Page 1] 2024 01 29 21:53:12+13:00 Anton Matthews is the director of Hustle Group, a company operating a bunch of restaurants and catering companies in Ōtautahi Christchurch. He's also a big advocate for people learning te reo Māori, also running online course Normalising Te Reo Māori. In the next in a weekly series, he shares a favourite whakataukī, or traditional Māori aphorism, with Emile Donovan. Ko te amorangi ki mua, ko te hāpai ō ki muri The leader at the front and the workers behind the scenes This simple whakataukī, or Māori proverb, is a multi layered favourite of Matthews. While he was fortunate to grow up immersed in te ao Māori, including being educated at kohanga reo and kura kaupapa, Matthews tells Nights anyone exposed to a lot of te reo Māori quickly learns that it’s a language rich in metaphor. “There’s the literal meaning of whatever has been said, but it often takes a couple of years (sometimes it never actually dawns on us), but there is a hidden meaning there as well. “That’s what I love about whakataukī is that yep, there's that kind of surface layer literally, what is the person saying? But what's the hidden meaning? What are they really trying to explain or what sort of message or idea are they trying to convey when they use the whakataukī? That's the beauty of language, not just te reo Māori, but any language has those kinds of beautiful nuances, I think.” Matthews says he loves all sorts of different whakataukī for different reasons and occasions, but his favourite is particularly appropriate to his work in the hospitality sector. Ko te amorangi ki mua, ko te hāpai ō ki muri has two parts to it, Matthews says. Amorangi is a term that refers to recognised iwi leaders, the ones who are front and centre when leading a pōwhiri, or welcome, onto the marae. “These are the familiar faces that everyone kind of knows… these people are highly respected. They have a lot of mana. We look to them when we need guidance.” Te hāpai ō referred to in the second part of the whakataukī is the complete opposite, Matthews says.

45.document_title: Waka Jumper, Mahi and Chilly Bin Added to Oxford English Dictionary
45.document_summary: The Oxford English Dictionary has added several New Zealand words and phrases to its latest update, including "waka jumper" (a member of Parliament who switches parties during a term), "mahi" (work or activity in Māori contexts), "chilly bin" (portable insulated container), and various te reo Māori terms like "tikanga," "kapa haka," and "Aotearoan." The addition reflects the increasing use of te reo Māori in New Zealand society and media. While experts celebrate the inclusion of Māori words as a sign of language normalization, some, including Māori Language Commission chief executive Ngahiwi Apanui, expressed concerns about "Aotearoan," viewing it as inconsistent with Māori orthographic conventions. Linguists note this represents the evolving and distinctive nature of New Zealand English.

[Page 1] Maaoridom has spent the week commemorating the eighth Maaori monarch Te Arikinui Kuini Nga wai hono i te po. The traditions and customs of the Kiingitanga trace back to the mid 1850s when iwi came together on the shores of Lake Taupoo to discuss the idea of appointing a King. The role was eventually offered to a rangatira of great mana, Pootatau Te Wherowhero who after initially declining, accepted the role. Today the home of Te Kiingitanga is Turangawaewae in Ngaaruawaahia and for many generations Waikato whaanau have devoted their entire lives to serving their monarch. One of those people is Rahui Papa, spokesperson or maangai mo te Kiingitanga. He talks to Mihingarangi at Turangawaewae.

48.text:
[Page 3] mothers, in particular Māori, keep their baby's placenta and return it to Papatūānuku. "[The lead carer] respected our choices. She understood tikanga without us having to explain it and when a hospital midwife made her negative comment about our choice to keep the placenta, the carer corrected her without her or us losing face, which is a skilled and culturally appropriate way to correct a mistake of that nature," the mother stated. A former midwife with no relation to this birth, now, a well child nurse Sharron Wipiti said it was "crazy" that there were cultural breaches because she only knew tikanga as being a strict practice. "We trained all the midwives to let people do their own tikanga, and that's for any nationality and religion." When Wipiti was younger, she said there was no consideration for tikanga when a māmā was in labour. "You got on the bed, you had your baby, and they just got rid of the placenta. I never knew there was such thing as keeping the placenta." But it is something she had learnt since "regaining being Māori," which is what got her and another midwife to create the Hapū Wānanga in Taranaki a programme to help wāhine hapū to reclaim traditional birthing practices. Regardless, Wipiti said consent everything. Communication and environment a point of concern The complaint stated the strategies staff and the obstetric used to "motivate" the woman to deliver her baby were damaging. Multiple staff members said the tone and manner of the experienced registrar were not unusual but can be taken as "unsympathetic" in a situation. "Everything [seems] more dramatic than needs be when you're in a heightened state of pain," Wipiti said. The interventions were necessary, the mother agreed, but raised concerns around the need for tikanga of manaakitanga. She stated that she did not want to risk not having the assisted birth, but she felt that there was time to be kind, respectful, and calm. As a result of the mother's complaint, Health NZ has since implemented nine changes including readily available information, two new roles created for Māori cultural education programmes, a dedicated Kaiāwhina position in Health NZ Southern Maternity Services, a 'Hua Oranga' midwifery performance appraisal tool, and cultural safety training. Health NZ Southern amended its policy on cord blood testing to include the consumer's right to informed consent prior to cord blood being taken for testing. 48.document_title: Health NZ Southern Made Multiple Breaches During Māori Mum's Labour - HDC Report
48.document_summary: A Deputy Health and Disability Commissioner report details multiple breaches by Health NZ Southern during a Māori mother's labour in 2017. The hospital staff dismissed the mother's cultural wishes regarding placenta retention and proceeded with an episiotomy without proper informed consent, leaving her feeling violated. Key breaches included: lack of consent for umbilical cord blood testing (violating Right 7(10) of the Code), failure to respect cultural safety and te ao Māori beliefs regarding tapu (sacred) practices, and inadequate communication during emergency procedures. The mother developed PTSD symptoms and received ACC compensation. In response, Health NZ Southern implemented nine changes including cultural safety training, new Māori cultural education roles, amended cord blood testing policies requiring informed consent, and the introduction of a 'Hua Oranga' midwifery performance appraisal tool to improve cultural competency and respectful care.

49.text:
[Page 1] From Tangata Whenua to Tangata Tiriti, from seasoned attendees to first time visitors, their visions for Aotearoa share a common theme kotahitanga. Waka mana wāhine inspire the next gen Out on the moana, Tanya Rogers stands as the kaihautū (captain) of Tī Eke Waka o Te Arawa, one of the few waka exclusively paddled by wāhine. Representing Ngāti Whakaue and Taranaki, she said the journey to Waitangi was hard work, but ultimately rewarding. "We practiced all through winter, through dry land paddles. For most of us, this was our first time paddling here, and it was absolutely magical," But she said their mission extends beyond the water. "Our job is to bring our rangatahi up. We hope we've been an inspiration to them so they can reach their aspirations of being wāhine toa." What she hopes for the future of Aotearoa she said, is kotahitanga. "I'd like to see more unity, more coming together, to see our Māori people standing together, being strong and taking us into the future. And again, our rangatahi are doing that." 'Paving the way for our mokopuna' Kataraina WiHongi, attending Waitangi with her mokopuna, envisions a future grounded in peace and justice. "If we aim for justice and peace for our tamariki and mokopuna, with their whakapapa and whakaaro, i raro i te humārie the humbleness and the peace then kia tau te rangimārie i roto i ngā mea katoa," While watching the waka celebrations with her mokopuna, she reflected on how much the space has changed. "When I was a little girl, I just swam here, because it was a Pākehā space. But now, it is very Māori. Our tamariki are growing up with te reo in kōhanga, in kura kaupapa and we need to embrace that." A space for all New Zealanders Pat Gray, Agnes Hermans, Ange Jones and Margo Irvine are representatives of Whangārei Network Waitangi, an organisation they said has spent decades educating Pākehā on Treaty issues. Their focus now is on constitutional transformation, guided by Matike Mai, a report envisioning a future where tino rangatiratanga is honoured. "We believe that an Aotearoa that upholds Te Tiriti benefits all New Zealanders," Hermans said. "A constitution based on Matike Mai would create a future for all of us." Jones added, "For us, tino rangatiratanga, honouring te tiriti is good for all New Zealand. Te ao Māori, the values, the values system care for the environment etcetera, this is what makes Aotearoa great." While being at Waitangi, kitted out in their 'Tangata Tiriti' kākahu, Hermans said they have received "lots of aroha and lots of support." "Particularly from tangata whenua, saying 'kia ora thank you for showing up' 'we really appreciate you being here." But they also received a lot of nods and smiles from Pākehā too, she said. "I think we are being a witness to something that is bigger than just the few of us, there is real base support." For Margo Irvine, attending Waitangi is an experience every New Zealander should have at least once. "I wish that all New Zealanders could experience the atmosphere here the passion, the fun, the colour, the kotahitanga. It is a very special thing." A first time visitor's whakaaro For one first time visitor from Tāmaki Makaurau, Waitangi was an unforgettable experience. "Waitangi is absolutely wonderful, it's inclusive, it's welcoming, I understand now why its so popular for Tangata Whenua and Pākehā like myself... Lifes an adventure and this is part of it." Looking ahead, she hoped for "a more cohesive society, one that respects tangata whenua." 50.text:
[Page 2] in 1860 and officially recognised in law by 1945, Māori wardens play a key role in supporting communities across the motu. The relationships they foster in their rohe enables them to anticipate the needs of their communities. Most wardens are just everyday people called to the role by wanting to serve te iwi Māori. For many, being a warden is in their whakapapa, with whānau serving before them. But Matarora Smith was not one of those. Growing up, she never imagined herself in the role she has today the chief executive of Tāmaki ki te Tonga District Māori Wardens. Instead, she was involved in peacekeeping of a different kind caring for her 13 siblings and felt her calling was to be a mother. "I got married, had children. At that time, hubby went to work and you stayed at home, looked after the kids and looked after the house." So when her daughter and grandchildren moved over to Australia, she followed them across the ditch. Settling in Sydney, Smith worked for an organisation supporting the homeless population, where she saw many similarities between the problems aboriginal peoples were facing and Māori back home. "All of a sudden a light bulb went on. My grandchildren moved back here [to New Zealand] and I thought, 'it's only me here, that's it, I'm going home'. And when I came back, I wanted to do the same work." Upon her return a friend suggested she help on an initiative called 'Project Walkthrough' in Manukau. Funded by the NZ Police in collaboration with Māori Wardens, their aim was to reduce alcohol consumption in public, and ensure that restaurants and bars were taking care of patrons, offering food, and not selling them more booze when they were already intoxicated. Smith jumped at the opportunity, excited to play a role in supporting people in need. The only catch: you had to be a registered Māori warden and Smith was not. 'I thought, 'what's a Māori warden?" But despite no prior knowledge of Māori wardens or what they did, she signed up. Since her first day all the years ago, she has worked hard starting on the front lines and rising the ranks to manage a team of wardens in her role as Chief Executive of her district. All wardens are volunteers and there are 10 Māori sub associations in the Tāmaki ki the Tonga District Smith works with, which runs from Howick to Māngere and Pukekohe in the south. no caption Her office and home in Tāmaki Makaurau is at the end of a long driveway. A metal gate opens onto a well manicured lawn where we are greeted by a loudly barking golden labrador, who turns out to be a big softie. Smith is not wearing her warden uniform but is dressed instead in a black polo shirt

[Page 1] Kotahitanga in action: Hundreds descend upon the Treaty grounds alongside the Kiingitanga and Rātana ByElla Stewart (Ngāpuhi, Te Māhurehure, Ngāti Manu) Longform Journalist, Te Ao Māori 2024 02 04 21:13:14+13:00 https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.ht ml?videoId=6346213822112 As the sun shone over the Waitangi Treaty Grounds on Sunday afternoon, up the hill came two of Māoridom's leading voices, Kiingi Tuuheita and Rātana Tumuaki Manuao, Te Kohamutunga Tamou, bringing with them iwi leaders from across the motu, a true sight of kotahitanga. Responding to the tono from Ngāpuhi rangatira, the Kiingitanga led hundreds onto the grounds, carrying with them the mauri from hui aa motu. Many from Tainui iwi travelled up to Paihia in one of the seven buses that the Kiingitanga organised, which left Waikato on Saturday. The Kiingitanga typically mark the day on its own whenua, but this year, they arrived in style. The sounds of the Rātana brass band overlapped with the haka of the kaihoe. As the manuhiri approached the atea the hau kāinga quickly put out more chairs to accommodate what seemed like a never ending ope. Read more: See how the day unfolded at Waitangi here. 51.document_title: Kotahitanga in Action: Hundreds Gather at Treaty Grounds with Kiingitanga and Rātana
51.document_summary: On February 4, 2024, hundreds of Māori gathered at the Waitangi Treaty Grounds in a powerful display of kotahitanga (unity). Led by Kiingi Tuuheitia and Rātana Tumuaki Manuao, iwi leaders from across the country assembled to voice concerns about the government's proposed Treaty principles bill. The pōwhiri featured speeches emphasizing unity and peaceful resistance, with leaders like Ngāpuhi Rangatira Matua Hone Sadler urging iwi to remain peaceful while standing firm. Bayden Barber referenced the 1990s kotahitanga movement, calling for continued strategic planning. Te Taepa Kameta criticized Minister Shane Jones's absence, while Rāhui Papa emphasized mobilizing under mana motuhake and ensuring He Whakaputanga receives equal standing with Te Tiriti. The gathering concluded with Tainui representatives singing in harmony, marking a historic moment of Māori solidarity.

1.fileDescription: Kaitiakitanga is a foundational Māori concept of guardianship and environmental stewardship rooted in the worldview that humans are part of nature. A kaitiaki is a guardian recognized by tangata whenua to care for natural areas such as lakes, forests, and waterways. Traditional conservation practices include temporary rāhui (resource restrictions), use of the lunar calendar (maramataka) for planting and harvesting, sustainable hunting and fishing, and blessing of mauri stones by tohunga (priests). Key spiritual concepts include mana (spiritual power), tapu (spiritual restriction), and mauri (life force). Today, kaitiakitanga is experiencing renewal as iwi (tribes) restore ecosystems and apply traditional knowledge in modern contexts. Practical examples include Ngāi Tahu's guardianship of pounamu resources, Ngāti Toa's fishery restoration at Pukerua Bay, and multi-tribal efforts to stop river pollution and protect endangered species. The document outlines challenges in collaborating with non-Māori stakeholders and details legislative frameworks such as the Resource Management Act 1991 and Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004 that incorporate kaitiakitanga principles. Kaitiakitanga offers perspectives on environmental stewardship and kinship with nature, enabling Māori to fulfill ancestral responsibilities while contributing to broader environmental sustainability.

chunkHighlights.text: By Te Ahukaramū Charles Royal

Understanding kaitiakitanga Kaitiakitanga means guardianship and
protection. It is a way of managing the environment, based on the Māori world view. A kaitiaki is a guardian. This can be a person or group that cares for an area such as a lake or forest. They are given that role by the local iwi . Māori world view In the Māori world view, people are closely connected to the land and nature. Kaitiakitanga is based on this idea of humans as part of the natural world. Traditional practices In the past, people followed traditional practices when they were hunting, fishing, growing or finding food. These helped them to care for the environment. They included: temporary bans (rāhui) on taking food from an area using the lunar calendar (maramataka) to decide when to plant and harvest taking only what was needed hunting and fishing only for food, not as sport using bird snares at the right time – for example, not when the birds were breeding. Mana, tapu and mauri Mana means spiritual power. If a forest has mana , it will have plenty of flowers, fruit and birds. Tapu can mean spiritual restriction. Sometimes rāhui (restrictions) are needed to help the mana of the forest. A rāhui might stop people taking birds, fish or fruit from a certain area, or at a certain time. Mauri means life force. This must be protected in forests, rivers, gardens, lakes and the sea. Special mauri stones, which tohunga (priests) said prayers over, were used to preserve this force. Kaitiakitanga today Today there is growing interest in kaitiakitanga. Iwi are restoring their environment and culture, and using traditional ideas in the modern world. Ngāi Tahu are guardians of pounamu (greenstone) in the South Island. Te Āti Awa ki Taranaki made a claim to the government to stop pollution in their fishing areas. Four iwi (Ngāti Kahungunu, Rangitāne, Muaūpoko and Ngāti Raukawa) have come together to stop the Manawatū River being polluted. The Te Rarawa people are working to save the kūkupa (New Zealand pigeon). Kaitiakitanga has also been included in some laws,
such as the Resource Management Act 1991.

7.fileDescription: Kaitiakitanga is a foundational Māori concept of guardianship and environmental stewardship rooted in the worldview that humans are part of nature. A kaitiaki is a guardian recognized by tangata whenua to care for natural areas such as lakes, forests, and waterways. Traditional conservation practices include temporary rāhui (resource restrictions), use of the lunar calendar (maramataka) for planting and harvesting, sustainable hunting and fishing, and blessing of mauri stones by tohunga (priests). Key spiritual concepts include mana (spiritual power), tapu (spiritual restriction), and mauri (life force). Today, kaitiakitanga is experiencing renewal as iwi (tribes) restore ecosystems and apply traditional knowledge in modern contexts. Practical examples include Ngāi Tahu's guardianship of pounamu resources, Ngāti Toa's fishery restoration at Pukerua Bay, and multi-tribal efforts to stop river pollution and protect endangered species. The document outlines challenges in collaborating with non-Māori stakeholders and details legislative frameworks such as the Resource Management Act 1991 and Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004 that incorporate kaitiakitanga principles. Kaitiakitanga offers perspectives on environmental stewardship and kinship with nature, enabling Māori to fulfill ancestral responsibilities while contributing to broader environmental sustainability.

chunkHighlights.text: Legislation

Kaitiakitanga has been included in some legislation. The Resource Management Act 1991 aims to enable sustainable management of environmental resources. It states that people managing resources under the act must take kaitiakitanga into account.

Kaitiakitanga was also included in the Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004, where it has the same meaning.

8.fileDescription: Kennedy Warne reflects on his deep personal connection to the Hauraki Gulf in New Zealand, tracing memories from childhood through his grandfather's swordfishing boat. He explores the concept of guardianship and stewardship through the Inuit legend of the mother of the sea—a story about how people's disrespect for the ocean causes the sea's bounty to disappear until a shaman restores harmony by combing her hair. Warne connects this ancient wisdom to the Māori concept of kaitiakitanga, arguing it represents a profound stewardship that goes beyond mere resource management. He observes a growing movement of individuals taking environmental responsibility into their own hands, becoming "ministers of the environment" by caring for wetlands, forests, and oceans. The essay emphasizes humanity's forgotten relationship with the sea and calls for a return to reverence and respect for the natural world.

In the next in a weekly series, he shares a favourite whakataukī, or traditional Māori aphorism, with Emile Donovan. Ko te amorangi ki mua, ko te hāpai ō ki muri The leader at the front and the workers behind the scenes This simple whakataukī, or Māori proverb, is a multi layered favourite of Matthews. While he was fortunate to grow up immersed in te ao Māori, including being educated at kohanga reo and kura kaupapa, Matthews tells Nights anyone exposed to a lot of te reo Māori quickly learns that it’s a language rich in metaphor. “There’s the literal meaning of whatever has been said, but it often takes a couple of years (sometimes it never actually dawns on us), but there is a hidden meaning there as well. “That’s what I love about whakataukī is that yep, there's that kind of surface layer literally, what is the person saying? But what's the hidden meaning? What are they really trying to explain or what sort of message or idea are they trying to convey when they use the whakataukī? That's the beauty of language, not just te reo Māori, but any language has those kinds of beautiful nuances, I think.” Matthews says he loves all sorts of different whakataukī for different reasons and occasions, but his favourite is particularly appropriate to his work in the hospitality sector. The relationships they foster in their rohe enables them to anticipate the needs of their communities. Most wardens are just everyday people called to the role by wanting to serve te iwi Māori. For many, being a warden is in their whakapapa, with whānau serving before them. But Matarora Smith was not one of those. Growing up, she never imagined herself in the role she has today the chief executive of Tāmaki ki te Tonga District Māori Wardens. Instead, she was involved in peacekeeping of a different kind caring for her 13 siblings and felt her calling was to be a mother. "I got married, had children. At that time, hubby went to work and you stayed at home, looked after the kids and looked after the house." So when her daughter and grandchildren moved over to Australia, she followed them across the ditch. Settling in Sydney, Smith worked for an organisation supporting the homeless population, where she saw many similarities between the problems aboriginal peoples were facing and Māori back home. "All of a sudden a light bulb went on. My grandchildren moved back here [to New Zealand] and I thought, 'it's only me here, that's it, I'm going home'. And when I came back, I wanted to do the same work." Upon her return a friend suggested she help on an initiative called 'Project Walkthrough' in Manukau. Funded by the NZ Police in collaboration with Māori Wardens, their aim was to reduce alcohol consumption in public, and ensure that restaurants and bars were taking care of patrons, offering food, and not selling them more booze when they were already intoxicated. Smith jumped at the opportunity, excited to play a role in supporting people in need. The only catch: you had to be a registered Māori warden and Smith was not. 'I thought, 'what's a Māori warden?" But despite no prior knowledge of Māori wardens or what they did, she signed up. Since h…

Responding to the tono from Ngāpuhi rangatira, the Kiingitanga led hundreds onto the grounds, carrying with them the mauri from hui aa motu. Many from Tainui iwi travelled up to Paihia in one of the seven buses that the Kiingitanga organised, which left Waikato on Saturday. The Kiingitanga typically mark the day on its own whenua, but this year, they arrived in style. The sounds of the Rātana brass band overlapped with the haka of the kaihoe. As the manuhiri approached the atea the hau kāinga quickly put out more chairs to accommodate what seemed like a never ending ope. Read more: See how the day unfolded at Waitangi here.
