## Te Tikanga o 'Kaitiakitanga'

Ko **kaitiakitanga** he kupu Māori e tohu ana ki te *guardianship*, te tiaki, te manaaki, me te ārai i te taiao. He ara whakahaere taiao tēnei, i runga i te tirohanga ao Māori. [[1]](cite://1/1)

### Te Pūtake o te Kupu

Ko te kupu **tiaki** te tūāpou o kaitiakitanga — he kupu e māmā ana, ko ōna tikanga he tiaki, he taunekeneke, he āhuru, he manaaki. Nō reira, ko te aroha me te tiaki i te taiao te ngākau o kaitiakitanga. [[2]](cite://2/1)

Ko te kupu **kai** he tāruarua kei mua i te kupu, e tohu ana ki tētahi e mahi ana i taua mahi. Ko te **kaitiaki** tērā — ko ia tētahi tangata, rōpū rānei e tiaki ana, e manaaki ana i tētahi wāhi, tētahi taonga rānei. [[3]](cite://3/1)

### Ko Wai te Kaitiaki?

- Ko te kaitiaki he tangata, he rōpū, he hapū rānei, e mōhiotia ana e ngā tangata whenua hei kaitiaki mō tētahi wāhi — mō tētahi roto, ngahere rānei. [[4]](cite://4/1)
- I ngā rā o mua, ko ngā atua o te taiao ngā kaitiaki tuatahi — ko Tāne, arā, ko ia te kaitiaki o te ngahere. Ko ērā atu kaitiaki katoa he imitanga nō ērā atua. [[3]](cite://3/2)
- Ka taea hoki e kaitiakitanga te āpiti ki ngā taonga tuku iho — ki ngā korowai (cloaks), ki ngā mere pounamu, ki ngā pukapuka whakapapa. Ka tiakina ēnei mea e te kaitiaki, mō ngā uri whakatipu katoa. [[5]](cite://5/1)

### Te Hononga ki te Ao Māori

I roto i te tirohanga ao Māori, he mea hono kaha ngā tāngata ki te whenua me te taiao. Ko kaitiakitanga te kōrero i tēnā hononga, ā, ka whakaahuatia i roto i ngā tikanga hou. [[6]](cite://6/1) He mea nui hoki ēnei ariā:

- **Mana** — ko te mana tohu ana i te hauora o te ngahere, o te awa rānei
- **Tapu** — ko ngā here wairua e tiakina ai te taiao (pērā i te rāhui)
- **Mauri** — ko te mauri o te awa, ngahere, moana rānei e tiakina ai [[1]](cite://1/2)

### Kaitiakitanga i Ēnēi Rā

E ai ki tētahi kōrero, ko kaitiakitanga he mahi — ehara i te kōrero noa iho: *"kaitiakitanga denotes action"* — nā reira, ka mahi ngātahi ngā iwi ki ngā kaunihera ā-rohe ki te whakaora i ngā wāhi tapu, i ngā awa, i ngā roto. [[7]](cite://7/1)

I roto i te ture, kua whakauruhia kaitiakitanga ki roto i te Resource Management Act 1991, e kīia ana ko ia *"the exercise of guardianship by the tangata whenua of an area in accordance with tikanga Māori in relation to natural and physical resources; and includes the ethic of stewardship."* [[8]](cite://8/1)

Ko tētahi āhua motuhake o kaitiakitanga: ehara ia i te ārai noa i te tangata — engari ko te tangata hei wāhanga o te taiao, ka tango, ka homai hoki. Ko tēnā te rerekētanga i waenganui i te kaitiakitanga Māori me te tirohanga taiao o te ao Pākehā. [[9]](cite://9/1)

I tua atu, ka āhei a kaitiakitanga ki te Māori me te kore-Māori — ko tōna kaupeka mo te Māori, he āta hono atu ki ngā tūmanako o ō rātou tīpuna; mō te kore-Māori, he whakaaro hou mō tō rātou whanaungatanga ki te taiao. [[10]](cite://10/1)

---

Ka pātai atu au — e hiahia ana koe ki te mōhio atu mō ngā tikanga ā-hapū, ā-iwi rānei o kaitiakitanga i tētahi wāhi ake o Aotearoa?

1.text:
[Page 1] By Te Ahukaramū Charles Royal Understanding kaitiakitanga Kaitiakitanga means guardianship and protection. It is a way of managing the environment, based on the Māori world view. A kaitiaki is a guardian. This can be a person or group that cares for an area such as a lake or forest. They are given that role by the local iwi . Māori world view In the Māori world view, people are closely connected to the land and nature. Kaitiakitanga is based on this idea of humans as part of the natural world. Traditional practices In the past, people followed traditional practices when they were hunting, fishing, growing or finding food. These helped them to care for the environment. They included: temporary bans (rāhui) on taking food from an area using the lunar calendar (maramataka) to decide when to plant and harvest taking only what was needed hunting and fishing only for food, not as sport using bird snares at the right time for example, not when the birds were breeding. Mana, tapu and mauri Mana means spiritual power. If a forest has mana , it will have plenty of flowers, fruit and birds. Tapu can mean spiritual restriction. Sometimes rāhui (restrictions) are needed to help the mana of the forest. A rāhui might stop people taking birds, fish or fruit from a certain area, or at a certain time. Mauri means life force. This must be protected in forests, rivers, gardens, lakes and the sea. Special mauri stones, which tohunga (priests) said prayers over, were used to preserve this force. Kaitiakitanga today Today there is growing interest in kaitiakitanga. Iwi are restoring their environment and culture, and using traditional ideas in the modern world. Ngāi Tahu are guardians of pounamu (greenstone) in the South Island. Te Āti Awa ki Taranaki made a claim to the government to stop pollution in their fishing areas. Four iwi (Ngāti Kahungunu, Rangitāne, Muaūpoko and Ngāti Raukawa) have come together to stop the Manawatū River being polluted. The Te Rarawa people are working to save the kūkupa (New Zealand pigeon). Kaitiakitanga has also been included in some laws, such as the Resource Management Act 1991. Kaitiakitanga means guardianship, protection, preservation or sheltering. It is a way of managing the environment, based on the traditional Māori world view.

1.document_title: Kaitiakitanga: Māori Guardianship, Environmental Stewardship, and Traditional Conservation Practices
1.document_summary: Kaitiakitanga is a foundational Māori concept of guardianship and environmental stewardship rooted in the worldview that humans are part of nature. A kaitiaki is a guardian recognized by tangata whenua to care for natural areas such as lakes, forests, and waterways. Traditional conservation practices include temporary rāhui (resource restrictions), use of the lunar calendar (maramataka) for planting and harvesting, sustainable hunting and fishing, and blessing of mauri stones by tohunga (priests). Key spiritual concepts include mana (spiritual power), tapu (spiritual restriction), and mauri (life force). Today, kaitiakitanga is experiencing renewal as iwi (tribes) restore ecosystems and apply traditional knowledge in modern contexts. Practical examples include Ngāi Tahu's guardianship of pounamu resources, Ngāti Toa's fishery restoration at Pukerua Bay, and multi-tribal efforts to stop river pollution and protect endangered species. The document outlines challenges in collaborating with non-Māori stakeholders and details legislative frameworks such as the Resource Management Act 1991 and Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004 that incorporate kaitiakitanga principles. Kaitiakitanga offers perspectives on environmental stewardship and kinship with nature, enabling Māori to fulfill ancestral responsibilities while contributing to broader environmental sustainability.

[Page 11] Legislation Kaitiakitanga has been included in some legislation. The Resource Management Act 1991 aims to enable sustainable management of environmental resources. It states that people managing resources under the act must take kaitiakitanga into account. The act defines kaitiakitanga as ‘the exercise of guardianship by the tangata whenua of an area in accordance with tikanga Māori in relation to natural and physical resources; and includes the ethic of stewardship’. Kaitiakitanga was also included in the Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004, where it has the same meaning.

[Page 7] The prefix kai means someone who carries out an action. A kaitiaki is a person, group or being that acts as a carer, guardian, protector and conserver. The gods of the natural world were considered to be the original kaitiaki for instance, Tāne, god of the forest, was the kaitiaki of the forest. All other kaitiaki emulate those original ones. Many hapū (sub tribes) and whānau (families) care for a place such as a lake or forest. They work to conserve the natural heritage, address environmental problems and reclaim traditional knowledge.

11.document_title: Pilgrim at Oakley Creek: Urban Nature, Memory, and Human Flourishing
11.document_summary: This comprehensive collection of interconnected essays by Kennedy Warne explores the transformative power of Oakley Creek (Te Auaunga) in Auckland, New Zealand, examining it through multiple lenses: personal pilgrimage, human psychology, historical memory, and place attachment. The work chronicles Warne's six-month photographic journey from winter to summer solstice, inspired by contemplative writers and Zen philosophy, demonstrating how mindful observation of urban nature fosters deep ecological connection. The essays apply Maslow's hierarchy of needs to show how urban green spaces fulfill fundamental human requirements—from physiological exercise and emotional security to social belonging and self-actualization—while highlighting the critical importance of preserving these spaces as Auckland's open space availability declines. Through archival research and personal narrative, Warne traces the layered histories converging at Oakley Creek, including indigenous Māori heritage, colonial discoveries, the legacy of Carrington Psychiatric Hospital, and the story of patient Rolfe Hattaway whose artistic vision inspired modernist artists. The collection advocates for kaitiakitanga (guardianship) and "locaphilia"—binding oneself to place through loving attention, storytelling, and ceremonial engagement—demonstrating how individuals can expand a place's narrative and experience meaningful homecoming through relationship-based environmental engagement.

12.document_title: Eyes in the Land: Dune Lakes, Wetlands, and Indigenous Stewardship in Northland
12.document_summary: This comprehensive collection explores New Zealand's dune lakes and wetlands in Northland, examining their ecological significance and cultural importance to iwi communities. The articles document indigenous stewardship and scientific conservation efforts, featuring Lake Ngatu and NIWA scientist Paul Champion's research on unique flora including kuta sedge and tuatara plants. Key threats include invasive species such as hornwort, Egeria densa, Gambusia affinis, and grass carp. The collection emphasizes kaitiakitanga (environmental stewardship) as the foundation for restoration, incorporating ecological and cultural dimensions. Monitoring strategies using the LakeSPI bio-assessment tool are detailed, alongside management approaches including herbicide applications and freshwater mussel restoration. The narrative incorporates the Māori proverb "Te roto tāpokopoko, he wai whakahuihui, he pukenga ora" (a dune lake is an oasis that gathers and grows life) and explores te mana o te repo (the mana of wetlands) as intermediaries between Tāne (forests) and Tangaroa (seas). Community engagement initiatives like "Get to Know Your Dune Lake" days link lake conservation to Māori traditions and reconnect communities with their ancestral lands.

13.document_title: A Gulf in my Thinking
13.document_summary: Kennedy Warne reflects on his deep personal connection to the Hauraki Gulf in New Zealand, tracing memories from childhood through his grandfather's swordfishing boat. He explores the concept of guardianship and stewardship through the Inuit legend of the mother of the sea—a story about how people's disrespect for the ocean causes the sea's bounty to disappear until a shaman restores harmony by combing her hair. Warne connects this ancient wisdom to the Māori concept of kaitiakitanga, arguing it represents a profound stewardship that goes beyond mere resource management. He observes a growing movement of individuals taking environmental responsibility into their own hands, becoming "ministers of the environment" by caring for wetlands, forests, and oceans. The essay emphasizes humanity's forgotten relationship with the sea and calls for a return to reverence and respect for the natural world.

14.document_title: Kōura: Māori Stewardship, Conservation, and Freshwater Ecosystem Restoration in Aotearoa New Zealand
14.document_summary: This comprehensive document collection explores the ecological, cultural, and conservation significance of kōura (New Zealand freshwater crayfish) through multiple interconnected narratives. It traces the historical role of kōura in Māori diet and culture, documenting how Māori ancestors practiced kaitiakitanga (environmental stewardship) by translocating crayfish across the country for centuries to ensure food security. The document examines kōura's ecological importance as ecosystem engineers that control invasive species and restore waterway health. It details the dramatic decline of kōura populations due to trout predation, forest clearing, invasive species (particularly brown bullhead catfish and marron), and water quality degradation, with some populations experiencing up to 99% decline. The collection highlights contemporary restoration efforts led by iwi and freshwater biologists using adapted traditional harvesting methods like the tau kōura technique. It features innovative approaches including John Hollows' professional kōura farming operations in Southland wetlands, which demonstrate sustainable aquaculture, and Kāti Huirapa rūnanga's initiatives to reconnect whānau with traditional food sources. The document emphasizes that mātauranga (Māori knowledge) remains essential for freshwater conservation and advocates for transferring ecosystem management responsibility back to indigenous communities.

The author argues that the traditional binary approach of designating areas for total protection or total exploitation is outdated. Drawing on Māori concepts of kaitiakitanga (stewardship), the piece advocates for a balanced approach that allows both protection and sustainable use of natural resources. The author acknowledges that reducing humanity's environmental footprint requires difficult choices and collective action, emphasizing the need for respectful dialogue and integration of diverse knowledge systems to develop a more sustainable approach to living in Aotearoa (New Zealand).

16.document_title: Between a Rock and a Hard Place
16.document_summary: This article examines the contentious Denniston Plateau mining debate, which pits resource extraction against environmental preservation. With 6.1 million tonnes of bituminous coal beneath a 150-hectare site, the proposed open-cast mine would generate 14 million tonnes of CO2 emissions when burned—equivalent to New Zealand's annual dairy herd emissions. The article explores the tension between economic benefits ($46 million in salaries for a struggling West Coast region) and environmental costs, including mercury, selenium, arsenic emissions, and climate change contributions. It presents three perspectives: exploitation versus preservation, and a Māori concept of land as taonga (treasure and resource), emphasizing guardianship (kaitiakitanga) and respect for the land's living essence. The author questions whether this traditional approach might offer a less-destructive path to prosperity.

[Page 8] interests, if the stewardship land process is an opportunity to ensure access to our lake bed, then we should certainly take advantage of that.” Zoom out from Mahinapua to the long green sweep of Te Tai Poutini/the West Coast, and there are many other such ancient places with contemporary significance on stewardship land. Pull back again to take in stewardship land nationwide, and you’ll find myriad similar sites: part of a deeper geography that lives on in the place names, practices and memories of local hapū. An increasingly vocal, self resourced Māori world is seeking to haul such places back into the light, and is asserting its right to have a say in how they’re managed. Given the vast majority of stewardship land is in Ngāi Tahu’s takiwā, and the majority of that is on Te Tai Poutini, it’s not surprising the iwi’s local and central leadership was paying close attention when reclassification process was announced. But to truly understand why they picked up the phone to call their lawyers, you have to go back even further. the [Chapter Break] In 1859, young Nelson settler and Crown agent James Mackay Jr was paddling the Māwhera when he upset his canoe. The river, also known as the Grey, is significant to Poutini Ngāi Tahu. The river’s path to the sea was forged by Aoraki’s nephew, Tūterakiwhānoa, to drain the wrecked hull of his uncle’s island sized waka. Later, in the time of mortals, the river was a trade and travel route. The principal kāinga of Ngāti Waewae was then at the river’s mouth. So it’s interesting that when Mackay had his mishap, among the items the river soaked was the freshly signed deed of sale for the entire West Coast. The signatures could still be read, but in places the ink had faded and bled. The history of outsiders making unilateral decisions about Poutini Ngāi Tahu’s territory had begun two years earlier, when Mackay first visited. He told one of the senior chiefs, Tarapuhi, that the government had already bought their territory from arch rivals Ngāti Toa in 1853 for £5000. The Crown had paid this and other amounts to various northern iwi for parts of Te Waipounamu, including portions of the Coast, without bothering to ascertain who actually owned the land. Tarapuhi and the other chiefs asserted their legitimate ownership. Stewardship land designations are at times nonsensically small and isolated. At Woodpecker Bay, a small comma shaped parcel of forest at the centre of the picture is stewardship land, while the remainder of the area behind the ridgeline is part of Paparoa National Park. Mackay then returned in 1858 with authorisation to purchase the entire West Coast from them for £200, and to leave the iwi with 200 hectares in reserves. His offer was met with the contempt it deserved. Chief Werita Tainui dismissed it as the price of a horse. When Mackay returned with a marginally better offer, he was well aware of the value of the land: there was significant demand for it, and the possibility of goldfields. Under Te Tiriti o Waitangi, the Crown had a duty to act in good faith, and had committed to actively protecting the chiefs’ ability to exercise chieftainship over their lands. As the Crown’s agent, if Mackay was aware of this conflict of interest, he didn’t let on. He made the Crown’s final offer: £300. The chiefs agreed—in part to assert their mana over the land in the face of Ngāti Toa’s claims. The price might not have mattered if Poutini Ngāi Tahu had been able to reserve from sale whatever lands they chose—a right guaranteed under Te Tiriti. The 151,757 hectares they wished to keep would have protected rights to pounamu and provided an economic base for future generations. But with few Māori on the Coast at the time and the balance of power tipped firmly in favour of settlers, the chiefs settled for a little more than 4000 hectares scattered across 58 reserves. (The Crown later described this allocation as “the bare minimum”, with “scant consideration” for future needs.) The chiefs did manage to insist on reserves at Māwhera (which later became Greymouth) and the banks of the Arahura, and secured ownership of the Arahura riverbed up to its source. Despite its dunking in the river, the Arahura Deed stood. The Crown acquired and then began to sell the land. Goldfields, mining, farming and logging built towns and a measure of prosperity for Pākehā. Meanwhile, many of the reserves, including the one at Māwhera, were taken from the iwi’s control and administered by government trustees. The trustees made some leases perpetual without the owners’ consent, and later fixed rents. Some land was sold off against the owners’ will. Parts of the Arahura Reserve were taken for roading and the railway line without compensation, because until well into the 20th century, the law didn’t require compensation to be paid when taking Māori land for public works. Other ancestral landscapes, such as Kaniere and Mahinapua, were put into scenic reserves. Today, 87 per cent of Poutini Ngāi Tahu’s takiwā is managed by DOC. Ngāi Tahu had little, if any, say in any of this. Ngāi Tahu is now in a position to insist on its rights. Socially and politically, there are signs of change as well. The law is now clear on the need for DOC to work with iwi as Treaty partners: section 4 of the Conservation Act requires DOC to give effect to the Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi—the strongest incorporation of the Treaty into any of New Zealand’s laws. A landmark Supreme Court case, Ngāi Tai ki Tāmaki v Minister of Conservation , affirmed DOC’s Treaty responsibilities in 2018. 17.document_title: Stewardship Land Reclassification in New Zealand: Conservation, Māori Rights, and the Old Ghost Road
17.document_summary: This comprehensive document collection examines New Zealand's stewardship land—nine percent of Aotearoa's total land area—through interconnected narratives spanning conservation policy, indigenous rights, and economic development. The collection begins with the Old Ghost Road project in the Mokihinui Gorge, illustrating how stewardship land's lower protection status both threatened and enabled conservation initiatives, ultimately generating $4 million annually for local communities after Meridian Energy abandoned its proposed dam project. The documents trace the government's 2021 fast-tracked reclassification process, which proposed appointing expert panels to assess stewardship land within eight months. This initiative sparked significant controversy, particularly from Ngāi Tahu iwi, who filed urgent High Court proceedings citing consultation breaches and Treaty of Waitangi violations. The historical context reveals how the Crown's 1859 acquisition of the West Coast from Poutini Ngāi Tahu for £300 left the iwi with only 4,000 hectares despite claiming 151,757 hectares, with 87% of their territory now managed by DOC with minimal iwi input. The collection explores the tension between traditional conservation frameworks and contemporary approaches that integrate mātauranga (Māori knowledge) and recognize Māori cultural values extending beyond preservation to include economic and commercial use on ancestral land. Through case studies such as Lake Mahinapua, the documents examine how mana whenua and national assessment panels are collaboratively developing integrated conservation models that respect rangatiratanga while addressing concerns about mining interests and the Stockton Coal Mine on Denniston Plateau.

18.document_title: Blue Carbon in New Zealand: Fiords, Coastal Wetlands, and Seagrass Restoration
18.document_summary: This comprehensive collection examines New Zealand's blue carbon ecosystems and their role in climate regulation. New Zealand's fiords, particularly Doubtful Sound and Dusky Sound, store approximately 2.24 billion tonnes of carbon—about one percent of the world's seabed carbon. These fiords bury organic carbon faster than similar ecosystems worldwide due to unique geography, steep valleys, heavy rainfall, and anaerobic mud conditions. Scientists at the Cawthron Institute are pioneering seed-based seagrass restoration methods, discovering that Zostera muelleri flowers more frequently than previously believed. Seagrass ecosystems capture carbon 55 times faster than tropical rainforests and store four times more carbon per hectare in soils. Coastal wetland restoration projects like Te Wahapū o Waihī integrate mātauranga Māori with coastal ecology, with five iwi collaborating on restoration efforts. Seaweed research reveals varying decomposition rates in deep-sea environments, though scientists raise concerns about accurately measuring seaweed's carbon removal potential. The research emphasizes protecting natural carbon sinks while addressing legal complexities involving Māori rights and rangatiratanga, highlighting kaitiakitanga (stewardship) and cultural significance of coastal ecosystem restoration.

19.text:
[Page 9] If everyone foraged, would we strip the land? Wellington author Johanna Knox (Ngāti Tukorehe, Ngāti Raukawa ki te Tonga, Ngāti Ranginui, Tangata Tiriti), who wrote the book on foraging in New Zealand, thinks that eating the environment is a pretty good way of reconnecting with it. She reckons foraging could resurrect the idea of the commons—not just the tragedy of it. It could bring back the concept of places that are used and maintained by people for each other—and for future generations. That idea has been largely lost from the Pākehā world, but it’s remained intact in te ao Māori. Despite the destruction of traditional food gathering areas, despite the theft of land, the depletion of resources, and the loss of kōrero about how different species are prepared—despite all of that, the philosophy of how to gather food sustainably remains intact. It’s the concept of kaitiakitanga. “A big difference between Western environmentalism and Māori kaitiakitanga is how they see humans in the environment,” says Knox. “So in Pākehā conservation, it’s like, ‘We must keep these areas pristine. Nobody can take anything from here,’ but in te ao Māori it’s like, ‘People are part of the landscape. It’s a reciprocal relationship, so of course we’re taking stuff.’ McKenzie and Mikhail Shatura, head chef at downtown Auckland restaurant Ahi, taste the morning’s foraging. Shatura assembles a dish of quail, chickweed, huruhuru whenua and ureure. Foraged ingredients don’t form the bulk of a dish, says McKenzie, but they bring the flavours of a place onto the plate. “These are supporting characters,” he says. “So I come at foraging from the perspective that if you get right out there and involve yourself in the landscape—which means taking what you can, but respectfully and sustainably and at the same time giving back—that’s just a really good way to do things.” Raglan ecologist and rongoā practitioner Mahuru Wilcox (Ngāti Awa, Ngāti Ranginui) echoes Knox. She forages native plants traditionally used for medicinal purposes for her small business, Hau Botanicals. “How can you teach people to value something if you can’t connect to it?” she asks. “These [plants] are valued because they were important as kai or as rongoā or they were important as ancestors, as tūpuna. If you’re really thinking of our world around us as our tūpuna, as our ancestors, how would you respect your tūpuna? So using those principles for how you connect.” Even in the most densely populated parts of the city, plants move through the cycles of the year. Retreating into their roots to conserve water, springing forth with new shoots. Exploding into colour for a week or two. “It’s such a reminder in your daily life as a human that everything has a season,” says Wilcox. Over time, you start to see it: the living calendar, the shifts in weather and sunlight reflected in the plants changing, day by day, in all the gaps between the fixed and immobile parts of the city.

19.document_title: The Weed Eaters: Urban and Rural Foraging in New Zealand
19.document_summary: This comprehensive article explores the growing practice of foraging in New Zealand, examining both urban and rural contexts. The piece follows multiple narratives: in Auckland, forager Bella Burgess leads a Facebook community group on Maungawhau/Mount Eden, teaching participants to identify and harvest edible wild plants including vetch, wild brassica, pūhā, nasturtium, oxalis, and onion weed while emphasizing ethical foraging practices. In Canterbury, Peter Langlands scouts for elderflower and wild parsnips for restaurants, demonstrating how roadsides and berms provide abundant biodiversity and foraged ingredients. The article features interviews with professional foragers like Nate McKenzie and Rico Birndt who maintain sustainable harvesting practices. It highlights the cultural and philosophical dimensions of foraging, connecting it to Māori philosophy of kaitiakitanga—a reciprocal relationship with the environment—and contrasting this with Western conservation approaches. The piece explores the underlying human desire for self-reliance and independence from modern systems, noting how the surge in foraging interest during COVID-19 lockdowns reflects deeper needs for connection and resilience. The article showcases how edible plants grow abundantly in plain sight throughout New Zealand's towns and cities, challenging cultural hesitation about harvesting from public spaces while advocating for sustainable practices and "feral parks" instead of manicured lawns.

20.text:
[Page 5] Margaret Orbell, author of The Natural World of the Maori and The Illustrated Encyclopedia of Maori Myths and Legends, notes that many family groups believed they had a special relationship with an ancestral spirit, which often took the form of a morepork. This owl guardian or kaitiaki was not recognised in just any morepork, but in one that exhibited unusual behaviour, such as sitting in a prominent place, fluttering against a wall or entering a house. Seeing such a bird might signify impending death, or merely announce the arrival of important visitors.

20.document_title: Morepork: New Zealand's Native Owl - Adaptations, Behavior, and Conservation
20.document_summary: This comprehensive document collection explores the morepork (ruru), New Zealand's native nocturnal owl. The first section provides personal observations of morepork hunting behavior, detailing their diet of insects, small birds, mice, and geckos through pellet analysis, with regional variations across different islands. Moreporks inhabit diverse environments including native bush, pine forests, and suburban areas, maintaining 3-5 hectare territories and navigating by memory. The second section examines remarkable sensory and behavioral adaptations enabling nocturnal hunting, including specialized night vision with rod-cell-dominated retinas 100 times more sensitive than pigeons' eyes, asymmetrical skull structures for precise sound localization, and silent flight through specialized feather structures. Research suggests moreporks may detect infrared light to locate warm-blooded prey. The third section details the complete life cycle, focusing on chick development from fledging through independence and territorial behavior. The collection highlights a significant conservation success story involving a nearly-extinct Norfolk Island boobook successfully bred with New Zealand moreporks, resulting in a growing population with potential reintroduction to Lord Howe Island. Additionally, the collection addresses Māori cultural perspectives, where moreporks held spiritual significance as ancestral guardians and messengers.

[Page 1] Māori AI expert Dr Karaitiana Taiuru shares his favourite whakataukī 2024 03 18 22:44:07+13:00 Dr Karaitiana Taiuru. Tino rangatiratanga: mō tātou, ā, mō kā uri ā muri ake nei. It is the whakataukī (Māori proverb) that means most to Māori data, AI and technology ethicist Dr Karaitiana Taiuru (Ngāi Tahu, Ngāti Kahungunu, Ngāti Toa). Translated to English, it means "the ability to create and control our destiny for generations to come". It links in well with his work and family life, Taiuru told RNZ Nights. For his work, it reminded Taiuru why he still does what he does and that there was a new generation of children who will not know life without AI and it was "our role to create the new normal for them". Taiuru applies a te ao Māori perspective to AI. https://www.rnz.co.nz/national/programmes/nig new generation of children who will not know life without AI and it was "our role to create the new normal for them". Taiuru applies a te ao Māori perspective to AI. https://www.rnz.co.nz/national/programmes/nig hts/audio/2018930609/whakatauki of the week with karaitiana taiuru Listen to the full interview on Nights "We already know that internationally, there's bias against minority peoples so what I do, in conjunction with international best practices with artificial intelligence and other technologies, is bring that Māori voice and Te Tiriti o Waitangi considerations to play." There were "a number" of cultural values that needed to be considered in terms of AI, he said. Many Māori have moko (facial tattoos) so understanding how that was considered with facial technologies was a big factor. In his personal life, the whakataukī applied to his whānau. "For me, I consider that I have an opportunity to create wealth and opportunities for my children and also for my grandchildren. "I live by that rule. I make that sure my children have the opportunities that I didn't always have, make sure they have access to education, financial resources, a home, and part of my planning in life is that my grandchildren will also have the same access and all going well in life, I should see my great grandchildren and maybe great great grandchildren whom I will also ensure that they have equal access. "And I know my children also that they consider the same sort of philosophies in life where they want to protect their whānau as well for the future." Taiuru said the whakataukī came out of working groups around the South Island when Ngāi Tahu was trying to identify a new tribal vision that would be carried into the future. It came after settlements with the Crown in 1996. "That whakataukī was the key whakataukī that came out of those hui." Related

34.document_summary: The Oxford English Dictionary has added several New Zealand words and phrases to its latest update, including "waka jumper" (a member of Parliament who switches parties during a term), "mahi" (work or activity in Māori contexts), "chilly bin" (portable insulated container), and various te reo Māori terms like "tikanga," "kapa haka," and "Aotearoan." The addition reflects the increasing use of te reo Māori in New Zealand society and media. While experts celebrate the inclusion of Māori words as a sign of language normalization, some, including Māori Language Commission chief executive Ngahiwi Apanui, expressed concerns about "Aotearoan," viewing it as inconsistent with Māori orthographic conventions. Linguists note this represents the evolving and distinctive nature of New Zealand English.

[Page 1] As well as being an award winning and critically acclaimed novelist and short story writer, Witi Ihimaera is also chair of Te Kaituhi Māori, the Māori writers' organisation within the New Zealand Society of Authors. Te Kaituhi Māori have just opened applications for its 2025 Kupu Kaitiaki and Kaituhi Māori programmes, fostering emerging and developing Māori writers. It's a "mighty mentor programme," Ihimaera told RNZ's Nights. https://www.rnz.co.nz/national/programmes/nights/audio/201897 7273/whakatauki of the week with witi ihimaera "In the past people like Paula Morris, people like Emma Hislop, Steph Matuku and Tanya Roxborogh have been the mentors. "And so, whoever goes in for this Māori mentor programme, they get the best teaching, and we hope will become the best in the next 20 years." Such mentor programmes didn't exist when Ihimaera was himself a young writer, but that may have helped him find his voice, he said. "I had to begin my career from a Māori perspective, and a Māori point of view. "Had I possibly had help from Pākehā institutions, then I possibly could have started to write in Pākehā ways and according to Pākehā frameworks." The Kaituhi Māori mentorship programme happened for the first time in 2024. When Ihimaera read through the work produced it brought him great joy, he said. "It was so incredibly awesome that, there are times when I almost wept with excitement and with joy, because I'm an old writer, I'm now 81 and to be able to see that there was a cohort of new rangatahi writers, fresh voices, refreshing ideas of who we were and people you know were mentoring them with so much generosity. [Page 1] 2024 01 29 21:53:12+13:00 Anton Matthews is the director of Hustle Group, a company operating a bunch of restaurants and catering companies in Ōtautahi Christchurch. He's also a big advocate for people learning te reo Māori, also running online course Normalising Te Reo Māori. In the next in a weekly series, he shares a favourite whakataukī, or traditional Māori aphorism, with Emile Donovan. Ko te amorangi ki mua, ko te hāpai ō ki muri The leader at the front and the workers behind the scenes This simple whakataukī, or Māori proverb, is a multi layered favourite of Matthews. While he was fortunate to grow up immersed in te ao Māori, including being educated at kohanga reo and kura kaupapa, Matthews tells Nights anyone exposed to a lot of te reo Māori quickly learns that it’s a language rich in metaphor. “There’s the literal meaning of whatever has been said, but it often takes a couple of years (sometimes it never actually dawns on us), but there is a hidden meaning there as well. “That’s what I love about whakataukī is that yep, there's that kind of surface layer literally, what is the person saying? But what's the hidden meaning? What are they really trying to explain or what sort of message or idea are they trying to convey when they use the whakataukī? That's the beauty of language, not just te reo Māori, but any language has those kinds of beautiful nuances, I think.” Matthews says he loves all sorts of different whakataukī for different reasons and occasions, but his favourite is particularly appropriate to his work in the hospitality sector. Ko te amorangi ki mua, ko te hāpai ō ki muri has two parts to it, Matthews says. Amorangi is a term that refers to recognised iwi leaders, the ones who are front and centre when leading a pōwhiri, or welcome, onto the marae. “These are the familiar faces that everyone kind of knows… these people are highly respected. They have a lot of mana. We look to them when we need guidance.” Te hāpai ō referred to in the second part of the whakataukī is the complete opposite, Matthews says.

This multi-layered aphorism illustrates the duality and balance fundamental to te ao Māori. The amorangi represents recognized iwi leaders at the front, while te hāpai ō (food carriers) work behind the scenes. Matthews emphasizes that both roles are equally important and worthy of mana, requiring constant communication and interdependence. He applies this philosophy to hospitality, arguing that all staff—whether in the kitchen or front-of-house—develop skills valued on the marae and contribute equally to organizational success. The whakataukī demonstrates that everyone has a vital place, and no role is more important than another.

38.document_title: Māori Landowners Take Crown to High Court Over Freshwater Rights
38.document_summary: Approximately 60 Māori Land Trusts, representing over 150,000 landowners, hapū, and iwi have filed proceedings in the High Court against the Crown over freshwater rights. The claimants argue the Crown has broken promises and failed to uphold Te Tiriti o Waitangi obligations regarding Māori proprietary and kaitiaki rights in freshwater and geothermal resources. They seek immediate action to stop water degradation, recognition of tikanga Māori rights, and a fair water allocation system enabling Māori to exercise kaitiakitanga. The case follows over a decade of Crown inaction despite 2012-2013 acknowledgments of Māori rights. The claimants criticize the current "first-in, first-served" allocation system and the dismantling of Te Mana o te Wai framework. Kingi Smiler, representing the claimant group, emphasizes the urgency of restoring balance and protecting waterways for future generations. The legal process is expected to take two to three years.

Responding to the tono from Ngāpuhi rangatira, the Kiingitanga led hundreds onto the grounds, carrying with them the mauri from hui aa motu. Many from Tainui iwi travelled up to Paihia in one of the seven buses that the Kiingitanga organised, which left Waikato on Saturday. The Kiingitanga typically mark the day on its own whenua, but this year, they arrived in style. The sounds of the Rātana brass band overlapped with the haka of the kaihoe. 39.document_title: Kotahitanga in Action: Hundreds Gather at Treaty Grounds with Kiingitanga and Rātana
39.document_summary: On February 4, 2024, hundreds of Māori gathered at the Waitangi Treaty Grounds in a powerful display of kotahitanga (unity). Led by Kiingi Tuuheitia and Rātana Tumuaki Manuao, iwi leaders from across the country assembled to voice concerns about the government's proposed Treaty principles bill. The pōwhiri featured speeches emphasizing unity and peaceful resistance, with leaders like Ngāpuhi Rangatira Matua Hone Sadler urging iwi to remain peaceful while standing firm. Bayden Barber referenced the 1990s kotahitanga movement, calling for continued strategic planning. Te Taepa Kameta criticized Minister Shane Jones's absence, while Rāhui Papa emphasized mobilizing under mana motuhake and ensuring He Whakaputanga receives equal standing with Te Tiriti. The gathering concluded with Tainui representatives singing in harmony, marking a historic moment of Māori solidarity.

[Page 1] Family Court appoints mokopuna as guardian after whānau battle over kaumātua’s care 2025 09 21 08:29:47+12:00 [repub:nzherald] Catherine Hutton, Open Justice reporter The kaumātua has dementia. A whānau is deadlocked over who should have guardianship of their much loved kaumātua, who has dementia. The man's daughter, who has overseen his care for the past few years, wants him to stay in Auckland, while his son and grandson want him to return to Te Tai Tokerau, where he's from. Now, the case has ended up in court, where a judge has been asked to decide who is best placed to be the man's guardian and where the 85 year old should live. Family Court judge Kevin Muir said the man's children and grandchildren undoubtedly had his best interests at heart. "The family is divided and for the whānau's long term wairua to thrive, they "may need to find a way to heal the mamae many of them now feel". According to a recently released decision, the once "great businessman and amazing cook" now lives in a hospital wing at a South Auckland retirement home, where he's incapable of making decisions about his personal welfare and care. The man's eldest daughter was appointed as an interim welfare guardian in 2022. At a hearing in June, she sought to have the order made permanent. The man's son opposed the order and his own son applied to replace his aunty as his koro's welfare guardian. The elderly man's son argued his sister's decision to move him to Auckland ignored the wishes their father had conferred in an ōhākī (last wishes). He was unable to give an exact time and place when this was made, but spoke in general terms about his father expressing a wish to be "home" in Te Tai Tokerau to a number of people on a number of occasions. In an affidavit prepared for the court, the son said: "My father directly conferred full and final authority upon me under tikanga and sacred law prior to any cognitive decline." He said his father expressly affirmed he held "tino rangatiratanga over his care decisions and end of life process". "[The son] considers the ōhākī is valid and binding, because it was expressed before his father's cognitive decline," the judge said in his decision. The daughter said their father always talked about going back to live on the whenua it was "peppered through his conversation". She viewed and continued to view the father's ōhākī as being something for the future. "It was his dying wish. He wasn't dying". The decision said the son and his whānau were distressed, when their father was moved to Auckland, and there was a confrontation, when they arrived at the facility. As a result, temporary protection orders were issued to protect the father and his daughter against his son and daughter in law. Another sister also obtained temporary protection orders. These remain in place, with the judge noting their existence had been seismic for the whānau. "There is a palpable sense of mistrust and some anger between them, which was evident during the hearing." At the end of the hearing, the judge encouraged the parties to call a hui, kanohi ki te kanohi (face to face), to try to bridge the differences between them, but said, "I cannot compel them to do that". Judge Muir stated he was unable to find, on the balance of probabilities, that the father expressed an ōhākī for his son to make decisions on his behalf or require him to be in a care facility in Te Tai Tokerau. The judge said this was because he had no reliable evidence that the concept of ōhākī could be extended or applied beyond the concept of a dying wish, and the man was very much alive. He also referred to a clinical assessment from 2018, which indicated the man preferred to place his trust in his daughter to make decisions about his personal care. 'I chose the option that is hopeful' The judge noted the daughter and the man's grandson were capable of being welfare guardians. In the daughter's case, she had shown herself highly capable of carrying out the duties in a satisfactory manner, but the judge said there was a real prospect that his grandson would be able to unite the four pillars of the whānau the kaumātua's four children and their children. "Sadly, the family remains fractured," he said. "Some of the wounds are deep, some of them seem to relate to the different relationships that the four children had with their mother." Explaining his decision to appoint the man's grandson as welfare guardian, he said: "I chose the option that is hopeful. "I find the father's wairua is likely to be better sustained, if responsibility is passed to his mokopuna." He also imposed conditions, including appointing the grandson as welfare guardian for a period of three years. He also ordered the man to remain at the Auckland facility and not return to Te Tai Tokerau, until a suitable care facility was found, medical professionals supported the move and whānau were consulted. 1.fileDescription: Kaitiakitanga is a foundational Māori concept of guardianship and environmental stewardship rooted in the worldview that humans are part of nature. A kaitiaki is a guardian recognized by tangata whenua to care for natural areas such as lakes, forests, and waterways. Traditional conservation practices include temporary rāhui (resource restrictions), use of the lunar calendar (maramataka) for planting and harvesting, sustainable hunting and fishing, and blessing of mauri stones by tohunga (priests). Key spiritual concepts include mana (spiritual power), tapu (spiritual restriction), and mauri (life force). Today, kaitiakitanga is experiencing renewal as iwi (tribes) restore ecosystems and apply traditional knowledge in modern contexts. Practical examples include Ngāi Tahu's guardianship of pounamu resources, Ngāti Toa's fishery restoration at Pukerua Bay, and multi-tribal efforts to stop river pollution and protect endangered species. The document outlines challenges in collaborating with non-Māori stakeholders and details legislative frameworks such as the Resource Management Act 1991 and Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004 that incorporate kaitiakitanga principles. Kaitiakitanga offers perspectives on environmental stewardship and kinship with nature, enabling Māori to fulfill ancestral responsibilities while contributing to broader environmental sustainability.

chunkHighlights.text: By Te Ahukaramū Charles Royal

Understanding kaitiakitanga Kaitiakitanga means guardianship and
protection. It is a way of managing the environment, based on the Māori world view. A kaitiaki is a guardian. This can be a person or group that cares for an area such as a lake or forest. They are given that role by the local iwi . Māori world view In the Māori world view, people are closely connected to the land and nature. Kaitiakitanga is based on this idea of humans as part of the natural world. Traditional practices In the past, people followed traditional practices when they were hunting, fishing, growing or finding food. These helped them to care for the environment. They included: temporary bans (rāhui) on taking food from an area using the lunar calendar (maramataka) to decide when to plant and harvest taking only what was needed hunting and fishing only for food, not as sport using bird snares at the right time – for example, not when the birds were breeding. Mana, tapu and mauri Mana means spiritual power. If a forest has mana , it will have plenty of flowers, fruit and birds. Tapu can mean spiritual restriction. Sometimes rāhui (restrictions) are needed to help the mana of the forest. A rāhui might stop people taking birds, fish or fruit from a certain area, or at a certain time. Mauri means life force. This must be protected in forests, rivers, gardens, lakes and the sea. Special mauri stones, which tohunga (priests) said prayers over, were used to preserve this force. Kaitiakitanga today Today there is growing interest in kaitiakitanga. Iwi are restoring their environment and culture, and using traditional ideas in the modern world. Ngāi Tahu are guardians of pounamu (greenstone) in the South Island. Te Āti Awa ki Taranaki made a claim to the government to stop pollution in their fishing areas. Four iwi (Ngāti Kahungunu, Rangitāne, Muaūpoko and Ngāti Raukawa) have come together to stop the Manawatū River being polluted. The Te Rarawa people are working to save the kūkupa (New Zealand pigeon). Kaitiakitanga has also been included in some laws,
such as the Resource Management Act 1991.

7.fileDescription: This comprehensive collection examines New Zealand's blue carbon ecosystems and their role in climate regulation. New Zealand's fiords, particularly Doubtful Sound and Dusky Sound, store approximately 2.24 billion tonnes of carbon—about one percent of the world's seabed carbon. These fiords bury organic carbon faster than similar ecosystems worldwide due to unique geography, steep valleys, heavy rainfall, and anaerobic mud conditions. Scientists at the Cawthron Institute are pioneering seed-based seagrass restoration methods, discovering that Zostera muelleri flowers more frequently than previously believed. Seagrass ecosystems capture carbon 55 times faster than tropical rainforests and store four times more carbon per hectare in soils. Coastal wetland restoration projects like Te Wahapū o Waihī integrate mātauranga Māori with coastal ecology, with five iwi collaborating on restoration efforts. Seaweed research reveals varying decomposition rates in deep-sea environments, though scientists raise concerns about accurately measuring seaweed's carbon removal potential. The research emphasizes protecting natural carbon sinks while addressing legal complexities involving Māori rights and rangatiratanga, highlighting kaitiakitanga (stewardship) and cultural significance of coastal ecosystem restoration.

9.fileDescription: This comprehensive article explores the growing practice of foraging in New Zealand, examining both urban and rural contexts. The piece follows multiple narratives: in Auckland, forager Bella Burgess leads a Facebook community group on Maungawhau/Mount Eden, teaching participants to identify and harvest edible wild plants including vetch, wild brassica, pūhā, nasturtium, oxalis, and onion weed while emphasizing ethical foraging practices. In Canterbury, Peter Langlands scouts for elderflower and wild parsnips for restaurants, demonstrating how roadsides and berms provide abundant biodiversity and foraged ingredients. The article features interviews with professional foragers like Nate McKenzie and Rico Birndt who maintain sustainable harvesting practices. It highlights the cultural and philosophical dimensions of foraging, connecting it to Māori philosophy of kaitiakitanga—a reciprocal relationship with the environment—and contrasting this with Western conservation approaches. The piece explores the underlying human desire for self-reliance and independence from modern systems, noting how the surge in foraging interest during COVID-19 lockdowns reflects deeper needs for connection and resilience. The article showcases how edible plants grow abundantly in plain sight throughout New Zealand's towns and cities, challenging cultural hesitation about harvesting from public spaces while advocating for sustainable practices and "feral parks" instead of manicured lawns.

chunkHighlights.text: If everyone foraged, would we strip the land? Wellington author Johanna Knox (Ngāti Tukorehe, Ngāti Raukawa ki te Tonga, Ngāti Ranginui, Tangata Tiriti), who wrote the book on foraging in New Zealand, thinks that eating the environment is a pretty good way of reconnecting with it. She reckons foraging could resurrect the idea of the commons—not just the tragedy of it. It could bring back the concept of places that are used and maintained by people for each other—and for future generations.

That idea has been largely lost from the Pākehā world, but it’s remained intact in te ao Māori. Despite the destruction of traditional food-gathering areas, despite the theft of land, the depletion of resources, and the loss of kōrero about how different species are prepared—despite all of that, the philosophy of how to gather food sustainably remains intact. It’s the concept of kaitiakitanga.

“A big difference between Western environmentalism and Māori kaitiakitanga is how they see humans in the environment,” says Knox. “So in Pākehā conservation, it’s like, ‘We must keep these areas pristine. Nobody can take anything from here,’ but in te ao Māori it’s like, ‘People are part of the landscape. It’s a reciprocal relationship, so of course we’re taking stuff.’

McKenzie and Mikhail Shatura, head chef at downtown Auckland restaurant Ahi, taste the morning’s foraging. Shatura assembles a dish of quail, chickweed, huruhuru whenua and ureure. Foraged ingredients don’t form the bulk of a dish, says McKenzie, but they bring the flavours of a place onto the plate. “These are supporting characters,” he says.

“So I come at foraging from the perspective that if you get right out there and involve yourself in the landscape—which means taking what you can, but respectfully and sustainably and at the same time giving back—that’s just a really good way to do things.”

Raglan ecologist and rongoā practitioner Mahuru Wilcox (Ngāti Awa, Ngāti Ranginui) echoes Knox. She forages native plants traditionally used for medicinal purposes for her small business, Hau Botanicals.

“How can you teach people to value something if you can’t connect to it?” she asks. “These [plants] are valued because they were important as kai or as rongoā or they were important as ancestors, as tūpuna. If you’re really thinking of our world around us as our tūpuna, as our ancestors, how would you respect your tūpuna? So using those principles for how you connect.”

Even in the most densely populated parts of the city, plants move through the cycles of the year. Retreating into their roots to conserve water, springing forth with new shoots. Exploding into colour for a week or two.
“It’s such a reminder in your daily life as a human that everything has a season,” says Wilcox.
Over time, you start to see it: the living calendar, the shifts in weather and sunlight reflected in the plants changing, day by day, in all the gaps between the fixed and immobile parts of the city.

# The History of New Zealand's National Parks

New Zealand's national parks are among the country's greatest treasures — spectacular landscapes preserved for all time, home to rare flora and fauna, and deeply intertwined with both Māori and Pākehā history. As of 2021, New Zealand has 13 national parks, protecting everything from volcanic peaks to ancient glaciers, fiords, river systems, and limestone caves. [[1]](cite://1/1)

## The Seeds of an Idea

The impulse to protect New Zealand's natural landscapes began taking shape as early as the 1860s and 1870s. Conservation historian Paul Star notes that naturalist T.H. Potts suggested in his essay *National Domains* that large tracts of land should be set aside as refuges for vulnerable native plants and animals — and even proposed converting predator-free islands into sanctuaries. [[2]](cite://2/1)

Several forces drove this early conservation thinking. Some settlers were alarmed that clearing forests for farms was destroying scenic landscapes. A handful of scientists worried about the loss of native birds and wildlife. And the government was beginning to recognise the tourism potential of New Zealand's natural wonders. [[3]](cite://3/1)

## Tongariro: The First National Park

The founding story of New Zealand's first national park is remarkable — and deeply rooted in Māori land rights and cultural identity.

In the 1880s, ownership of the central North Island's volcanic peaks was being fiercely contested in the Māori Land Court. Ngāti Tūwharetoa's paramount chief, Horonuku Te Heuheu, understood the danger clearly, reportedly saying:

> *"If our mountains of Tongariro are included in the blocks passed through the Court in the ordinary way, what will become of them? They will be cut up and perhaps sold... They will become of no account, for the tapu will be gone. Tongariro is my ancestor, my tupuna; it is my head; my mana centres around Tongariro."* [[4]](cite://4/1)

In 1887, on the advice of his son-in-law, the Tauranga politician Lawrence Marshall Grace, Horonuku signed a deed with the Crown ensuring the volcanic peaks of Tongariro, Ngāuruhoe, and Ruapehu could never be sold. [[5]](cite://5/1) The government subsequently purchased additional Māori land to supplement the mountaintops, and Tongariro National Park was formally established by Act of Parliament in 1894. [[4]](cite://4/2)

Today, at 78,618 hectares, it remains New Zealand's most visited national park — a landscape of volcanic mountains, barren lava flows, snowfields, and hot springs side by side. [[6]](cite://6/1)

Both growing support among Pākehā for conservation and Māori determination to protect their ancestral lands provided the context that made the creation of this first national park possible. [[7]](cite://7/1)

## Early Expansion: The Turn of the Century

Momentum built quickly after Tongariro's establishment. By 1900, national parks had also been created on Taranaki (then known as Mt Egmont), and large areas of South Island mountain country had been set aside at Aoraki/Mt Cook and Arthur's Pass. In 1905, almost a million hectares was reserved in Fiordland. [[8]](cite://8/1)

The Scenery Preservation Act of 1903 — championed by parliamentarian Harry Ell — provided a commission to investigate which areas were suitable for preservation, and was amended in 1908 to establish scenic reserves boards. By the time Ell left Parliament, more than 500 reserves had been created, up from fewer than 100 when he entered. Many of these early reserves, such as at Aoraki/Mt Cook and the Paparoa Range, later formed the basis of future national parks. [[9]](cite://9/1)

Abel Tasman National Park came about through a different kind of advocacy: Nelson conservationist Perrine Moncrieff successfully campaigned for it to be created in 1942, to mark the tercentenary of Dutch explorer Abel Tasman's arrival in New Zealand. [[10]](cite://10/1)

## Tourism vs Conservation: An Enduring Tension

From their earliest days, New Zealand's national parks were pulled in two directions — as havens for native wildlife, or as playgrounds for visitors. Until the 1940s, the parks were managed predominantly as places for recreation and tourism. [[11]](cite://11/1)

The American model, which prioritised visitor pleasure over nature conservation, heavily influenced New Zealand's approach. [[12]](cite://12/1) This occasionally led to extraordinary decisions: between 1914 and 1924, Police Commissioner John Cullen spread tonnes of Scottish heather seed throughout Tongariro National Park to encourage grouse hunting. Critics were scathing, with one declaring: *"We do not wish to turn Tongariro National Park into something that does not exist on earth and I trust does not exist in heaven."* [[12]](cite://12/2)

The tourism infrastructure grew ambitiously. In the late 1920s, entrepreneur Rodolph Wigley built the grand Chateau Tongariro, complete with a gymnasium, cinema, and central heating — but the Depression bankrupted him just a year later. The Tourist Department took over in 1931, and by 1938, some 20,000 overseas visitors were arriving, 61% of them Australians. World War II brought all of that to an abrupt halt, with the Chateau itself converted into a hospital. [[12]](cite://12/3)

## The National Parks Act 1952: A Turning Point

In the 1920s, boards were established to manage Tongariro and Egmont national parks, but there was no coordinated national framework. By the 1940s, organisations such as the Forest and Bird Society and the Federated Mountain Clubs were pressing for central control. [[13]](cite://13/1)

This advocacy led to the landmark National Parks Act (NPA) 1952, which established the National Parks Authority to provide guidance and policy, with individual boards overseeing each park alongside the Department of Lands and Survey and its park ranger service. Crucially, the Act emphasised the preservation of native plants and animals, and the control or eradication of introduced species. [[13]](cite://13/2)

The effect was dramatic. The number of national parks grew from four to 10 within a few years of the Act's passage, with new parks created through the 1950s and 60s. [[14]](cite://14/1) The 1950s also saw the government embark on a massive hut-building and track-cutting programme — in 1960 alone, the Forest Service built an average of one backcountry hut per week. Between 1957 and 1972, it constructed 680 huts and shelters, 166 footbridges and cableways, and 4,000 kilometres of tramping tracks. [[14]](cite://14/2)

Fiordland National Park — New Zealand's largest, at more than 1.2 million hectares — was formally established in 1952 as part of this expansion. Its features include glaciated terrain with deep lakes and sounds, the country's highest rainfall, and the remarkable takahē bird, found almost nowhere else. [[15]](cite://15/1)

## Wilderness Areas: A New Concept

As the backcountry became more accessible, a new debate emerged: was it being over-developed? Purists began calling for 'wilderness areas' — places entirely free of huts, tracks, bridges, and even helicopter access. [[14]](cite://14/3)

New Zealand's first wilderness area, Otehake (12,000 hectares), was established in 1955 within Arthur's Pass National Park. Others followed in Tongariro in the early 1960s. [[16]](cite://16/1) From 1988, wilderness areas were also created outside the national park system — including the Raukumara on the East Cape and the Tasman Wilderness Area in what is now Kahurangi National Park. There are now 11 wilderness areas in New Zealand. [[17]](cite://17/1)

## Legislation Evolves: 1980 and Beyond

It wasn't until 1980 that new national park legislation allowed parks to be created specifically for ecological or scientific values — not just as scenic tourist destinations. [[18]](cite://18/1) This opened the door for parks like Kahurangi, in the northwest of the South Island, which lacked the iconic glaciers or fiords of other parks but possessed extraordinary ecological richness. Kahurangi's path to national park status was long, with mining interests a major obstacle; a campaign against Australian mining company CRA's 1981 road-building application helped galvanise conservation support. [[10]](cite://10/2)

## Māori Involvement and Treaty Claims

The relationship between iwi and national parks has been complex and often fraught. Although Tongariro National Park was born from an act of Māori guardianship, iwi involvement in its management was progressively diminished after 1914, when the park was transferred to the Tourist Department. [Page 12] Tongariro National Park Tongariro was New Zealand’s first national park. In 1887 Horonuku Te Heuheu, paramount chief of Ngāti Tūwharetoa, signed a deed with the Crown to safeguard the volcanic peaks of Tongariro, Ngāuruhoe and Ruapehu. More land was added, and the park was established by statute in 1894. In 2019 its total area was 78,618 hectares. It is New Zealand’s most visited national park, and one of the most visible on a fine day its snow covered peaks are an arresting sight for people travelling through the central North Island by road, rail or air. The park’s landscapes are diverse. As well as the volcanic mountains, barren lava flows, snowfields and hot springs exist side by side.

4.text:
[Page 9] From their earliest days New Zealanders have debated whether national parks should be havens for native plants and animals or adapted for the enjoyment of visitors. For 10 years from 1914, sporting enthusiast and Police Commissioner John Cullen spread tonnes of Scottish heather seed in Tongariro National Park to encourage grouse hunting and beautify the landscape. A critic asserted, ‘We do not wish to turn Tongariro National Park into something that does not exist on earth and I trust does not exist in heaven.’ 2 National parks in New Zealand were developed on the American model that prioritised pleasure for visitors over nature conservation. Yet shortage of funds meant that the huts in national parks suited only those ‘with the scouting spirit’. 3 In the late 1920s Wigley made a bold move to construct a hotel in Tongariro National Park. The Chateau was grand and its modern facilities included a gymnasium, a cinema and central heating. Wigley hoped that being close to Rotorua and midway between Wellington and Auckland on the main trunk railway line would ensure profitability. He also believed that successful tourist operators needed a chain of businesses in both North and South islands. Tourism in the Depression The timing was bad for grand ventures, and the economic depression bankrupted Wigley a year later. The Tourist Department took over the resort in 1931, publicising weekend excursions and importing European ski instructors. In 1938 there were 20,000 overseas visitors, 61% of them Australians. The outbreak of the Second World War in 1939 brought an immediate halt in travel for pleasure. The Chateau’s transformation into a hospital symbolised a tourist industry in ‘cold storage’. 4 Wartime petrol rationing brought resorts like Franz Josef close to bankruptcy. Government takeovers kept hotels open for an expected boom after the war. In the early 20th century most New Zealanders could afford only one or two day excursions. In the 1920s the Railways Department aggressively promoted weekend excursions which drew crowds to places like Caroline Bay in Timaru, Arthur’s Pass, Rotorua, Te Aroha , Waitomo Caves and Waihī Beach. In the 1930s, with New Zealand now one of the most motorised countries in the world, families explored further afield from South Island lakes to Far North beaches.

4.document_title: New Zealand Tourism: A Comprehensive History from the 1880s to the 2020s
4.document_summary: This comprehensive document traces the evolution of New Zealand's tourism industry from the late 19th century through the 2020s. The narrative begins with the government's establishment of Rotorua as a spa resort in the 1880s, inspired by European spa culture, and the pioneering efforts of Māori entrepreneurs in tourism services. Early tourism was driven by wealthy travelers from Britain, Australia, and the United States attracted to natural landscapes including Rotorua's geysers, the Southern Alps, and Milford Sound. Key historical figures include Thomas Donne (first government tourist superintendent), Dr Arthur Wohlmann (balneologist), and Freda Du Faur (pioneering female mountaineer). The industry faced significant challenges through the World Wars, with the Treasury skeptical of tourism's economic value in the 1950s. The transformative shift came with long-haul jet aircraft service beginning in the 1960s, making New Zealand accessible to international tourists. Major developments included Auckland International Airport (1966), the Māori Arts and Crafts Institute (1963), and the Agrodome (1969). The 1980s brought deregulation and extreme adventure tourism, exemplified by bungy jumping (1988). In 1999, Tourism New Zealand launched the iconic "100% Pure New Zealand" global campaign. By 2019, nearly 3.9 million international tourists visited annually, contributing $25 billion to the economy, with tourism becoming New Zealand's top export earner. The COVID-19 pandemic halted inbound tourism in March 2020, creating uncertain long-term impacts.

The new law set up the National Parks Authority to provide guidance and policy. Boards oversaw individual parks in conjunction with the Department of Lands and Survey, which provided day to day management through a park ranger service. 10.document_title: New Zealand's Mountains: Comprehensive Guide to Geology, Ecosystems, Culture, and Recreation
10.document_summary: This comprehensive document explores New Zealand's mountains across both the South Island and North Island. It covers the geological formation of major mountain ranges including the Southern Alps (containing all 23 peaks over 3,000 metres, with Aoraki/Mt Cook as the highest at 3,724 metres), North Island volcanoes (Mt Ruapehu, Mt Taranaki, and Mt Ngāuruhoe), and other significant ranges. Mountain formation is driven by tectonic plate collision between the Pacific and Australian plates, causing rapid uplift (up to 10mm/year in the Southern Alps) and counteracted by heavy rainfall and erosion exceeding 10,000mm annually on western slopes. Glaciation over the past two million years has shaped valleys, fiords, and lakes. The alpine ecosystems feature over 600 endemic plant species above the treeline (93% endemic) and unique fauna including the kea parrot, rock wren, giant wētā, and the world's only alpine gecko. Introduced species have significantly impacted native biodiversity. Mountains hold profound cultural significance in Māori tradition as sacred places with spiritual importance and tribal identity connections. The document covers European exploration and mountaineering achievements, mountain settlement patterns (typically not exceeding 600-700 metres altitude), extensive recreation and tourism infrastructure with approximately 500,000 annual visitors to Aoraki/Mt Cook and 800+ back-country huts, and mountains' representation in art, photography, and literature.

11.text:
[Page 7] Piecemeal management The environmental management of New Zealand’s fiords was hindered by the absence of a single co ordinating agency. Fiordland’s terrestrial environment is protected under the National Parks Act 1980; however, its jurisdiction stops short of the water, at the high tide mark. The marine ecosystem is excluded from both Fiordland National Park and the Southwest New Zealand Te Waipounamu World Heritage Area.

11.document_title: Fiordland's Marine Ecosystem: Glacial Formations, Species Diversity, and Conservation Management
11.document_summary:
This comprehensive document explores New Zealand's 14 fiords in the south-west of the South Island, examining their geological origins and unique marine ecosystems. Fiords are long, narrow sea inlets with steep sides carved by glaciers approximately 20,000 years ago. When glaciers melted, seawater filled these formations, creating distinctive ecosystems characterized by a layer of fresh water from heavy rainfall sitting above salt water, which reduces sunlight penetration and creates dark conditions similar to deep ocean environments. This enables "deep water emergence," allowing deep-water species to thrive at shallow depths.

The Fiordland marine ecosystem supports exceptionally diverse marine life including over 150 fish species such as the brotula fish, Jock Stewart fish, scorpion fish, and deep-water wavyline perch, along with sponges, corals, sea stars, sea urchins, and marine mammals including New Zealand fur seals and a resident pod of 60 bottlenose dolphins in Doubtful Sound. Life concentrates in distinct zones: the upper zone (0-15m) with hardy organisms like mussels and barnacles, the lower zone (15-40m) dominated by sponges and corals, and deep basins (40m+) with sparse life.

Conservation challenges include fragmented management due to jurisdictional gaps between terrestrial and marine authorities, commercial fishing targeting blue cod, crayfish, and pāua, and increasing tourism pressures. Conservation efforts began in 1995 with the Guardians of Fiordland Fisheries and Marine Environment, followed by the Fiordland Marine Management Act 2005, which established 928,000 hectares as a special management area with eight new marine reserves.

12.text:
[Page 10] Tongariro National Park In the 1880s land was being sought by numerous claimants around the Lake Taupō area. Because the Tūwharetoa chief Horonuku had joined both Waikato and Te Kooti in fighting against the British Crown, some claimants believed this was reason enough for the Crown to treat the Taupō blocks as rebel land. Horonuku could see that he might lose the land. So in 1887, on the advice of his son in law (the Tauranga politician Lawrence Marshall Grace), he signed a deed with the government which ensured that the mountain block could never be sold. The land became New Zealand’s first national park.
{}

12.document_title: Ngāti Tūwharetoa: History, Leadership, Cultural Heritage, and Contemporary Development
12.document_summary: This comprehensive document provides an in-depth overview of Ngāti Tūwharetoa, a Māori iwi (tribe) from the central North Island of New Zealand. It traces the tribe's origins to the Te Arawa canoe and ancestral explorers Ngātoroirangi and Tia, whose legendary journeys shaped the cultural landscape of the Taupō region. The document details Chief Tūwharetoa, a 16th-century warrior and skilled carver, and the subsequent rise of the Te Heuheu dynasty as paramount chiefs in the 18th century. Key historical narratives include tribal warfare establishing Tūwharetoa mana, Māori mythology about mountain warriors competing for the maiden mountain Pīhanga, and Chief Horonuku's 1887 deed protecting the mountain block, which became New Zealand's first national park in 1894. The document describes the traditional diet based on native fish species including kōkopu, īnanga, kākahi, koura, and kōaro, which were largely displaced by introduced trout in the early 1900s. It documents the establishment of the Ngāti Tūwharetoa Trust Board in 1926 and the tribe's economic development through forestry investments and education initiatives. The document highlights geographic divisions within the iwi, particularly Ngāti Tūwharetoa ki Kawerau in the Bay of Plenty, and notes the leadership of paramount chief Sir Tumu Te Heuheu (1997-2025) and his successor Gerrard Te Rangimaheu Te Heuheu. Significant treaty settlements are documented: a 2003 settlement worth $10.5 million for Ngāti Tūwharetoa ki Kawerau, and a 2017 settlement of $25 million for the broader iwi. Census data from 1991-2013 shows tribal identification growth from 24,066 to 35,877 members.

13.text:
[Page 8] Acknowledging the need for conserving representative areas, the Guardians proposed making the whole of Sutherland Sound a marine reserve. In response, the New Zealand government passed the Fiordland Marine Management Act 2005, which ensured that 928,000 hectares were set aside as a special management area, and created eight new marine reserves. With the continued support of government and an increasing public awareness of conservation issues, there is a good chance that the fiords will remain a rich and unique environment.
{}

Life concentrates in distinct zones: the upper zone (0-15m) with hardy organisms like mussels and barnacles, the lower zone (15-40m) dominated by sponges and corals, and deep basins (40m+) with sparse life.

Conservation challenges include fragmented management due to jurisdictional gaps between terrestrial and marine authorities, commercial fishing targeting blue cod, crayfish, and pāua, and increasing tourism pressures. Fiords are long, narrow sea inlets with steep sides carved by glaciers approximately 20,000 years ago. When glaciers melted, seawater filled these formations, creating distinctive ecosystems characterized by a layer of fresh water from heavy rainfall sitting above salt water, which reduces sunlight penetration and creates dark conditions similar to deep ocean environments. This enables "deep water emergence," allowing deep-water species to thrive at shallow depths.

They will be cut up and perhaps sold, a piece going to one pakeha and a piece to another. They will become of no account, for the tapu will be gone. Tongariro is my ancestor, my tupuna; it is my head; my mana centres around Tongariro.’ 1 The first national park Tongariro In 1887, following suggestions from some prominent Pākehā , the paramount chief of the Ngāti Tūwharetoa tribe, Horonuku Te Heuheu, made an agreement wirh the Crown that the central North Island volcanoes would become a national park. 16.document_title: Te tāpoi Māori – Māori Tourism: Evolution, Cultural Preservation, and Business Development in New Zealand
16.document_summary: This document traces the evolution of Māori involvement in New Zealand tourism from the 19th century through the early 2000s. Initially, Māori controlled thermal tourism in the central North Island, earning substantial income as guides and operators. The Pink and White Terraces near Rotorua were major attractions until Mt Tarawera's 1886 eruption destroyed them. By the early 20th century, the government had purchased most thermal lands, shifting power from Māori to the Department of Tourist and Health Resorts. Māori transitioned from independent operators to employees and cultural exhibits. The Māori Arts and Crafts Institute, established by Parliament in 1963 at Whakarewarewa, became central to preserving and promoting Māori culture through carving traditions and performance arts. By the early 2000s, Māori tourism experienced significant resurgence with diverse businesses like Whale Watch Kaikōura and Tamaki Tours, representing a return to Māori control. By 2008, over 350 Māori tourism businesses operated in New Zealand, with 65% being self-employed operations. Tourism has significantly contributed to maintaining Māori language and cultural practices while generating economic opportunities.
